First, FERC must revise its 1994 transmission pricing policy within 270 days and then complete a rulemaking requiring utilities to charge these loads both embedded and incremental transmission costs, crediting the incremental payments against the utility’s revenue requirement to prevent double recovery. Loads accepting non-firm (interruptible) service would receive a lower rate.

Second, a new Federal Power Act Section 228 establishes a “ratepayer protection floor” for loads of 20 MW or more, counted across commonly owned sites and phased projects so that loads cannot be split to stay below the threshold: no portion of the incremental cost of serving them, including generation, storage, transmission, and distribution, may be recovered from other customers. Covered loads must post financial assurances before facilities are built and remain liable for unrecovered costs if they exit early. States may also charge covered loads above cost and credit the surplus to other customers, allocate service through announced application windows, and require loads to bring their own generation or accept limited service.

Implications

The central question that Section 2107 on ratepayer protection addresses is whether households and small businesses end up paying for the generation and grid buildout needed to exclusively serve large loads. The bill makes clear that utilities cannot build assets for a data center and pass on the associated costs to other customers. If the data center leaves the grid early, it would still need to pay those costs. These rules could address the stranded-asset risk that regulators worry about, particularly where load forecasts are uncertain.

Whether they translate into lower bills for other customers depends on several factors. First, the floor covers only costs incurred by the utility serving the load. In restructured markets such as PJM, a principal way data centers raise household bills is through higher wholesale capacity and energy prices, which the floor does not address and which would be left to states and market operators. Second, the floor applies only to loads that interconnect after enactment. Existing data centers and arrangements approved before enactment fall outside its scope, which may prompt a rush to secure approvals while the bill is pending. The new transmission pricing, by contrast, applies regardless of when a load connects, but could take up to two and a half years to finalize. Third, incremental cost is a one-time estimate made when the load comes online. Regulators must approve that estimate, but cost overruns after that point could still fall on other ratepayers.

Moreover, while these changes can go a long way toward assuaging concerns about cross-subsidization, policymakers will also need to strike a careful balance between ensuring that large loads pay their fair share of network costs and not charging them so much that they push more data centers off the grid. That said, recent experience suggests that speed to power, more than price, drives these decisions. Faster interconnection, in addition to community acceptance, may therefore matter more than cost allocation in determining where this load is served.

Finally, Section 228 raises a jurisdictional question: who decides which large loads gain access to the transmission grid, and on what terms? In most respects, the section confirms powers that states already have. State utility commissions already approve special tariffs for large customers that include collateral requirements, exit fees, interruptible service, and requirements to procure generation, and in vertically integrated states data centers are served as ordinary retail customers of the local utility. In three respects, however, the section goes further than current law:

Transmission service terms. In states with bundled retail service or organized wholesale markets, transmission service is governed by tariffs FERC approves. Section 228 would let a state condition a data center’s service on the type of transmission service it takes, for example by requiring it to accept interruptible service or capping how much firm capacity it receives.

Interconnection priority. Section 228 would let states decide which data centers may connect, and in what order, through competitive solicitations rather than the grid operator’s queue. This would apply even where interconnecting large loads to the transmission system may fall under FERC’s authority.

Protection from preemption. Section 228 applies “notwithstanding” any FERC rule or order, so neither power could be challenged as conflicting with the Federal Power Act or FERC’s rules.

This approach diverges from the direction of recent federal action. DOE’s October 2025 advance notice of proposed rulemaking proposed that FERC assert jurisdiction over connecting large loads to the transmission system.[lxi] FERC’s June 2026 show-cause orders to all six grid operators then pressed for rules that apply to all large loads regardless of type.[lxii] While the bill and the federal process agree on several aspects, Section 228 departs from the federal approach in two ways: it gives states a role in controlling access, and it applies only to data centers, expressly permitting them to be treated less favorably than other large customers. Enacting it could narrow FERC’s options as it develops region-wide procedures for connecting large loads to the transmission system.

The bill states that it confirms rather than creates state authority, and courts may rely on that statement to limit the “notwithstanding” clause to traditional retail matters. Until courts resolve the question, the line between state retail authority and federal open access will remain unsettled, creating legal uncertainty for data center developers and the grid operators planning to serve them. In vertically integrated states outside organized markets, where state control over retail service is already the norm, the change would be modest.

Grid Data, Reporting, and E-Permitting

Several of BAAJA’s less prominent provisions address a problem that underlies many of its larger reforms: the data needed to plan the grid, study interconnection requests, and manage federal reviews is often incomplete, inconsistent, or inaccessible.

The first concerns data center demand. Section 2114 would require the Energy Information Administration to revise its annual utility survey (Form 861) to report electricity consumption by data centers, including facilities used for AI training and inference, cloud computing, and cryptocurrency mining, beginning with the first reporting cycle after enactment. No consistent federal data on data center electricity use currently exists, which makes it harder for utilities, regulators, and policymakers to forecast load growth and plan the investments needed to serve it.

The second concerns the data used in interconnection studies. Section 2111 would require transmission providers to obtain, maintain, and use the grid data needed for generator and load interconnection studies. It would also require owners and operators of the bulk power system to provide requested data within 15 days and in usable formats, subject to confidentiality rules governing how data is shared but not permitting it to be withheld. Noncompliance would be treated as a reliability matter subject to civil penalties, and FERC would be mandated to act on complaints within 60 days. Within one year, FERC and DOE would have to publish a reference specification identifying the data categories, formats, and validation standards needed to fully automate interconnection studies. Together with Section 2110’s direction to FERC to promote the use of AI and automation in processing interconnection requests, these provisions are intended to lay the groundwork for faster, more standardized studies.

The third concerns data on federal permitting processes. Section 1121 would direct the Council on Environmental Quality to establish common data standards for environmental reviews and, where practicable, develop a unified interagency permitting system by December 1, 2028, built around a single digital portal hosted by the General Services Administration. Project sponsors would submit all required documentation through the portal, collaborate with agencies in real time, and track the status of their reviews. The portal would also track performance metrics, including review timelines before and after BAAJA’s enactment, and give Congress direct access to performance data. Separately, Section 1132 would create a public tracker for major projects that reports quarterly on whether agencies are meeting their schedules and whether delays stem from the agency or the project sponsor. Section 1133 would authorize $20 million annually through FY2033 for a fund to improve the performance of permitting agencies.

Implications

These provisions are among the least controversial in BAAJA, but the bill’s larger reforms depend on them. Consolidated planning, published interconnection locations, and automated studies all require accurate, interoperable data, and Section 2111 is the first statutory requirement that such data be provided on a deadline, backed by reliability penalties. The data specification would also arrive within one year, before regions file their consolidated planning processes.

C. Permit Durability

Developers usually commit large sums only after receiving federal permits, but permit approvals have not always held. The Biden administration revoked the cross-border permit for the Keystone XL pipeline in 2021, citing inconsistency with U.S. climate goals. In December 2025, the Trump administration suspended work on five offshore wind projects, citing national security risks, but courts have since blocked these suspensions, finding that the government had not adequately justified them.[lxiii] Under current law, a permit holder in that position can argue that the agency acted arbitrarily. But damages are generally unavailable, and no statute limits the grounds on which a federal agency may reopen a permit it has issued.

BAAJA attempts to address both problems. Under Section 1401, an agency could not revoke, suspend, or amend any federal permit in effect on or after September 16, 2026. Nor could it take “any other action to interfere with or prevent” the construction or operation “at full capacity” of a project that holds all its federal approvals. The exceptions are limited to cases such as court orders, material breaches of the permit, fraud, requests from the project sponsor, or actions needed to prevent “specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm” to life, property, national security, or defense based on new information obtained since the permit was issued. In these cases, the agency would carry the burden of proving that an exception applies, and if it fails, the project’s sponsor would be entitled to have the permit reinstated, a bar on further interference without approval from the same judge, attorney fees, costs associated with the delay, and an additional payment equal to 25 to 50 percent of its costs to date.

BAAJA’s Section 1402 also attempts to address the problem of administrations disfavoring a whole category of projects. An applicant for one of dozens of listed energy and mining project types could sue over a denial or a delay of more than 60 days past a deadline caused by a pattern of disparate treatment. The bill defines such a pattern in part by reference to an empirically demonstrated, substantial, and persistent increase in denials or unreasonable delays compared with the five most recent calendar years of data for the relevant project category. Official statements and executive orders can serve as supporting evidence of a pattern, which must result from an intentional federal course of action. If the applicant succeeds, remedies include economic damages and an award of 50 to 100 percent of the project’s expected construction cost, which remains conditional upon the sponsor moving forward with the project. Developers would not be allowed to collect damages and abandon the project at the same time. These awards would be paid from the federal Judgment Fund, outside the regular appropriations process—creating a potential uncapped financial liability for the federal government.

Implications

Together, Sections 1401 and 1402 aim to reduce regulatory risk and encourage investment by making federal approvals more durable. Without these changes, recent federal interference with already permitted projects could deter future investment. Lenders and investors also price into contracts the chance that an approval will be reversed or stalled after capital is committed, so greater certainty should lower financing costs and therefore allow more projects to get off the ground. The protections are deliberately technology neutral. They respond most directly to recent federal actions against wind and solar, but they would also constrain a future administration seeking to reverse fossil fuel approvals.

The central question is how far permit durability should extend. Critics warn of “forever permits,” where one administration approves projects, including in sensitive areas, that the next administration could not revisit. Proponents counter that Congress could still reverse a permit by statute, and that permits issued unlawfully could still be challenged and set aside in court.

A related concern with Section 1401 is its broad scope, which extends beyond prohibiting formal revocation or suspension to include actions that “interfere with” construction or operation at full capacity. As Michael Gerrard notes, the language could generate disputes over whether generally applicable requirements governing air pollution, methane emissions, noise, or worker safety are permissible when they affect a covered facility’s operation.[lxiv] Although Congress may intend to protect specific project approvals without immunizing facilities from otherwise applicable law, Gerrard argues the text’s breadth could invite challenges to regulatory actions that project owners claim undermine their permits.

Revisions to Section 1401 could avoid overly broad interpretation by, for example, expressly preserving authority to enforce independent statutory requirements and generally applicable environmental, public health, and safety standards, while defining more clearly which targeted actions against a particular permitted project are prohibited.

Questions have also been raised about Section 1402’s disparate-treatment provision. This provision measures disparate treatment against the five most recent calendar years of data for the relevant project category. It does not specify, however, whether that window precedes the filing of the lawsuit or the onset of the alleged pattern. Under either reading, a claim against a future administration would largely be measured against the current administration’s approval rates, including for fossil fuel projects. Gerrard argues that an administration that shifted priorities and denied more such projects could therefore face disparate treatment claims.[lxv] The historical baseline could thus entrench past permitting patterns by making substantial departures from them evidence of discrimination, even when an administration invokes different policy priorities or new circumstances.

That possibility is not necessarily an unintended consequence. Section 1402 is specifically intended to prevent administrations from using permitting decisions to systematically favor some technologies and disadvantage others. From this perspective, constraining politically motivated reversals is part of the bill’s purpose, and some short-term friction when administrations change course may be an acceptable tradeoff for greater policy stability over time.[lxvi]

The question is whether the provision can distinguish deliberate obstruction of lawful projects from legitimate policy changes, such as those responding to changed economic circumstances. As drafted, BAAJA’s Section 1402 may struggle to do so.

The greatest risk lies in how the bill treats denials versus delays. Delay claims are tied to fixed deadlines, which offer an objective benchmark. By contrast, the bill never defines what makes a denial “improper.” In project categories with few decisions or no prior denials, such as emerging technologies, even one or two denials could show a ‘substantial increase’ in the share of permits denied for that project type and support a claim. The intent requirement may offer limited protection, as an applicant could argue that a deliberate policy shift was itself an intentional course of action that created the pattern.

Several clarifications could help draw the distinction between deliberate obstruction and legitimate policy change. The most direct solution would be to remove the denial provision and keep the delay provision. Courts can already overturn unlawful denials, so the denial provision adds little protection while creating most of the risk. If Congress keeps the denial provision, it could at a minimum define “improper” to cover only denials that violate the law. To make the comparison meaningful, Congress could require a minimum number of past decisions before the numbers can support a claim, since many listed technologies have few or none. It could also specify whether the five-year period runs backward from the lawsuit or from when the alleged pattern began.

Finally, the scale of the potential damages available to project sponsors under Section 1402 warrants consideration. Damages equal to 50–100 percent of expected construction costs could impose substantial liabilities on the federal government, even when the dispute concerns a denial or delay rather than the revocation of an existing permit, because awards would be payable from the Judgment Fund rather than through the regular appropriations process. Facing that risk, agencies may approve projects they would otherwise reject, potentially including projects they consider unsafe. Congress could tie awards more closely to a developer’s actual losses while keeping enough of a penalty to deter deliberate abuse.

These provisions address a legitimate problem: developers need confidence that lawful approvals will not be withdrawn arbitrarily after substantial investments are made. The challenge is to provide that confidence without inadvertently limiting legitimate environmental, health, safety, and other regulatory obligations or making future policy changes prohibitively expensive. More precise language governing generally applicable regulation, changed circumstances, the statistical baseline, and damages could better preserve the bill’s investment-certainty objective while reducing unintended constraints on future administrations.

D. Energy Supply and Infrastructure-Specific Reforms

Beyond its crosscutting reforms, BAAJA includes targeted provisions for mining, geothermal, hydropower, and oil and gas. Most of these provisions address specific legal gaps or duplicative federal requirements rather than restructuring how these resources are developed.

Critical Minerals and Mining

Under Section 2215, BAAJA addresses two longstanding constraints on domestic critical mineral development: the lack of a leasing framework for hardrock minerals on federally acquired lands and legal uncertainty surrounding the use of federal land for mining-related activities beyond extraction.

name: Clean Energy
title: The Senate Permitting Deal Could Lock in Fossil Fuel Dominance for Generations
description:
BAAJA undermines bedrock environmental laws while granting the fossil fuel industry more power, more access to public lands, and less accountability.
Federal Backstop Authority The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has long had authority to resolve interstate transmission siting disputes, but the process has never functioned effectively.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act might accelerate transmission deployment and benefit some renewable energy projects down the road, but it will lock in fossil fuel projects now and well into the future.
The fossil fuel industry and its allies are profiting from our current energy system while minimizing competition from cheaper, cleaner competitors.
Instead of righting this imbalance, the Senate permitting deal will lock it in place for generations to come.
text:
To address the energy affordability crisis and climate crisis, what’s needed most are critical improvements to the power grid that will accelerate deployment of clean energy across the country. Instead, the Senate Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) sponsored by Senators Capito (WV), Whitehouse (RI), Lee (UT), and Heinrich (NM)—also known as S. 5653 or the Senate permitting deal—is warped in favor of fossil fuels and would harm people, communities, and the environment if enacted.

BAAJA undermines bedrock environmental laws while granting the fossil fuel industry more power, more access to public lands, and less accountability. In return, the package includes tenuous renewable energy and transmission provisions, many of which could be achieved under current law. Without significant improvements, which seem unlikely, enactment of BAAJA could be worse than the status quo.

The status quo is already terrible

Senate negotiators appear to have “compromised” between the Trump administration’s harmful current energy policy and something worse, rather than undoing recent attacks on clean energy and environmental and community protections.

In 2023, as part of a bipartisan deal to raise the debt ceiling, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) was amended to narrow the scope of the statute and insert arbitrary time and page limits on environmental reviews. The Trump Administration then issued an Executive Order revoking the authority of the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) to promulgate NEPA regulations. The Supreme Court then further narrowed the scope of the law in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (145 S. Ct. 1497 (2025)).

The courts, this Congress, and the Trump administration have taken similar steps to undermine decades of settled law and practice under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and Clean Water Act (CWA). Rather than demand that BAAJA reverse any of these trends, Senate negotiators appear to have accepted the Trump administration’s position as a new baseline and then agreed to even more dangerous backsliding as the price to help modernize our antiquated grid.

Small “wins” are even smaller than they appear

To be clear, the package includes provisions to speed deployment of transmission lines and renewable energy projects, which should be enacted.

Federal Backstop Authority

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has long had authority to resolve interstate transmission siting disputes, but the process has never functioned effectively. The new bill would remove bureaucratic and technical challenges that have rendered this federal “backstop” siting authority ineffective and would empower FERC to approve interstate transmission projects that provide benefits to consumers and are in the public interest.

Order 1920

In 2024, FERC issued Order 1920 to mandate robust, forward-looking regional grid planning and cost allocation, but compliance has been slow and multiple court challenges to the Order are pending. The Senate bill would write a similar regional and interregional planning mandate into law, strengthen it to help ensure beneficial projects actually get built, and add further ratepayer protections to the process. If enacted, this provision would achieve the goals of Order 1920, regardless of the outcome of pending litigation.

Advanced Transmission Technologies

Advanced transmission technologies (ATTs) are widely recognized as a quick and cost-effective way to get more from the existing grid, but utilities have long resisted installing ATTs, preferring larger new investments that provide more (and more certain) profits. The Senate bill would require deployment of cost-effective ATTs when building new lines or upgrading existing lines that would provide a pathway for relatively quick cost savings for consumers and improved reliability of the existing system.

eNEPA

The legislation also includes “eNEPA” provisions, directing CEQ to implement a program to put uniform standards, definitions, and metrics online, so that permitting agencies can better coordinate reviews, and to provide public access and transparency. While a funding source for the project is not identified, this program, if implemented, would help streamline and standardize the federal permitting process.

Data Centers

Finally, the legislation would require FERC to revise its transmission pricing policies to require utilities to charge data centers for cost increases they cause and prohibit those costs from being passed on to other customers. The provision would require cost recovery to continue until the full cost is paid, even if the data center ends its contract, to protect other ratepayers from being on the hook for potential “stranded assets.”

Most of the remaining provisions in the transmission title of BAAJA, while positive, are achievable using authority FERC or other agencies already have in law. Even the new federal backstop authority and regional planning mandate could be underused or even abused by the Trump administration.

Overall, the transmission title is a collection of provisions with potential, long-term benefits, dependent on adequate funding and good-faith implementation by this Administration. What is sorely needed, and missing from BAAJA, are transmission investments that would provide a host of benefits in addition to access to clean energy. Better reliability, improved public health, greater resilience to extreme weather, strengthened national security, expanded economic development, and lower energy costs as more people access renewable energy resources are among the many benefits that aggressive, smart grid investments would deliver.

What is unclear is why negotiators failed to think bigger and why the transmission and clean energy improvements that are included in the bill require devastating, pro-fossil fuel provisions as “offsets” to secure bipartisan support in Congress.

Project (un)certainty

BAAJA includes language billed as providing certainty for federal permittees. Supporters highlight this provision as one of the main strengths of the bill and claim the language would prevent President Trump from continuing to cancel approved wind and solar projects. Unfortunately, the provision appears to provide more permanence for fossil fuel projects than renewables.

On its face, the revocation provision (section 1401) is simple—federal agencies can’t revoke, suspend, alter, or “interfere with” permits in effect on or after September 16, 2026. If they do, the agency must prove one of a few narrow exceptions using “clear and convincing evidence,” or pay the developer a percentage of its sunk costs. A separate provision (section 1402) lets developers who prove a “pattern of disparate treatment” against certain types of projects recover 50–100% of their expected construction costs.

An obvious flaw is that these provisions do nothing to restore permits cancelled by the Trump administration before September. My colleague, John Rogers, documents some of the offshore wind projects already sabotaged by the Administration here and points out that these actions are likely already illegal.

And going forward, a permit applicant would have to prove disparate treatment for their category of projects compared to the baseline over the previous five years. Because that five-year baseline is already skewed by this administration, future administrations could keep denying or slow-walking wind and solar with little consequence, while facing damage awards if they revisit fossil fuel projects approved by the Trump administration.

Fracturing the bedrock

If enacted as currently drafted, BAAJA would be the most significant reversal in environmental and community protections in decades.

NEPA

The bill redefines the phrase “major federal action,” – the trigger for NEPA – to add a raft of new categories of projects no longer covered by the law (including pipeline expansions in existing corridors, drilling on lands with mixed federal and non-federal ownership, and projects using federal grant or loan funding but not run by federal agencies).

When added to the hollowing out of the law already achieved by the Trump Administration and SCOTUS, NEPA would be reduced to a discretionary table-top exercise, not subject to timely or meaningful judicial review or public input. The requirements that federal agencies consider alternatives when reviewing permit applications, and solicit and consider public input on those alternatives, would become little more than a formality.

CWA

Section 101(b) of the Clean Water Act reads in part:

It is the policy of the Congress to recognize, preserve, and protect the primary responsibilities and rights of states to prevent, reduce, and eliminate pollution, to plan the development and use (including restoration, preservation, and enhancement) of land and water resources . . .

In practice, this means states can require reasonable conditions on CWA permits and the burden is on applicants to overcome those objections. The Senate permitting proposal destroys this basic concept of cooperative federalism. States could deny certification only by providing “clear and convincing evidence” that no condition could make the project comply with the law, and any condition they do impose must be the “least burdensome” option. Both standards are designed to be difficult, if not impossible, to meet.

For interstate gas pipelines and transmission lines, state water quality certification would be limited to direct point-source discharges, excluding the stream and wetland crossings, sedimentation, and construction runoff that have been the basis for past state denials.

These changes, combined with provisions limiting judicial review under the CWA, could speed development of transmission corridors, but absolutely would speed development of natural gas pipelines by depriving states (and Tribes) of the ability to place reasonable conditions on permits impacting their water quality.

ESA/Historic Preservation/Mining

BAAJA would also make sweeping changes to existing protections for endangered species, historic and cultural resources, and public lands.

The bill would limit agency consultation under the ESA and delegate federal authority to states, many of which do not have the scientific expertise to manage listed species.

Similarly, review of permits pursuant to the National Historic Preservation Act would be limited, leading Tribal Leaders, among others, to express strong opposition to the bill because it “fail[s] to respect our inherent sovereignty, self-determination, and Indigenous Knowledge.”

The Senate package would also change decades of precedent and effectively overturn a recent federal court decision by authorizing mining companies to dump mining waste on land not covered by their mining claims. International mining conglomerates already enjoy broad access to US public lands under the outdated Mining Law of 1872, and the Senate proposal would expand that access to vast swaths of new land for waste dumping.

Process fouls

The Senate bill was largely crafted behind closed doors without meaningful input from broad categories of stakeholders, including environmental groups, scientific experts, Tribal governments, and Environmental Justice communities. Bill sponsors have announced a plan to forgo hearings or mark-ups in any of the committees of jurisdiction and place the bill on the Senate floor immediately after the November elections.

Such a flawed process is perhaps fitting for legislation that would enshrine reckless speed, limited transparency, and lack of accountability into law.

It does not have to be this way

UCS is not alone in raising serious concerns regarding the Senate proposal. A review of the bill by the Natural Resources Defense Council may be found here, and a statement from WE ACT for Environmental Justice is here. A review by Earthjustice is here, and an assessment of the bill’s impact on public lands by The Wilderness Society may be found here.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act might accelerate transmission deployment and benefit some renewable energy projects down the road, but it will lock in fossil fuel projects now and well into the future. Senate negotiators argue they have no choice but to agree to a deal largely on President Trump’s terms, and that the President will follow the new law if it is enacted. Neither claim is convincing.

The fossil fuel industry and its allies are profiting from our current energy system while minimizing competition from cheaper, cleaner competitors. Instead of righting this imbalance, the Senate permitting deal will lock it in place for generations to come.

It does not have to be this way. An efficient permitting process, rooted in science and public participation, can get us to the cleaner, more affordable energy future we desperately need. We know the targets we need to hit, and we have the technology to get us there—we just need the will.

Collaboration brings the potential for engineering, procurement, construction, modularization and supply-chain capabilities into NANO Nuclear's platform as the University of Illinois KRONOS MMR™ project advances through NRC review

Framework creates a pathway from first-of-a-kind project planning to potential A/E, EPC, fabrication, U.S. manufacturing and future fleet-deployment support

New York, N.Y. and Seoul, Republic of Korea, Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NANO Nuclear Energy Inc. (NASDAQ: NNE) ("NANO Nuclear" or the "Company"), an advanced nuclear energy and technology company developing microreactors, nuclear fuel cycle capabilities and nuclear transportation solutions, today announced that it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding ("MOU") with Hyundai Engineering Co., Ltd. ("HEC") to establish a framework for potential collaboration to advance the KRONOS MMR™ Energy System project at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign ("U. of I.") and to evaluate broader cooperation on future NANO Nuclear manufacturing and deployment activities.

The MOU brings together NANO Nuclear's advanced reactor development program with HEC's engineering, procurement, construction, project-management, supply-chain, modularization, logistics and industrial-project capabilities. The parties initially intend to focus on project-execution planning, conventional and site-related work, procurement readiness, constructability, modularization, logistics, supply-chain development and U.S. localization planning for the U. of I. project, while preserving clear interfaces with the U. of I., existing expected contractors and applicable public-procurement requirements.

The collaboration is designed to give NANO Nuclear a structured pathway to bring experienced project-execution capability into the KRONOS MMR™ project at an increasingly important stage of development. Subject to technical and commercial evaluation, availability of scope, U. of I. and regulatory requirements and separate definitive agreements, the parties may later expand HEC's role to include architecture and engineering ("A/E"), engineering and procurement ("EP"), engineering, procurement and construction ("EPC"), construction management, equipment or component fabrication, and support for future KRONOS MMR™ reactor fleet deployment.

Figure 1: NANO Nuclear Energy Inc. Signs MOU with Hyundai Engineering Co., Ltd. to establish a framework for future collaboration

Building an Industrial Project-Execution Platform Around the KRONOS MMR™ System

NANO Nuclear and HEC expect to designate a working team and begin preparing a preliminary responsibility and interface matrix. That work is intended to define potential project packages, clarify design and procurement interfaces, identify presently unassigned work for the project, and establish a disciplined basis for future contracting as the U. of I. project progresses.

Anticipated workstreams identified in the MOU include conventional facility constructability and modularization studies; construction sequencing and site mobilization; civil and site packages; supplier identification and prequalification; long-lead-item planning; U.S. and Korean supplier mapping; domestic-content and localization planning; heavy-haul and construction logistics; commissioning and turnover support; and procurement-readiness, cost and schedule benchmarking. Any compensated scope would be implemented under a separate definitive agreement with the appropriate contracting parties.

The MOU also contemplates future cooperation on U.S. reactor-component and core-manufacturing facility planning, modular-factory and production-line development, standardization and replication for future KRONOS MMR™ system deployments, U.S.-Korea supplier-development initiatives, and potential financing, export-credit, insurance and industrial-participation pathways. These areas are intended to help NANO Nuclear build not only a first deployment at the U. of I., but the industrial infrastructure and a repeatable project model required for a future commercial fleet.

The collaboration also builds on more than a decade of HEC familiarity with the underlying MMR technology. HEC began collaborating with Ultra Safe Nuclear Corporation ("USNC") and the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute ("KAERI") on high-temperature gas-cooled reactor and MMR technology in 2012, and later supported MMR engineering and procurement activities, including support for a specific opportunity in Canada. NANO Nuclear subsequently acquired USNC's MMR technology in 2025 and now advances the system as the KRONOS MMR™ Energy System. NANO Nuclear believes this history provides valuable continuity and institutional familiarity with the technology as KRONOS advances through licensing, project execution and toward future deployment.

"NANO Nuclear is deliberately assembling the industrial capabilities required to move advanced nuclear technology from design into repeatable deployment.” said Jay Yu, Founder and Chairman of NANO Nuclear Energy. “Our objective is not simply to develop an advanced microreactor; it is to build the broader platform around it. This includes engineering, manufacturing, fuel, transportation, project execution and the necessary supply chain that can support real projects at scale. Hyundai Engineering brings project-delivery capabilities that can become increasingly valuable as the KRONOS MMR™ system advances from design to regulatory licensing and into construction and ultimate commercialization."

"The next phase of advanced nuclear will be defined by execution.” said James Walker, Chief Executive Officer of NANO Nuclear Energy. “As our KRONOS MMR™ system progresses through NRC review, constructability, procurement, logistics, modularization, interfaces and a qualified supply chain become just as important as the reactor design itself. This MOU gives us a framework to bring HEC into that work early, while creating a pathway from the first U. of I. project toward a standardized and repeatable fleet-deployment model."

"This MOU establishes a foundation for cooperation with a promising advanced nuclear developer. By participating in demonstration and first-of-a-kind project opportunities, we aim to build valuable project experience, strengthen our capabilities across the advanced nuclear project lifecycle and continuously identify new business opportunities in the global market." said Woo-Jeong Joo, Chief Executive Officer of Hyundai Engineering.

A Collaboration Designed to Scale Beyond a Single Project

NANO Nuclear and HEC view the U. of I. project as a potential foundation for a broader relationship. The MOU provides a framework to evaluate future NANO Nuclear projects in the United States, including manufacturing and deployment activities, and to explore ways in which Korean and U.S. industrial capabilities can be combined to support localization, supplier development, project financing and future fleet execution.

The parties may also evaluate future conventional balance-of-plant and infrastructure support for industrial heat, hydrogen, desalination, maritime and other applications. Any future project scope, fabrication activity or commercial award will remain subject to applicable regulatory, quality, export-control, procurement and commercial requirements and to separately executed definitive agreements.

The MOU is non-exclusive and does not itself award any specific work package or commit either party to funding or construction. It establishes the commercial and technical framework through which defined scopes can be evaluated and, where appropriate, advanced under future contracts.

text:
Dynamic in-motion wireless charging may help address gaps in EV charging infrastructure by moving power delivery into the transport corridor, according to analysis from GlobalData.

The research and analytics company points to a magnetic coupling wireless power transfer (WPT) road system co-developed by Honda R&D, Taisei Corporation and Taisei Rotec. Initial demonstration tests of the system are slated for 2027. The release does not say where the tests will take place.

Constraints on EV adoption

GlobalData says growth in key EV markets is constrained by charging infrastructure gaps, grid capacity limits and consumer concerns about battery range and charging times. Automakers and infrastructure operators face pressure to deliver scalable solutions that reduce the time vehicles spend stationary at plug-in charging points.

By continuously transmitting power to vehicles while they are moving, dynamic WPT avoids the reliability and downtime issues associated with public chargers, according to the company. It adds that, if commercialised effectively, in-motion charging infrastructure could ease range anxiety, reduce queueing at chargers and cut the physical battery capacity needed in each vehicle, which would lower production costs and purchase prices.

“From Honda’s strategic perspective, integrating dynamic charging technology creates long-term operational leverage across both commercial logistics and mass-market passenger vehicles,” said Madhuchhanda Palit, senior automotive analyst at GlobalData. “While deploying WPT in heavy transit corridors and logistics fleets offers immediate commercial utility, its eventual expansion into passenger segments will allow automakers to downsize onboard battery packs without sacrificing operational range.”

GlobalData notes that establishing foundational intellectual property in vehicle-to-infrastructure power transfer gives Honda an engineering advantage, while competitors remain tied to stationary fast-charging partnerships.

Palit added: “For prospective EV buyers who lack access to dedicated residential overnight charging, widespread dynamic charging may potentially provide the predictability needed to encourage the mainstream transition from internal combustion engines.”

What the 2027 trial must prove

“Dynamic in-motion charging represents a structural shift from standalone charging stations toward integrated energy-transport infrastructure,” Palit continued. “While the technological trial scheduled for 2027 must first prove cost-effectiveness, grid stability, and road-surface durability under continuous traffic load, successful deployment could accelerate EV market penetration by eliminating stationary charging bottlenecks and redefining the economics of EV battery sizing.”

text:
DENVER – The most prominent glaciers in Colorado thinned dramatically over the past year due to record low mountain snow and record warm temperatures, according to new research.

Their shrinking is on par with recent observations of glacier loss across the planet as warmer temperatures accelerate melting and less snow falls to replenish their ice, threatening water sources, increasing mountain hazards and contributing to sea level rise.

While glaciologists typically measure changes over longer intervals, glaciologist Dan McGrath at Colorado State University sought to find out what happened over 2026 since it was such an exceptional year. The state’s worst snowpack on record, followed by record summer heat, left the year-round ice masses in the Rocky Mountains exposed.

The Andrews Glacier thinned by more than 12 feet (3.7 meters) in this single year, the Arapaho Glacier lost nearly 10 feet (3 meters), and the Isabelle Glacier lost about 6.5 feet (2 meters) — doubling their rate of thinning from the prior five years, McGrath said. In the decade before that, the thinning measured a foot or less per year.

St. Mary's Glacier, a perennial snowfield popular among hikers and skiers, melted completely in September.

“What we’re witnessing is the loss of that part of Colorado’s identity. And it’s not just Colorado,” said McGrath, who specializes in glacier dynamics. “Obviously we see it in the Alps and we’re seeing it in other mountain ranges in the western U.S., the European Alps and globally. There are very clear, consistent patterns across these ranges.”

Climate change is shrinking glaciers faster than ever

More than 7 trillion tons of ice (6.5 trillion metric tons) has been lost worldwide since 2000, according to research, a slow-motion disaster that sometimes provokes sudden devastation: More than 1,300 people were killed in August after a massive section of rock and overlying glacier collapsed near Nepal’s border with China.

Glaciers in Switzerland lost 5.5% of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record, due to heat waves and low winter snowfall. The GLAMOS Swiss glacier monitoring service and Swiss Academy of Sciences said this month that alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving long-term under such conditions. Switzerland is home to the most glaciers in the Alps.

In Washington state, researchers with the North Cascade Glacier Climate Project have surveyed six glaciers on Mount Baker during an annual summer trip. Director Mauri Pelto said this year's survey shows the fastest average retreat since 1950 with the collapse of several large ice caves, which form as warm air circulates in retreating glaciers.

Mountain glaciers in the contiguous United States average just 0.16 square miles (0.41 square kilometers), or about 100 acres (about 40 hectares), and are widely distributed at high elevations. Since the mid-1900s, about one-quarter of them have disappeared and the remnants have lost a third of their area and volume, according to a new study co-authored by Brian Menounos, an earth sciences professor at the University of Northern British Columbia.

The runoff supplies water to high alpine and downstream ecosystems across the western United States, and eventually these areas may become more vulnerable to extreme drought as the glaciers disappear, he added.

And in a “one-two punch,” wildfires also are hastening the melting by darkening the surfaces of glaciers with soot and dust, Menounos said, making them more vulnerable to absorbing sunlight.

Glaciers could re-form if carbon pollution declines substantially and temperatures drop enough to enable snowfall to build year-round, eventually compressing again into glacial ice, but that may take several hundred years, Menounos added.

Colorado's glaciers may not have much time left

Looking at how much ice Colorado's remaining glaciers have lost, McGrath thinks they could soon disappear. The Andrews Glacier has already lost half of its ice since 2017, he said.

“This past decade has showed us that these glaciers are out of balance with the climate here in Colorado, in the western U.S., and they’re thinning at a rate that could lead to their demise in the next 20 years,” he said.

Harlan Ulmer, 20, is a student at Colorado State University who has photographed the glaciers annually since 2022 and volunteers with McGrath’s research project. He said it's sad to see their decline, but important to record.

“Being Gen Z, I came in too late to ever see the glaciers at their largest,” he said. “But I think we have the opportunity, I have the opportunity, to sort of document the changes that are taking place in my time to preserve them for future generations and for posterity.”

___

McDermott reported from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaigners - The Guardian
description:
Andy Burnham will “sleepwalk” into climate disaster if he fails to get a grip on a series of important policies whose combined impact could scupper plans to reach net zero, campaigners have said.
Big decisions on North Sea drilling, the expansion of Heathrow airport, electric vehicles (EVs) and grants for heat pumps are awaiting decisions from ministers.
Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace, said: “The Burnham government is facing a series of big decisions over the next few months that could define its legacy on climate.
Airlines are also pressing for an expansion of Heathrow, which the chancellor, John Healey, strongly favours in the belief that it could increase economic growth.
Campaigners challenge this analysis, arguing the UK is already embarking on airport expansion at Gatwick.
text:
Andy Burnham will “sleepwalk” into climate disaster if he fails to get a grip on a series of important policies whose combined impact could scupper plans to reach net zero, campaigners have said.

Big decisions on North Sea drilling, the expansion of Heathrow airport, electric vehicles (EVs) and grants for heat pumps are awaiting decisions from ministers.

But they should be considered in the context of their cumulative impacts rather than be taken separately by different government departments, according to Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth (FoE) in a letter to the prime minister.

Taken together, the emissions resulting from approving drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, expanding Heathrow airport, watering down the UK’s EV targets and cutting heat pump grants would be 402m tonnes of CO2 over the next 25 years, the letter says.

The emissions would be greater than those of 106 coal plants running for a year, more than enough to prevent the UK meeting its carbon budgets and net zero.

Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace, said: “The Burnham government is facing a series of big decisions over the next few months that could define its legacy on climate. This administration seems to get the urgency of cutting the emissions causing deadly heatwaves and droughts, but there’s a real risk they could still sleepwalk into reversing the strong progress the UK has made so far.”

Last week, the government gave the go-ahead to drill the Jackdaw gasfield, despite warnings that it would create only 27 new jobs, fail to cut the cost of living, and add little to UK tax revenues. Now, the North Sea fossil fuel industry is pressing for a green light to the more controversial Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, which would produce higher emissions.

Car manufacturers have lobbied hard for the government to water down its mandate to ensure all new car and van sales are electric by 2035, by allowing as many as half of sales to be petrol or diesel in 2030, which would mean falling far short of the current target of 80% electric by then. Given the long life of vehicles, this could produce future emissions equal to about 60% of the emissions from Rosebank, according to analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank.

Airlines are also pressing for an expansion of Heathrow, which the chancellor, John Healey, strongly favours in the belief that it could increase economic growth. Campaigners challenge this analysis, arguing the UK is already embarking on airport expansion at Gatwick.

In his budget on Wednesday, Healey is also likely to cut the boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants to households installing heat pumps in place of gas boilers, despite the savings on gas use that it represents and the slow speed of the transition to electric heating so far.

Parr said: “Decisions about Rosebank, Heathrow expansion, electric vehicle targets or heat pump funding should not be rushed through or made in isolation – ministers need to be far-sighted and keep track of their cumulative impact on our climate. The carbon bill may take a while to turn up, but there’s hell to pay when it does.”

If Burnham were to reject these high-carbon plans, the UK could build a cleaner, more equal and more prosperous society, added Imogen Dow, climate lead at FoE. Renewable energy could bring down bills, particularly amid soaring oil and gas prices, and the net zero economy has grown faster than the rest of the economy, according to the CBI.

Dow said: “Delivering on our climate goals is not solely a win for the planet – it will also strengthen the economy, lower household bills, improve public health and protect the places we call home.

“At a time when powerful vested interests are pushing the world towards climate catastrophe, it’s more important than ever that governments like the UK stand strong.”

A government spokesperson said: “Reindustrialisation will never mean reneging on our climate obligations and net zero. Over the past two years, clean power has secured £110bn in announced investment and supported thousands of jobs through our record renewable energy auctions.”

Brazil’s national oil company, meanwhile, had a brutal day of trading on the stock market following left-wing Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise surge to reelection in Sunday’s runoff. Shares of Petrobras plunged 14% on the New York Stock Exchange by the time trading ended Monday evening. While conservative candidate Flávio Bolsonaro had promised more privatization and fewer environmental regulations, Lula has ramped up drilling, particularly offshore, as he seeks to capitalize on South America’s oil boom.

2. A natural gas megamerger creates America’s new No. 1 producer

A hot deal. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

EQT Corporation bills itself as “America’s only large-scale, vertically integrated natural gas producer.” Soon it will also be the largest gas company in the nation. On Monday, the company announced plans to acquire Range Resources Corporation in a deal to create a North American gas giant worth more than $50 billion. The all-stock transaction would also establish the biggest gas producer in the U.S. by output. Combined, EQT and Range pump out 9 billion cubic feet of natural gas equivalent per day. The next largest shale gas producer in the U.S. is Expand Energy, at 7.5 billion cubic feet per day. The merged company would also command a network of pipelines and other midstream infrastructure that tops 3,700 miles. “This transaction brings together two of the highest-quality, longest-duration asset bases in North America and creates a company uniquely positioned for the next era of natural gas,” EQT CEO Toby Z. Rice said in a statement. “We believe this combination creates a must-own energy company capable of generating durable, through-cycle free cash flow while compounding value for shareholders for decades to come.”

The deal is a sign “U.S. gas consolidation is accelerating,” Salih Yilmaz, a senior oil analyst at the consultancy Bloomberg Intelligence, wrote in a post on X. “The bigger theme is consolidation: scale, concentration, and infrastructure control are becoming increasingly important in US gas, especially as LNG exports and power demand grow.”

3. U.S. wind turbine orders surged by nearly 3 gigawatts this spring

U.S. orders for wind turbines vaulted to 2.8 gigawatts in the second quarter of this year — the highest since the end of 2023 — as developers scrambled to meet the deadlines to qualify for expiring tax credits, according to a new market analysis by the consultancy Wood Mackenzie. New Mexico saw the biggest surge as the SunZia megaproject, the largest wind farm ever built in the U.S., came online, raising the state to the top of the list of capacity additions. Despite the Trump administration’s efforts to kill or slow walk permits for wind projects, the industry is on track to add 39 gigawatts of new onshore wind farms by 2030. More than half the projects set to come online over the next two years are already under construction, meaning there’s little risk of disruption. Offshore wind, by contrast, tops out at 5 gigawatts, all of which is on course to be delivered in the next two years. “Policy is the variable with the greatest impact on wind installations,” Wood Mackenzie analyst Tyler Gifford said in a statement. “With tax credit expirations on the horizon, developers are prioritizing projects that can be operational by 2030, so the five-year onshore wind installation outlook remains stable.”

On the other side of the Atlantic, exports of wind turbines are booming. While Europe is still debating how to deal with the sudden rise of China’s wind companies, as I told you last week, the European Union's exports of wind turbines spiked by nearly 11% to $3.4 billion last year, Renewables Now reported.

Sign up to receive Heatmap AM in your inbox every morning:

4. Exclusive: Clean Air Task Force is out with its new strategy for climate advocacy

The climate movement, as virtually anyone involved will tell you, is broken. Even those who are part of it want to stop talking about “climate change,” according to the results of this year’s Heatmap Insiders Survey. Clean Air Task Force, one of the more pragmatic groups in the policy arena fighting for clean energy, is out with a new memo detailing the strategy it plans to use through the end of the decade. Dubbed CATF Forward, the plan is “designed to drive the global adoption of climate solutions, orienting around three clear impact priorities and rooted in the attributes that have made” the group “uniquely effective” since its launch 30 years ago. “The world’s increasingly complex climate and energy challenges require sober thinking and sharper focus,” Armond Cohen, CATF’s founder and executive director, said in a statement. “How do we protect climate in a world turned upside down?”

His answer:

Prevent pollution by reducing the most damaging emissions at a global scale.

Advance clean power by calling for more energy and more options.

Transform complex systems by grappling with the nuances different industries face and working to shift away from them.

All of that seems fairly straightforward. But the document is defined as much by what it omits as what it includes. Amid a growing debate over whether climate activists should keep targeting fossil fuel infrastructure, which my colleague Robinson Meyer aired out nicely on a recent episode of our podcast Shift Key, CATF isn’t pushing for boycotts of fossil fuels or, you know, committing crimes in the name of saving the planet.

5. An Indian solar giant is investing $525 million to take on China

India’s solar factories have boomed in recent years as the world’s most populous country turns to photovoltaics to meet surging domestic electricity demand and supply overseas buyers looking for alternatives to China. But the subcontinent has struggled to take on China’s dominance of the solar supply chain’s upstream elements. On Monday, Noida-based Jakson Solar announced plans to invest over $525 million into manufacturing solar cells, ingots, and wafers. The company plans to commission a 3-gigawatt cell factory by the end of next year, managing director Ivan Saha told Reuters on the sideline of a conference. The company then plans to stand up a 3-gigawatt ingot and wafer plant by the third quarter of 2028. That will all feed into Jakson’s existing 1.2-gigawatt module-making factory.

THE KICKER

Indonesia and Malaysia have launched more than 100 cloud-seeding missions this year in an attempt to engineer rain to quench parched lands as El Niño worsens droughts. The worst wildfire season in decades has shrouded the region in devastating toxic smog. But the high cost of the effort, including using dry ice to break up warm air that traps smog on the ground, “have so far brought little in the way of lasting results,” Bloomberg reported. “Sometimes, there’s a lot of political pressure to do things that may not be really well-founded scientifically,” Steven Siems, a professor at Monash University in Melbourne and the co-chair of an expert team on weather modification at the World Meteorological Organization, told the newswire.

The approach aims to solve a persistent logistics problem. Economics dictate that commodity producers typically locate near a high-volume source of feedstock or a pipeline that can deliver it. But for captured methane — a potential feedstock for lower-carbon fuels, chemicals, and fertilizers — that’s often not an option. The potent greenhouse gas escapes from geographically dispersed landfills, farms, and wastewater treatment plants, many of which are too small to support a large gas-to-liquids facility and too far from existing pipelines. Trucking the gas to a centralized plant is generally prohibitively expensive, often leaving operators to either flare it or let it escape unabated.

“We are really kind of burning money, creating a lot of emissions when we could be capturing this and making high-value products,” Emmanuel Kasseris, Emvolon’s CEO, told me in an August conversation about the company’s technology, which it spun out of MIT.

“We really try to flip the script completely,” Kasseris said of the startup’s modular approach. Rather than one large facility, the company aims to produce “a few tons to maybe tens of tons per day” of methanol for the $40 billion global market. For comparison, conventional gas-to-liquid facilities can produce hundreds of times more product daily.

Emvolon’s technology is “engine agnostic,” running on repurposed engines from used cars and diesel generators as well as new builds modified for the startup’s purposes. The engines take in captured methane from landfills, farms, or gas-flaring sites. But instead of burning the fuel completely like a standard combustion engine, Emvolon limits the oxygen supply, triggering only partial combustion of the methane to produce a mixture of hydrogen and carbon monoxide known as syngas. The company then feeds that mixture into a conventional reactor, where a catalyst converts it into liquid methanol that can be shipped in standard tanker trucks.

The process requires relatively few modifications to standard internal combustion engines, Kasseris told me, thereby bringing the economics of mass production to small-scale chemical production. “You’re taking something that comes from an assembly line, you repurpose it — changing sensors, controls, simple things that require a lot of [intellectual property] but are not expensive — and you build the plant around it,” he explained. The goal is to offer customers a four-year payback period sans low-carbon fuel subsidies.

Emvolon is now attempting to push that logic a step further. For the second stage of the conversion process, the company is working to swap out its conventional reactor with another modified engine in order to “replace even more one-off process equipment” with mass-produced components. The Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy awarded Emvolon a $2.3 million grant to develop this part of its system.

But the startup doesn’t need to have this additional piece of technology dialed in to start securing customers. In August, global commodities merchant Freepoint Commodities signed on as the startup’s primary buyer, securing priority rights to purchase at least $450 million worth of Emvolon’s biomethanol for use across maritime shipping, aviation, heavy transport, and specialty chemicals. The agreement also gives Freepoint priority rights to invest in or lend to future Emvolon projects, a provision Kasseris described as the anchor for the startup’s project financing platform.

The company’s first commercial projects are designed to produce up to 50,000 metric tons of biomethanol annually across multiple sites, with the Freepoint agreement structured to scale that output to 300,000 metric tons per year. Because each plant should cost only “a few million dollars,” Kasseris said, the company can spread out its risk rather than bet on “the half a billion dollar e-fuels plant” common to the alternative fuels industry. If one plant runs into trouble, the setback should be manageable, and the company can keep churning out and deploying its modular units elsewhere.

“This is great for scaling,” Kasseris told me. “It’s just very different. It’s just more boxes.”

That is an abysmal finding for technology companies and would-be developers of the computing facilities. But it actually represents an improvement from previous polling, and it suggests one of the fastest shifts in public opinion in recent memory may be tapering off.

That shift has been swift. As recently as September of last year, about 43% of Americans said they would support a data center being built near where they live, and Americans broadly appeared to be evenly split on the infrastructure, according to Heatmap Pro polling. Eleven months later, 75% of Americans told the same poll that they would oppose a nearby data center — a 32 point shift. That monumental turnaround helped make data centers a defining issue in this election cycle.

That backlash has transformed the economics of the data center boom, the largest infrastructure buildout in recent U.S. history. The overwhelming majority of data center projects now face some degree of community opposition, Heatmap Pro reporting suggests. More than $260 billion in proposed data centers have been canceled this year after meeting local opposition. The artificial intelligence company Anthropic even flagged the infrastructure slowdown on Monday when it filed for its initial public offering, which is widely expected to be among the largest ever.

Now our new survey shows that Americans’ rejection of the enormous computing facilities may itself be slowing. The small observed drop, which only slightly exceeds the survey’s margin of error, was driven by a four-point decline in the share of Americans who said they would “strongly oppose” the technology.

While Americans of all parties improved their view of data centers, the change was most pronounced among Republicans. In August, 23% of GOP voters said that they would support a data center being built near where they live. In the new poll, conducted after weeks of favorable campaigning by President Trump, 34% of Republicans said they would support a data center slated for their area, while the share of Republicans who said they would oppose it fell from 66% to 58%. Data centers’ standing among independents improved by nine points during the same period.

Democrats remain largely unified against the infrastructure, and data centers’ improvement among that group was just outside the margin of error.

While Americans of every age, race, gender, and partisan ID remain more opposed to local data center development than in favor of it, their standing has also improved among men since the summer. In August, 21% of men said they would support a data center being built near where they live. Now, 28% of men would support one.

text:
Democrats hoping to win back Congress are split over whether to revive a Biden-era tax break for electric car buyers.

Rank-and-file House Democrats want to restore the $7,500 credit Republicans ended in 2025, but party leaders have not committed to it, Politico reported Monday. Democratic Ohio Rep. Greg Landsman introduced a bill Oct. 22 to double the credit to $15,000 and make it permanent, according to his office.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

“The credit is not good policy,” Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, said in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation.

Michel said estimates of the Inflation Reduction Act-era credits indicate roughly seven in 10 recipients would have purchased an electric car without one.

He noted the Joint Committee on Taxation’s projection that repealing the old credit would save more than $19 billion in fiscal 2032, the last year of projected savings.

“If we simply double that figure and multiply it by the budget window, a credit twice as large as the one Congress repealed could cost about $380 billion over a decade, possibly more,” Michel said.

Ending the credit for buyers of new electric cars is projected to save the federal government $77.8 billion from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2034, according to Joint Committee on Taxation estimates cited in a December 2025 Congressional Research Service report.

“Repealing it was the wrong decision,” Democratic California Rep. Mike Levin told Politico. “The whole thing is a giant self-own by this administration, and it does no good for the American auto industry.”

A Democratic adviser who works on energy, granted anonymity by Politico, said the credit has “become kind of synonymous with elite, liberal, coastal, kind of out-of-touch policy and politics.”

The credit has gained a reputation for helping Americans who could already afford an electric car, party insiders told the outlet. (RELATED: Trump Admin Kills Biden’s Fuel Economy Rules, Says New Cars Will Cost $1,300 Less)

“The credit primarily benefited high-income households, those making over $150,000 annually,” Jonathan Lesser, senior fellow at the National Center for Energy Analytics, said in a statement to the DCNF.

“If the subsidy were revived, it would mean lower-income Americans would be again forced to subsidize higher-income ones,” Lesser added.

Mark Mills, the center’s founder and executive director, said in a statement to the DCNF that “high-income households are the overwhelming majority of electric vehicle (EV) buyers and thus the subsidy to those households is a reverse Robin Hood.”

Peter Z. Grossman, a visiting fellow at the center and a professor of economics emeritus at Butler University, said in a statement to the DCNF that his understanding is most of the credit’s beneficiaries were “wealthy people who bought an EV as a second/third/fourth car as a virtue signal and (if it was a Tesla) a status symbol.”

“For taxpayers it would continue to be a subsidy for the wealthy although it would depend on how the subsidy was structured,” Grossman said.

Levin and Democratic Illinois Rep. Sean Casten’s Energy Bills Relief Act, which Casten introduced March 18, would repeal the part of the 2025 reconciliation law that ended the clean energy tax credits, including the electric car credit, according to the bill text.

The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and eight other committees, according to the Government Publishing Office.

More than 160 House Democrats back the bill, but House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is not a cosponsor, Politico reported.

In March remarks to the League of Conservation Voters, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York called for restoring clean energy credits for sources such as wind and solar but did not explicitly mention electric cars, Politico reported.

Neither Schumer’s nor Jeffries’ office answered the outlet’s repeated questions about their positions on the electric car credit.

“We’ve made unbelievable progress just from the momentum that we’d already created from 2020 to 2024,” Hickenlooper said, according to Politico. “We’ve got to assess how much momentum and how much benefit we got from it.”

Democratic Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she is “open to tax credits” but wants “a comprehensive strategy” on energy, Politico reported.

“There are still elements within the Democratic coalition who are still fighting the last battle of the [Inflation Reduction Act],” said Tré Easton, vice president for public affairs at the Democratic think tank d Institute, according to Politico.

The centrist group Third Way has proposed a $7,500 point-of-sale rebate aimed at “working and middle-class families,” criticizing the old credit for allowing “wealthier households to use the credit to buy luxury vehicles,” according to Politico.

“We need to incorporate lessons learned and the reality of the 2026 and 2027 economies into the proposals we’re offering,” Josh Freed, Third Way’s senior vice president for climate and energy, said, according to Politico.

Half of the benefits of the credit’s predecessor went in 2022 to taxpayers with adjusted gross incomes of $200,000 or more, the top 8 percent of taxpayers by income, according to a separate Congressional Research Service report.

Democrats have also cooled on electric cars themselves. Forty-seven percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they would give serious thought to buying one in a Pew Research Center survey of 3,524 U.S. adults taken March 16 to 22, down from 58 percent in 2022.

The question went to about half the sample, and the margin of error for Democrats and Democratic leaners who were asked it is plus or minus 3.7 percentage points, according to Pew.

Sixty percent of Democrats and Democratic leaners said the federal government should encourage electric car use, down 10 points from 2022, according to Pew, which gives a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points for that group.

text:
Clean Air Task Force today launched CATF Forward, a new, sharpened strategy to innovate and scale global climate solutions into 2030 and beyond.

Find the full strategy here.

CATF Forward is designed to drive climate action in a changed and changing world – where geopolitical fragmentation, rising energy demand, and shifting political priorities have rendered traditional approaches outdated. It’s designed to drive the global adoption of climate solutions, orienting around three clear impact priorities and rooted in the attributes that have made it uniquely effective over the past three decades.

“The world’s increasingly complex climate and energy challenges require sober thinking and sharper focus,” said Armond Cohen, CATF’s founder and Executive Director. “How do we protect climate in a world turned upside down? That question inspired CATF Forward, our new strategy to accelerate the global adoption of the highest-impact climate solutions. It’s a gameplan built for the decades ahead, drawing on CATF’s signature DNA of out-of-the-box thinking, pragmatic solutions, a relentless focus on economics, respected advocacy, and patient coalition building.”

CATF’s work is now organized around three interconnected impact priorities:

Prevent Pollution: Reducing the most damaging emissions quickly and at global scale, while building the rules and institutions that keep our air clean.

Advance Clean Power: Building clean power the world can count on. More energy. More solutions.

Transform Complex Systems: Grappling with complexity across industry, transportation, and land to unlock breakthrough solutions to common challenges.

These priorities are mutually reinforcing. Preventing super pollutants slows warming in the near term, buying time for clean power solutions to scale. Advancing clean power enables emissions reductions across other parts of the economy. Transforming industrial, transportation, and land systems creates further opportunities to reduce emissions and accelerate innovation.

Climate change is an interconnected challenge that demands coordination across borders, institutions, and markets. CATF works to accelerate the global adoption of highest-impact technologies, policies and practices across three core geographic focus areas:

United States: Protect hard-earned climate progress, expand pathways for durable action, and advance the technologies, policies, and markets that can drive impact at home and around the world.

Europe: Advance solutions that address the interconnected challenges of decarbonization, energy security, and industrial competitiveness, while shaping policies and markets with global influence.

Growth Regions: Deepen our engagement across Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America, where future energy demand, infrastructure investment, innovation, and economic growth will decisively shape global climate progress.

CATF connects across these regions, helping technologies, policies, capital, and best practices move across borders and adapt to local political, institutional, and economic realities.

“This new strategy helps support CATF’s unique combination of independent technical expertise, pragmatic policy-maker engagement, and agenda setting,” said Jonathan Banks, Chief of Programs and Advocacy at CATF. “Taken together, these capabilities allow us to identify the right solutions, build support for their deployment, and ultimately help drive their adoption around the world.”

“CATF Forward leans into our distinctive commitment to innovation, one that has delivered outsized impact over 30 years,” said Anastasia Marceau, Managing Director, Clean Air Task Force. “We’ll continue to put more real world options on the table, take an integrated systems approach to the hardest climate and energy challenges, and pursue breakthrough solutions alongside those we can deploy today.”

CATF is recommended by Giving Green, Founders Pledge, and Vox as one of the most effective climate organizations in the world and holds a four-star Charity Navigator rating, the highest possible rating. It is independent and nonpartisan, taking no government funding and no money from the industries it works to change.
