Led by John Douglas, whose development experience includes the $8 billion Champlain Hudson Power Express, the collaboration brings major North American energy infrastructure expertise to MAX Power’s growing Lawson Natural Hydrogen Discovery and commercialization strategy.

Strategic MOU targets Canadian-built AI data centers in Saskatchewan and potential electricity markets through a proposed 2,000 MW First Nations-controlled energy corridor.

REGINA, Saskatchewan, Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- – MAX Power Mining Corp. (CSE: MAXX; OTC: MAXXF; FSE: 89N) (“MAX Power” or the “Company”) is pleased to announce a strategic Memorandum of Understanding (“MOU”) with Douglas Capital Inc. (“DCI”), bringing major North American energy infrastructure development expertise (transmission projects, operating industrial power plants, and hydrogen-fired generation engineering) to the Company’s emerging Natural Hydrogen commercialization strategy.

The collaboration will evaluate opportunities to connect MAX Power’s Saskatchewan Natural Hydrogen Discovery with Canadian-built AI data centers, industrial power generation, and potential electricity markets through a proposed interprovincial energy corridor.

DCI is led by John Douglas , founder of Transmission Developers Inc., the developer behind the C$8 billion, 1,250 MW Champlain Hudson Power Express , which entered commercial operation in June 2026, delivering Québec hydroelectricity to New York City. Together with Dr. Denis Steyn , a former Siemens power transmission lines and high-voltage direct current (“HVDC”) executive, Mr. Douglas also co-founded Public Energy Inc., which operates power generation facilities serving industrial customers in Ontario, including Magna International.

The collaboration with DCI comes as MAX Power advances technical evaluation of its Lawson Natural Hydrogen discovery and Saskatchewan positions itself for substantial investment in AI infrastructure. With growing demand for reliable electricity and new data center developments facing increasing pressure to secure dedicated power supplies, the collaboration provides a framework for evaluating how a potential new Canadian energy source could be connected to emerging domestic and broader North American electricity markets.

Highlights

Natural Hydrogen to AI: Evaluate a connected network of next-generation data centers of varying capacities across Saskatchewan, intended to be entirely Canadian-built and powered by electricity generated from MAX Power’s Natural Hydrogen, subject to technical and commercial validation;

A broader route to market: Explore potential electricity supply opportunities through DCI’s proposed CANVergence Energy Way, an Alberta-to-Ontario energy corridor intended to be 100% First Nations-controlled and to include a 2,000 MW multi-terminal HVDC transmission system;

Development and operating experience: Combine MAX Power’s exploration and subsurface expertise with DCI’s experience in project development, permitting, financing, transmission, distributed generation and prospective customer engagement;

Defined next steps: The parties intend to agree on a joint feasibility work plan, budget and timetable within 30 days of the MOU’s effective date, addressing hydrogen supply requirements, generation infrastructure, data center sizing, potential customers and definitive commercial arrangements.

Mr. Chad Levesque, MAX Power President, commented: “Natural Hydrogen has the potential to become an entirely new primary energy source, the first since uranium, but realizing that opportunity requires more than a discovery. It requires the infrastructure, expertise and commercial relationships to bring that energy to market. John Douglas and his team have been involved in developing some of North America’s most significant energy projects. Bringing that experience together with what we are advancing at Lawson represents an important step in building the commercial pathways for Natural Hydrogen in Canada.”

Major Energy Infrastructure Experience

Mr. Douglas, CPA, CA, CBV, has more than 30 years of investment banking and energy infrastructure experience. He founded Transmission Developers Inc. in 2008, served as its CEO through 2010 and remained a director until 2022. TDI originated and developed Champlain Hudson Power Express, which was built under Blackstone ownership following its acquisition of TDI. The approximately 550-kilometre underground and underwater transmission project provides a major new connection between Québec’s hydroelectric supply and New York City’s electricity market.

Mr. Douglas also founded Lake Erie Power Corp., developer of the proposed 1,000 MW Lake Erie Connector between Ontario and Pennsylvania, and Ventus Energy Inc., which developed a portfolio of wind projects before its acquisition by GDF Suez in 2007. His earlier career included serving as Head of Investment Banking at Sprott Securities.

Dr. Steyn, P.Eng., PhD, brings more than 25 years of high-voltage engineering and energy management experience, including leadership of Siemens’ power transmission lines business in Germany and HVDC business development in Canada. He is also CEO of Verdyn Inc., a Canadian power electronics company developing technologies for industrial power quality, energy storage and high-density data center loads.

Through Public Energy, Mr. Douglas and Dr. Steyn have developed, financed, built and operated natural gas-fired generation facilities supplying Ontario industrial customers under long-term agreements. Their hydrogen-focused company, Current H2 Inc., has completed front-end engineering and design for a proposed 25 MW reference plant in Owen Sound, Ontario. The proposed plant is designed to use hydrogen produced by on-site electrolysis; its engineering experience is relevant to evaluating hydrogen-fired power generation, while the proposed collaboration with MAX Power would examine naturally occurring hydrogen as a potential fuel source.

Mr. John Douglas, President and CEO of Douglas Capital, commented: “The opportunity is to connect a potential new Canadian energy source with infrastructure designed around the needs of its customers. Our team brings experience across generation, transmission and project finance, and we see a compelling reason to evaluate how that experience could support MAX Power’s Natural Hydrogen opportunity. The work ahead is to match the characteristics of the hydrogen supply with the right power systems, project scale and commercial arrangements.”

Canadian AI Data Centers and a Potential National Energy Connection

The data center initiative would evaluate a connected network of Saskatchewan facilities of varying capacities, using advanced power electronics and modular generation systems. DCI is advancing a portfolio of Saskatchewan data center opportunities, with the intended solution made, constructed and installed by Canadian companies. Project sizing would be informed by MAX Power’s hydrogen composition, quantity and flow data, alongside customer requirements and technical, commercial and environmental feasibility.

A second initiative would examine potential customers and offtake arrangements for Natural Hydrogen-derived electricity through CANVergence Energy Way. The proposed corridor extends from Alberta to Ontario and is intended to include a 2,000 MW multi-terminal HVDC transmission system. DCI would lead engagement with First Nations along the proposed corridor and near potential project sites. The 2,000 MW figure refers to the corridor’s proposed transmission capacity.

The MOU contemplates DCI leading project development, financial modelling, prospective customer solicitation and efforts to raise development capital for data center projects. MAX Power would contribute the subsurface and hydrogen supply information required to evaluate and size potential developments. A joint steering committee, with a senior representative from each company, would oversee the proposed work plan and discussions toward definitive agreements.

Mr. Rob Norris, MAX Power CEO, commented: “MAX Power is advancing the technical work at Lawson while building the relationships needed to pursue commercial development. Saskatchewan’s growing AI infrastructure ambitions give that work added urgency. This collaboration brings experienced energy developers into the process of evaluating how a new source of Natural Hydrogen could serve Canadian customers, and what it would take to develop those opportunities at a scale supported by our results.”

Why This Matters To Investors

MAX Power is assembling the capabilities needed to move from Natural Hydrogen discovery toward a commercial energy business. DCI brings experience with the decisions that shape that transition: How to size a power project, connect it to a customer, secure approvals and structure its financing. Its principals’ record across major transmission development and operating industrial generation gives MAX Power a credible counterpart for evaluating those commercial pathways as the Company advances Lawson’s technical validation.

The two initiatives address different potential markets. Saskatchewan data centers could provide local demand for dedicated generation sized to the hydrogen supply that testing may establish. A future interprovincial corridor could provide another route to electricity customers beyond Saskatchewan. Evaluating both gives MAX Power a broader basis for assessing where its potential energy supply could create value, while retaining control of its resource and the ability to pursue other commercial relationships.

The timing is significant. MAX Power has established Canada’s first confirmed subsurface Natural Hydrogen system at Lawson and holds approximately 2.5 million permitted acres across Saskatchewan. This collaboration brings a proven energy infrastructure development experience into MAX Power’s “Months to Molecules” strategy as the Company evaluates how Natural Hydrogen could serve Canadian customers and potentially reach broader North American markets. This parallel approach could help shorten the pathway from discovery to commercial development, should the necessary technical and economic conditions be established.

MOU Framework

The MOU is non-binding other than certain customary provisions. No definitive agreement has been entered into, and there can be no assurance that either initiative will proceed. Any development remains subject to technical, commercial and environmental feasibility, financing, permitting, required approvals and definitive agreements.

The MOU does not establish a legal partnership or joint venture, commit either party to project financing, or grant MAX Power any ownership, capacity or access rights in DCI’s proposed corridor or data center sites. It does not grant DCI rights to MAX Power’s resources, production or offtake. Each party retains its assets and rights, and any joint expenditure requires advance written agreement. The proposed ownership, governance, economics, supply and offtake arrangements would be negotiated in definitive agreements, if the parties determine to proceed beyond the MOU.

description:
Battery Demand Could Reach 100,000 MW Pakistan is seeking to build local battery manufacturing capacity as demand for energy storage and electric vehicles rises.
The EDB estimates that demand for battery energy storage systems could reach 100,000 megawatts by June 2030, depending on economic growth.
Pakistan Plans Four to Five Gigafactories The EDB estimates that grid stabilization alone could require 3,000 to 5,000 megawatts of battery storage capacity.
The government has prepared a lithium battery manufacturing policy that was submitted to the Ministry of Industries in March and is awaiting approval.
The EDB expects the new automotive policy to support demand for battery storage as Pakistan seeks to shift from imported fuel toward electric mobility.
text:
Pakistan is preparing to launch a $2.25 billion lithium-ion battery manufacturing project in Rawalpindi, with a factory owned by the military-run Margalla Heavy Industries Limited (MHIL) expected to begin production within six to eight months of the government approving a policy for the sector.

According to Arab News, the project involves Chinese manufacturers and a local private sector investor, with construction and equipment installation already completed. Hamad Ali Mansoor, chief executive of the Engineering Development Board (EDB), told Arab News that the facility was awaiting government approval before production could begin.

The proposed factory is located at Heavy Industries Taxila in Rawalpindi district, where MHIL manufactures defense equipment and other products, including unmanned drones, electric vehicle buses, two-wheelers and battery energy storage systems.

The project was signed in July with a Chinese company that Mansoor described as one of China’s leading manufacturers, alongside a local investor. He said the factory would manufacture lithium ion cells, with an initial production capacity of 200 to 300 megawatts before gradually reaching its planned annual capacity of more than 1,000 megawatts.

Battery Demand Could Reach 100,000 MW

Pakistan is seeking to build local battery manufacturing capacity as demand for energy storage and electric vehicles rises. The EDB estimates that demand for battery energy storage systems could reach 100,000 megawatts by June 2030, depending on economic growth.

Mansoor said demand could reach 100,000 megawatts if Pakistan’s economy grows by 5 percent or more, while growth below 3 percent could limit demand to around 80,000 megawatts. The projected requirement includes households, commercial buildings, industrial facilities and electric vehicles, ranging from two wheelers to buses and trucks.

Pakistan Plans Four to Five Gigafactories

The EDB estimates that grid stabilization alone could require 3,000 to 5,000 megawatts of battery storage capacity. Meeting the country’s projected demand could require four to five gigafactories, each costing approximately $1 billion to $1.25 billion.

The government has prepared a lithium battery manufacturing policy that was submitted to the Ministry of Industries in March and is awaiting approval. The plan envisages four major factories, with three in Punjab’s Lahore, Faisalabad and Rawalpindi divisions and another in Karachi.

Government Policy Awaits Approval

The proposed policy would require battery manufacturers to export a specified share of their production, although Mansoor declined to disclose the target before the policy is approved. He said the framework incorporates international safety and performance standards.

The development follows Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s approval of the Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026 to 2031, which is awaiting International Monetary Fund approval over proposed tax incentives and their potential impact on government revenue. The EDB expects the new automotive policy to support demand for battery storage as Pakistan seeks to shift from imported fuel toward electric mobility.

Pakistan Seeks to Replace Imported Components

Pakistan currently assembles around 3,000 to 4,000 megawatts of batteries and related components, including motors, controllers and chargers, according to Mansoor. However, the country remains dependent on imports and is seeking to develop domestic manufacturing capacity to reduce costs and strengthen its engineering industry.

Mansoor said the government wanted to move toward manufacturing these components entirely within Pakistan by next year. The planned battery factories are expected to support local production for electric vehicles and energy storage while creating opportunities to export locally manufactured cells.

text:
Renewable energy supplied 28.1% of total US electricity generation during the first eight months of this year, with output from renewable sources rising by 10.2% year-on-year, according to data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), reviewed by the SUN DAY Campaign.

According to the data, renewable generation has grown significantly faster than overall US electricity production, which increased by 2.6% over the same period.

‘Unstoppable growth’

“The growth of solar, wind, and battery storage has become unstoppable,” commented Ken Bossong, executive director, SUN DAY Campaign. “Meanwhile, the share of the nation’s electrical generation and generating capacity provided by fossil fuels and nuclear continues to shrink.”

According to EIA data, utility-scale solar generation increased by 20% over the eight-month period, while small-scale solar rose by 12%. Wind generation increased by 7.8%, hydropower by 4.2% and geothermal generation by 3.8%.e

By comparison, electricity generation from natural gas increased by 2.6% and nuclear generation by 1.3%, while coal-fired generation fell by 8.7%.

In the period from January to August 2026, wind and solar together accounted for more than a fifth (21.1%) of US electricity generation, with combined wind and solar generation accounting for 662,486 gigawatt-hours, compared with 531,031 GWh from nuclear power and 458,609 GWh from coal.

In addition, over the past year – i.e. between September 2025 and August 2026 – renewable energy capacity increased by 43,497.9 megawatts (MW), including 27,141.7 MW of utility-scale solar, 6,526.1 MW of small-scale solar and 9,979.1 MW of wind capacity.

Projections from the EIA suggest that utility-scale renewable capacity will increase by a further 53,117.3 MW during the 12 months to August 2027, led by solar (+44,603.1 MW).

Renewable generation

If small-scale solar is included, the SUN DAY Campaign estimates that renewable generating capacity could reach around 550,000 MW by September 2027. This compares with projected natural gas capacity of around 518,313 MW.

The turnaround comes amid pushback against the massive $900 million Amtrak maintenance facility from residents in Bridgeport and Chinatown and accusations of a bait and switch from local officials.

The dispute is over a 60-acre freight yard along Canal Street between 33rd and 35th streets, which Amtrak, backed by multi-million dollar federal grant, wants to turn into a massive 24-hour passenger coach and maintenance hub.

RELATED: South Side residents voice opposition to proposed Amtrak maintenance facility at public meeting

The project was originally granted a categorical exclusion, meaning it could bypass rigorous environmental checks, but now the Federal Railroad Administration reversed that and is now requiring a formal environmental assessment.

Area residents have threatened lawsuits and are demanding transparency claiming they were kept in the dark and misled, thinking the site would just be used to park train cars, not be an around-the-clock heavy industrial repair yard.

SEE ALSO: Justin Ishbia says White Sox stadium decision rests with Reinsdorf as ownership transition awaits

Opponents of the proposal remain critical of the entire deal because moving the rail yard from its current South Loop location at 14th Street to the neighborhood would free up prime real estate for a highly controversial new Chicago White Sox stadium back by a billionaire developer and tied to team ownership.

In a statement, Alderwoman Nicole Lee, , whose 11th Ward includes the proposed facility location, writes, "We should not have had to scream, fight and pound on the doors of power just to get the basic transparency about the environmental effects this plan could have on our residents,"

In response to the decision, Amtrak and developer Canal Edge said in a joint statement, "We believe a deeper public review process will help stakeholders better understand the need for the new facility and associated viaduct repair work as well as the environmental impact of the project,"

The federal environmental study is expected to be wrapped up by the end of the year and includes a mandatory 30 day public comment period and at least two public meetings.

title: Türkiye could electrify 85% of its energy use | Ember
description:
To accelerate this transition, Türkiye has announced a pledge to raise electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035.
For Türkiye, electrification points to a very high potential for transformation in final energy consumption, particularly in transport and buildings.
In Türkiye, around 85% of final energy demand could be met by electric technologies already in use today.
Today, existing technologies already make it possible in Türkiye to electrify 100% of energy use in buildings, 96% of transport and 58% of industrial energy consumption.
But as the number of electric vehicles grows, fossil fuel consumption falls and electricity’s share of total energy consumption rises faster.
text:
The International Energy Agency (IEA) and International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) scenarios show that, to limit global temperature rise to 1.5C, electricity’s share of global final energy consumption needs to rise from 23% today to 35% by 2035.

Accordingly, at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference of the Parties (COP31), which Türkiye hosts this year, the target of 35% electrification by 2035 is expected to be on the agenda. In Türkiye, where this share stood at 22% in 2024, electrification needs to gain momentum for the target to be reached.

Electricity’s share is 30% in buildings and industry, but below 1% in transport

Türkiye’s clean energy transition has so far taken place mainly in electricity generation. The share of renewables in electricity generation rose from 32% to 43% between 2015 and 2025. Over the same period, the share of solar and wind alone grew from 4.5% to 22%, showing that the energy transition in the power sector has gained significant momentum. Yet while electricity increasingly comes from renewable sources, energy needs in buildings, transport and industry are still met mainly by fossil fuels.

Spreading the progress in electricity generation across the wider economy depends on electricity replacing fossil fuels in buildings, transport and industry – in other words, on raising electricity’s share of final energy consumption. To accelerate this transition, Türkiye has announced a pledge to raise electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035.

For Türkiye, electrification points to a very high potential for transformation in final energy consumption, particularly in transport and buildings. In Türkiye, around 85% of final energy demand could be met by electric technologies already in use today. Electric vehicles in transport, heat pumps in buildings, electric cooking instead of gas stoves and electric production technologies in industry can replace fossil fuels with more efficient and cleaner electricity.

Today, existing technologies already make it possible in Türkiye to electrify 100% of energy use in buildings, 96% of transport and 58% of industrial energy consumption. The share that does not appear suitable for electrification comes largely from aviation and shipping in transport, from high-power machinery such as combine harvesters in agriculture and from some high-temperature processes and fuels used as feedstock in industry.

The growing share of renewables in electricity generation is reducing the power system’s dependence on fossil fuels. However, electricity makes up only 22% of final energy consumption. Most of the remainder consists of fossil fuels burned directly in transport, buildings and industry. Cutting the use of fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal in these sectors requires wider use of electricity. Supplying the electricity demand created by the electrification with renewable energy will enable clean energy to spread across the wider economy. Replacing fossil fuels with electricity from renewable sources will also strengthen Türkiye’s energy security by reducing its import dependence.

On current trends, electrification falls short of 35% in 2035

Between 2014 and 2024, final fossil fuel demand in Türkiye grew by an average of 2.5% a year, and electricity demand by 4%. If these trends continue, the electrification rate will reach 24.4% in 2035, around 11 percentage points short of the 35% target. This shows the need for a transition that goes beyond current trends and accelerates the replacement of fossil fuels with electricity.

If fossil fuel consumption keeps growing at its current pace, electricity demand needs to grow by 9% a year

In a scenario where fossil fuel consumption keeps growing at its current pace, raising electricity’s share of total final energy consumption to 35% requires a very large technological transition. In this case, reaching the 35% target would mean 19 million electric cars and 6.5 million electric commercial vehicles on the road in 2035, heat pumps in 20 million homes and around 12 GW of electric heat generation capacity in industry.

This scenario requires an average of 1.7 million new electric cars to take to the road every year. That is around 1.5 times the total number of cars sold in Türkiye in 2025. Moreover, only 17% of new sales in 2025 – 190,000 cars – were electric. The 19 million electric cars needed by 2035 are also more than two and a half times the 7 million projected by the Energy Market Regulatory Authority (EMRA) in its high scenario for 2035. The scenario also requires heat pumps to be installed in 1.8 million homes every year. This is equivalent to almost all of Ankara’s residential gas subscribers switching to heat pumps every year. Yet around 1 million gas boilers are sold in Türkiye each year. The targeted transition would therefore require installation rates far above current boiler sales and a rapid change of the heating market.

The electricity generation required by this scenario is equally large. Without any fall in fossil fuel consumption, this transition would increase final electricity consumption by 480 TWh compared with 2024, to 790 TWh in 2035 – 2.6 times today’s level. Meeting this additional consumption with the current mix of generation capacity would require around 200 GW of additional capacity to be brought online by 2035. That means commissioning new generation capacity 1.5 times the size of today’s installed capacity by 2035. If current investment trends continue, however, capacity growth on this scale by 2035 does not appear feasible.

For electricity consumption to reach 790 TWh, it would need to grow by an average of 9% every year until 2035. This is more than double the 4% average annual growth Türkiye recorded over the past ten years. Türkiye last achieved annual electricity consumption growth of 9% in the 1970s, when electricity was being brought to every village.

In a scenario where fossil fuel consumption stays flat at its 2024 record level, electricity consumption would need to grow by an average of 6.7% a year to reach the 35% target by 2035. Yet this rate is higher even than the strong growth Türkiye last achieved between 1996 and 2007, when consumption was a third of today’s level.

However, as in every maturing power system, electricity consumption growth in Türkiye is slowing over time. Annual growth of more than 9% in 1972–1980 has fallen by around 1.5 percentage points each decade, to 4% in 2014–2024. Reaching the 35% target without reducing fossil fuel consumption, purely by increasing electricity consumption, would require today’s mature system to recapture growth rates typical of the early period when access to electricity was expanding. The path to the 35% target therefore lies not in increasing electricity consumption far above current rates, but in concrete steps to shift the services that fossil fuels provide today to electricity.

The electrification rate understates early progress

In the early years of the shift from fossil fuels to electricity, the electrification rate can paint a misleading picture of slow progress. Because electric technologies use 2–4 times less energy to do the same job, total energy consumption falls when a service previously met by fossil fuels switches to electricity. As a result, electricity’s share of total energy consumption rises more slowly in the early years than the share of services actually switching to electricity, then climbs rapidly once the transition passes a certain threshold.

Cars clearly illustrate this gap. An internal combustion engine car uses around 3.6 times as much energy as an electric car to travel the same distance. As a result, the transition measured by number of vehicles and the electrification rate measured by energy diverge markedly.

In a fleet of 100 internal combustion engine cars, converting 10 to electric represents a 10% transition by number of vehicles, but raises the energy-based electrification rate to only 3%. Converting half the fleet takes the rate to 21%, while converting 80 cars brings it to just 52%. Converting the final 20 cars takes the rate to 100%.

In the early stages, the spread of electric vehicles raises the electrification rate slowly; as most vehicles become electric, the rate rises faster. This is because electric vehicles use far less energy than petrol or diesel vehicles to travel the same distance. When the first vehicles switch to electric, most of the total energy consumption still comes from fossil fuels. But as the number of electric vehicles grows, fossil fuel consumption falls and electricity’s share of total energy consumption rises faster.

The electrification rate can therefore make progress look slower than it is in the early stages of the transition, and faster than it is in later stages. To understand the real pace of the transition, indicators such as electric vehicle sales, heat pump installations and industrial production capacity switching to electricity need to be tracked alongside the electrification rate.

Reaching Türkiye’s 35% electrification target requires cutting fossil fuel use and expanding electricity in industry, transport and buildings. To track this transition, the national target should be broken down into sectoral roadmaps with absolute targets. This would set the pace at which each sector needs to transform and make it possible to measure whether current progress is in line with the target. These targets would also provide a basis for forecasting future electricity demand and for planning clean generation capacity and grid investment to match.

The Climate Law, which entered into force in 2025, made expanding electrification one of the duties of public institutions and requires them to align their plans with electrification targets by the end of 2027. Assigning interagency coordination and progress tracking to the Carbon Market Board established by the Law would speed up the process without the need for a new institutional structure.

Heat pumps need higher electricity tariff thresholds

Residential heat pumps are among the technologies that could make a large contribution to the national electrification target, 11 percentage points on their own. However, their uptake depends on running costs being competitive with gas.

The current tiered electricity tariff and the 4,000 kWh annual consumption threshold for the last resort supply tariff (SKTT) quickly push households using heat pumps into high-cost bands and onto the SKTT. Compared with subsidised gas prices, the unit cost of electricity in the upper tier is three times higher, and four times higher under the last resort tariff, which weakens the economic case for heat pumps. To reduce fossil fuel dependence and encourage electrification, raising the consumption threshold in the tiered tariff for households using heat pumps would limit the increase in electricity costs and make heat pumps more competitive with gas.

The public sector can lead the shift to electric vehicles

Road transport alone accounts for around a third of energy imports in Türkiye. With the Hormuz crisis expected to add $5.2 billion to oil import costs for road transport in 2026, the shift to electric vehicles offers a major opportunity to cut oil demand and import dependence. This shift could be accelerated by a scrappage scheme that requires end-of-life fossil fuel vehicles to be replaced only with electric equivalents. Old, inefficient cars would be taken off the road, and because these cars would have been replaced anyway, users would face no additional cost.

In addition, making the public sector’s new fossil fuel vehicle purchase ban, which expires in May 2027, permanent and extending it to vehicle leasing would generate significant savings in the public budget. Over the long term, this policy would also contribute directly to the central government budget by lowering the public fleet’s fuel and maintenance costs.

Meanwhile, diesel, which makes up two-thirds of fuel consumption in road transport, is pushing up transport costs and Türkiye’s import bill as global oil prices rise. Converting heavy-duty vehicles to electric could cut energy costs and oil imports, helping to reduce the trade deficit. Türkiye has signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging that at least 30% of new truck and bus sales are zero-emission by 2030 and that all are zero-emission by 2040, but it has not yet reflected these targets in national strategy documents. In addition, compared with their diesel equivalents, electric light commercial vehicles – where the transition could happen faster – are subject to a higher Special Consumption Tax.

Measures such as a gradually increasing electric requirement for new urban passenger buses purchased from 2027, together with Special Consumption Tax and Motor Vehicle Tax advantages and motorway toll discounts for electric heavy-duty vehicles, would extend electrification beyond private use to commercial transport. By creating a steady and predictable market, this move would also accelerate domestic commercial vehicle production and investment in charging infrastructure for heavy-duty vehicles.

Mapping industrial potential can unlock concrete projects

Industrial heat demand of up to 200C degrees can already be met with existing electric technologies. However, the specific conditions of each facility and production process mean that electrification options and investment needs must be assessed case by case. Publicly supported feasibility studies would lay the groundwork for investment decisions by identifying facilities’ technical potential and suitable technology options. Building the project development capacity of facility staff would speed up the conversion of this potential into viable projects. As a result, existing transition support could be directed to processes with high electrification potential.

Meanwhile, the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) entered its financial obligation phase in 2026. In a high scenario, it is estimated that CBAM’s annual cost to Türkiye could reach €2.5 billion. Moreover, the EU’s preparations to extend CBAM to other sectors that account for a significant share of Türkiye’s exports, such as chemicals, plastics, glass and ceramics, suggest that this cost could rise.

The way to reduce these costs is to accelerate the clean energy transition that cuts industrial emissions, with electrification at its core. Quickly setting the emissions cap and price corridor in the Türkiye Emissions Trading System (ETS), which entered into force in 2026, to create a predictable carbon price would encourage industry to invest in electrification. Channelling ETS revenues into industry’s clean energy transition would help keep in Türkiye the resources that would otherwise leave the country through CBAM.

Electrification and clean electricity generation capacity need to be planned together

Meeting rising electricity demand with fossil fuel power plants would increase emissions and energy imports, even if it raised the electrification rate. The 35% electrification target should therefore be considered together with renewable energy targets.

Türkiye’s target to triple its wind and solar installed capacity – currently over 40 GW – by 2035 provides a strong foundation for the clean electricity supply this transition will need. To support this target, realising Türkiye’s 120 GW of rooftop solar potential would both make a significant contribution to additional capacity needs and support the expansion of distributed electricity generation.

Strengthening transmission and distribution grids, expanding interconnection capacity and planning battery storage and demand side flexibility solutions at the same time are essential to carry this new capacity and rising demand through the system reliably and efficiently. This integrated approach to infrastructure would ensure that rising demand is met reliably and at low cost.

However, strengthening the grid and increasing clean electricity generation are only the first step. Achieving the 35% electrification target depends on clean electricity replacing fossil fuels in sectors such as transport, buildings and industry. As holder of the COP31 Presidency in 2026, Türkiye can take a leading role in the energy transition by extending its progress in renewable electricity across the whole economy through electrification.

The electrification rate refers to the share of electricity in total final energy consumption. Non-energy uses in final energy consumption are excluded from the total. Calculations use the energy balance tables published by the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources. Global and regional rates were compiled using the same definition from the International Energy Agency’s World Energy Balances dataset.

The electrification-ready share was calculated by matching sectoral and fuel-specific final consumption data from the energy balance table with the technology readiness levels in the IEA’s Clean Energy Technology Guide. All uses with an electric alternative at level 9 – the highest readiness level in the guide, meaning commercially mature – were considered electrifiable.

Scenario assumptions to 2035

The first scenario assumes that final fossil fuel demand grows at its current annual rate for 2014–2024. In this scenario, the 35% target is reached solely through growth in electricity demand. The second scenario assumes that fossil fuel consumption stays flat at its 2024 level.

Electricity demand in the scenarios refers to final demand. The gross amount to be met on the generation side was calculated assuming 15% transmission and distribution losses. Additional electricity needs were assumed to be met in proportion to today’s installed capacity mix.

Electricity consumption growth rates used in historical comparisons were calculated from national energy balance tables covering 1972–2024.

Data from the automotive distributors’ association ODMD and the Turkish Statistical Institute (TURKSTAT) were used for car sales and electric vehicle shares, data from the gas appliance industry association DOSİDER for gas boiler sales and EMRA’s 2035 high-scenario projection for the electric vehicle comparison.

For the calculation in which all new car sales are electric, new car sales in Türkiye – an average of one million a year in 2023–2025 – were assumed to continue at the same level from 2027 to 2035, with all of them electric.

The energy-based electrification rate for cars was calculated assuming that each vehicle in the fleet travels the same distance each year and that an internal combustion engine car uses 3.6 times as much energy as an electric car for the same distance. In calculating this transition’s contribution to Türkiye’s overall electrification rate, all final energy consumption other than cars was held constant at 2024 levels; the fossil fuel consumption replaced by converted vehicles was subtracted from total final consumption, and their electricity consumption was added to both electricity consumption and total final consumption. The same method was applied to the case where the entire current fleet becomes electric.

The calculation for Türkiye’s current fleet used petrol, diesel, LPG and electricity consumption by cars from the 2024 balance tables (around 150 TWh in total), together with TURKSTAT figures of 18 million cars and a 2.7% electric vehicle share as of September 2026.

Efficiency of electrification

To estimate the technologies behind the additional electricity consumption in the scenarios, the 4% annual growth in electricity demand that would occur anyway if trends continued was first separated out, and additional fossil fuel uses above this were assumed to be converted to electricity. The electricity required was calculated by dividing the fossil fuel consumption replaced by each converted use by the relevant efficiency factor. Electric cars were assumed to be 3.6 times more efficient than internal combustion engine cars, electric heavy-duty vehicles 1.5 times more efficient than diesel equivalents, heat pumps in buildings 2.5 times more efficient than gas boilers and electric heat generation in industry twice as efficient as fossil fuel systems. The transition to 2035 was distributed across technologies in proportion to their current consumption shares.

Sectoral contributions were calculated separately for each technology, holding the 2024 consumption structure constant. When several sectors transform simultaneously, the denominator shrinks faster, so the total effect will differ from the sum of the individual contributions. In homes, all heating, hot water and cooking were assumed to switch to heat pumps and electric cookers.

text:
A new federal rule could make it harder for Utah farmers to finance projects related to clean energy.

The regulations require farmers to complete projects and document a year of energy savings before applying for funding. The U.S. Department of Agriculture said the changes are intended to streamline its Rural Energy for America Program and ensure funding decisions reflect actual project performance.

Chad Hughes, senior associate attorney at the Environmental Law and Policy Center, said requiring farmers to cover costs up front could put federal assistance out of reach for smaller operations.

"Only those that can afford to carry those costs for over a year without knowing whether or not they're going to be reimbursed are going to be able to apply for [the program]. So it's going to make the program just much less accessible," Hughes contended.

Hughes pointed out the changes also limit wind projects on certified cropland. They took effect Oct. 16.

Farmers and rural businesses can comment on the rule online through Nov. 2. Although the rule is already active, the Department of Agriculture said the feedback could influence future program revisions.

The guidelines follow earlier agency restrictions on solar funding, which applied retroactively to pending applications. The Environmental Law and Policy Center sued the agency in September, arguing the policy conflicts with Congress’ intent for the program to support renewable energy projects. Hughes stressed the agency cannot restrict renewable energy to favor fossil fuels.

"The law has these basic principles of fairness baked in. You can't just change the rules in the middle of the game like that unless you have a really good reason to do so, and [the Agriculture Department] just has not identified such reason," Hughes underscored.

text:
By Simon August, DCNF Reporter, Daily Caller News Foundation

Democrats hoping to win back Congress are split over whether to revive a Biden-era tax break for electric car buyers.

Rank-and-file House Democrats want to restore the $7,500 credit Republicans ended in 2025, but party leaders have not committed to it, Politico reported Monday. Democratic Ohio Rep. Greg Landsman introduced a bill Oct. 22 to double the credit to $15,000 and make it permanent, according to his office.

“The credit is not good policy,” Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, said in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation.

Michel said estimates of the Inflation Reduction Act-era credits indicate roughly seven in 10 recipients would have purchased an electric car without one.

He noted the Joint Committee on Taxation’s projection that repealing the old credit would save more than $19 billion in fiscal 2032, the last year of projected savings.

“If we simply double that figure and multiply it by the budget window, a credit twice as large as the one Congress repealed could cost about $380 billion over a decade, possibly more,” Michel said.

Ending the credit for buyers of new electric cars is projected to save the federal government $77.8 billion from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2034, according to Joint Committee on Taxation estimates cited in a December 2025 Congressional Research Service report.

“Repealing it was the wrong decision,” Democratic California Rep. Mike Levin told Politico. “The whole thing is a giant self-own by this administration, and it does no good for the American auto industry.”

A Democratic adviser who works on energy, granted anonymity by Politico, said the credit has “become kind of synonymous with elite, liberal, coastal, kind of out-of-touch policy and politics.”

The credit has gained a reputation for helping Americans who could already afford an electric car, party insiders told the outlet.

“The credit primarily benefited high-income households, those making over $150,000 annually,” Jonathan Lesser, senior fellow at the National Center for Energy Analytics, said in a statement to the DCNF.

“If the subsidy were revived, it would mean lower-income Americans would be again forced to subsidize higher-income ones,” Lesser added.

Mark Mills, the center’s founder and executive director, said in a statement to the DCNF that “high-income households are the overwhelming majority of electric vehicle (EV) buyers and thus the subsidy to those households is a reverse Robin Hood.”

Peter Z. Grossman, a visiting fellow at the center and a professor of economics emeritus at Butler University, said in a statement to the DCNF that his understanding is most of the credit’s beneficiaries were “wealthy people who bought an EV as a second/third/fourth car as a virtue signal and (if it was a Tesla) a status symbol.”

“For taxpayers it would continue to be a subsidy for the wealthy although it would depend on how the subsidy was structured,” Grossman said.

Levin and Democratic Illinois Rep. Sean Casten’s Energy Bills Relief Act, which Casten introduced March 18, would repeal the part of the 2025 reconciliation law that ended the clean energy tax credits, including the electric car credit, according to the bill text.

The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and eight other committees, according to the Government Publishing Office.

More than 160 House Democrats back the bill, but House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is not a cosponsor, Politico reported.

In March remarks to the League of Conservation Voters, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York called for restoring clean energy credits for sources such as wind and solar but did not explicitly mention electric cars, Politico reported.

Neither Schumer’s nor Jeffries’ office answered the outlet’s repeated questions about their positions on the electric car credit.

“We’ve made unbelievable progress just from the momentum that we’d already created from 2020 to 2024,” Hickenlooper said, according to Politico. “We’ve got to assess how much momentum and how much benefit we got from it.”

Democratic Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she is “open to tax credits” but wants “a comprehensive strategy” on energy, Politico reported.

“There are still elements within the Democratic coalition who are still fighting the last battle of the [Inflation Reduction Act],” said Tré Easton, vice president for public affairs at the Democratic think tank d Institute, according to Politico.

The centrist group Third Way has proposed a $7,500 point-of-sale rebate aimed at “working and middle-class families,” criticizing the old credit for allowing “wealthier households to use the credit to buy luxury vehicles,” according to Politico.

“We need to incorporate lessons learned and the reality of the 2026 and 2027 economies into the proposals we’re offering,” Josh Freed, Third Way’s senior vice president for climate and energy, said, according to Politico.

Half of the benefits of the credit’s predecessor went in 2022 to taxpayers with adjusted gross incomes of $200,000 or more, the top 8 percent of taxpayers by income, according to a separate Congressional Research Service report.

Democrats have also cooled on electric cars themselves. Forty-seven percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they would give serious thought to buying one in a Pew Research Center survey of 3,524 U.S. adults taken March 16 to 22, down from 58 percent in 2022.

The question went to about half the sample, and the margin of error for Democrats and Democratic leaners who were asked it is plus or minus 3.7 percentage points, according to Pew.

Sixty percent of Democrats and Democratic leaners said the federal government should encourage electric car use, down 10 points from 2022, according to Pew, which gives a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points for that group.

name: Congress
title: A 'Bipartisan' Bill to Dismantle the Nation's Bedrock Environmental Law
description:
Once stripped of its deceptive branding, the bill is an out-and-out assault on the National Environmental Policy Act, the bedrock environmental law that has for more than 50 years required the federal government to look before it leaps.
Often called the “Magna Carta” of environmental law, NEPA has been emulated worldwide.
It expands the categories of proposals that aren’t “major Federal actions,” reducing agencies’ responsibility to prepare in-depth environmental impact statements.
Congress passed NEPA because development-minded agencies often treated environmental concerns as obstacles.
This bill hands those agencies — and the developers they serve — the keys to making the go or no-go decisions.
text:
This op-ed was originally published by The Revelator. Reprinted under Creative Commons license CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

Washington has a gift for cloaking unpopular ideas in appealing names. One recent example is the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA, a sweeping “permitting reform” measure introduced this September by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, Mike Lee, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Martin Heinrich. Once stripped of its deceptive branding, the bill is an out-and-out assault on the National Environmental Policy Act, the bedrock environmental law that has for more than 50 years required the federal government to look before it leaps.

NEPA’s genius is its modesty. As the Supreme Court has repeatedly noted, it’s a purely procedural statute. It dictates no outcomes but requires agencies to stop and think — to generate, consider, and disclose the potential environmental consequences of their actions before shovels hit the ground. Often called the “Magna Carta” of environmental law, NEPA has been emulated worldwide.

BAAJA keeps NEPA’s title while hollowing out nearly everything that makes it work: detailed review of environmental risks, rigorous analysis of available alternatives with less harmful effects, meaningful public input before agencies commit to harmful actions, and — most dangerously — the ability of courts to enforce any of it.

The bill has a minor positive or two; it would restore some of the authority of the Council on Environmental Quality that two courts in 2024 appeared to strip away, allowing the Council to standardize federal agencies’ NEPA procedures. The deal, however, is terribly lopsided and devalues NEPA’s essential purposes.

BAAJA dramatically expands NEPA’s “categorical exclusions,” removing scrutiny and shutting the public out of commenting on excluded projects. It expands the categories of proposals that aren’t “major Federal actions,” reducing agencies’ responsibility to prepare in-depth environmental impact statements. The newly excluded categories could cause significant harm, including projects such as electric transmission facilities, methane gas pipelines, and water resources and geothermal energy development programs.

When review does occur, the bill guts its substance. It instructs agencies to eliminate alternatives that don’t “meet the goals of an applicable non-Federal project sponsor.” The comparison of alternatives is the heart of an EIS, but the bill would let developers define that heart out of existence. The bill then freezes the science: Agencies could ignore research that becomes available after it publishes a project’s notice of intent to prepare a NEPA document.

The bill also imposes rigid deadlines that trace back to a report the Congressional Research Service thoroughly debunked. The real culprits delaying infrastructure projects are inadequate financing, local opposition, and under-resourced agencies. Arbitrary clocks will pressure agencies to cut corners, inviting project-slowing litigation while doing little or nothing to address the most important causes of delay.

Congress passed NEPA because development-minded agencies often treated environmental concerns as obstacles. This bill hands those agencies — and the developers they serve — the keys to making the go or no-go decisions. A project sponsor could force an agency to veto deadline extensions and dictate which alternatives get studied. This is the essence of agency capture, transforming a public safeguard into a private convenience.

The most alarming provisions concern courts. Building on the Supreme Court’s vilification of NEPA in its Seven County Infrastructure Coalition decision, BAAJA forces judges to give “substantial deference” to agency determinations in NEPA documents. This ignores an important impetus for NEPA’s adoption: the incentives of development-oriented agencies to sweep adverse effects under the rug if they threaten project implementation.

Even when a plaintiff wins, courts generally could not halt projects pending preparation of NEPA-compliant documents. By the time they’re completed, the projects may already have caused irreparable environmental harm. These measures go well beyond the already restrictive judicial limits in recent permitting legislation and the Seven County decision and remove agency incentives to conscientiously apply NEPA’s requirements.

The bill also penalizes agencies for protecting the public. If an agency suspends or revokes a permit, it would need to prove that doing so “is necessary to prevent specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm or damage to life, property, national security, or defense” — but not, perversely, to the environment!

A defeat for a NEPA plaintiff would enable private project proponents to recover a significant percentage of all project costs they incurred. Faced with that exposure, no rational agency would ever correct a mistaken approval. A law meant to improve decisions would instead make them irreversible.

It doesn’t have to be this way. Real reform would fund agencies properly, reserve any streamlined track for projects that genuinely benefit the environment, make mitigation binding and monitored, and preserve the public’s access to courts to redress statutory violations.

We should build clean energy and critical infrastructure faster, but not bulldoze the one law that makes sure we know what we’re building before it’s too late to change course. Before Congress votes on whether to “reform” NEPA — which is scheduled to happen immediately after the midterms — its members need to heed the statute’s original vision and look before they leap.

title: YPCCC Partnerships: Interview with GreenLatinos' Mark Magaña
description:
Originally founded in 2008 as the National Latino Coalition on Climate Change, GreenLatinos has become a key voice in shaping how climate issues are communicated within and beyond Latino communities.
At the time, my journey to climate work was just about improving living conditions.
I started an organization called the National Latino Coalition on Climate Change to encourage the passage of one of the first major federal bills on climate change.
So, in 2012, I built on the momentum from the National Latino Coalition on Climate Change to establish GreenLatinos.
Mark: YPCCC’s research has been incredibly valuable to help us understand how different audiences perceive climate change and which messages resonate.
text:
Mark Magaña is the Founding President & CEO of GreenLatinos, a national comunidad of Latino/a/e environmental, conservation and climate justice leaders and advocates. Originally founded in 2008 as the National Latino Coalition on Climate Change, GreenLatinos has become a key voice in shaping how climate issues are communicated within and beyond Latino communities. They advocate for environmental policies that support Latino communities, from building sustainable communities with clean air and water, to urban forestry, to combating extreme heat in Latino neighborhoods.GreenLatinos secured $2.65 million for urban greening initiatives in Latino-populous cities across the US, like Albuquerque, Chicago, and Los Angeles.

Prior to founding GreenLatinos, Mark was the first Latino to serve as Senior Policy Advisor to the House Democratic Caucus and as Special Assistant to President Clinton for Legislative Affairs at the White House. Mark also successfully founded and led the strategic consulting firm Hispanic Strategy Group.

Helena Souffrant from YPCCC’s Partnerships Program recently interviewed Mark Magaña to learn about GreenLatinos’ approach to achieving climate justice, cultivating Latino representation in environmentalism, and their partnership with YPCCC.

Helena: How did you get involved with climate work?

Mark: My journey started with community, not necessarily with climate policy or advocacy work. I grew up in the Los Angeles area, and at that time, the air was really polluted. I also grew up in between three freeways: the 405, the 605, and the 22. In the mornings, we’d listen to the weather and the air quality report. Most days, the air was too unhealthy for children and the elderly to go outside and exert themselves. Of course, we didn’t listen to that. Kids are kids, so we went out and played. But we had to take asthma inhaler breaks. We had to know where the nearest house with a parent was to be able to run over there if one of the kids was having trouble breathing. We knew the risks. We didn’t think it was odd at the time. But now, I think about how just going out to play could be life-threatening.

Now I have two kids, and I am able to afford air and water purifiers – and even organic food sometimes. They are my motivation for why I do this work. But I can see my grandmother smacking me upside the head with a chancla for how much money I spend just to breathe clean air, drink clean water, and eat clean food. At the time, my journey to climate work was just about improving living conditions.

It became a professional journey in 2008 when Congress was preparing a cap-and-trade bill, the ​​American Clean Energy and Security Act, which sought to allow the government to set a limit on the amount of greenhouse gases that could be emitted annually. I started an organization called the National Latino Coalition on Climate Change to encourage the passage of one of the first major federal bills on climate change.

Helena: Is the National Latino Coalition on Climate Change still in existence? Does it support the work of GreenLatinos?

Mark: Ultimately, the American Clean Energy and Security Act bill died and in the process of building support for that piece of legislation, I found that Latinos in the sector felt isolated, siloed, unwelcomed, and ignored. I realized this was an issue I really wanted to engage with beyond just this piece of legislation. I thought we needed a hub for Latinos to convene, support each other, provide resources for each other, advocate together, and feel like they really belonged in the climate movement. So, in 2012, I built on the momentum from the National Latino Coalition on Climate Change to establish GreenLatinos.

Helena: What role does GreenLatinos play in advocacy and in the climate communication landscape?

Mark: Very little of the content produced about climate change resonates with the Latino community. I didn’t learn about environmentalism from traditional environmental content. I learned most of my environmental education at the back of a chancla. You could see your grandmother or your tía smacking you because you left the fridge open, or you didn’t eat all your food, or you left the light on, or you threw something out instead of repairing it. When we eat, we use all parts of the animal: lengua, sesos, intestines, todo. This is part of who I am. This is part of my culture. We learned conservation and how to live in tandem with this environment. So from this perspective, my aunts and uncles were conservationists. I was raised not to waste, to reuse, repurpose, repair. If I don’t convey these values to my children, then it’s gone. It’s history. Maintaining this culture of conservation is vital. But many Latinos don’t see themselves as conservationists or environmentalists because of how it’s framed in the media. When we ask Latinos if they see themselves as people who want to protect the land, water, or air, more than 70% say yes. But when we ask them if they see themselves as environmentalists, many of them say no because they don’t associate with that word. They think it’s academic or for other people. Being able to do effective storytelling and connect environmental issues to issues that are important to them, like children’s health, energy costs, jobs, and safety can help them see how these issues are directly affecting them every day. Language is also an important consideration, whether it’s Spanish or jargon. This helps to build trust between decision makers and frontline communities. This also allows us to be catalysts for more advocacy work within the community.

Helena: What strategies does GreenLatinos use to communicate environmental issues and rally support?

Mark: We focus on communicating values that are important to Latinos. For our communities, the values are family, our children, health, jobs, and opportunities for future generations. We [GreenLatinos] don’t lead with technical language. We address how climate policies affect real life and immediate issues. We embrace trusted messengers, whether it’s local leaders or organizers, priests, or celebrities like Bad Bunny. Rather than top-down narratives we use values-driven storytelling that connects to real community experiences.

Helena: How have you utilized YPCCC data, resources, or insights to advance GreenLatinos’ strategic communication and advocacy work?

Mark: YPCCC’s research has been incredibly valuable to help us understand how different audiences perceive climate change and which messages resonate. We’ve used their insights on values-based framing, audience segmentation, and public opinion trends to refine how we talk about clean air, extreme heat, and a just energy transition with Latino communities.

Their research has also helped us demonstrate to funders and policymakers that climate action has broad public support when framed around health, economic opportunity, and community resilience. This, in turn, strengthens our advocacy strategies by giving us data to back up what we’re seeing on the ground — that when you connect climate to these key issues that are relevant to them, people respond.

Helena: How do you remain hopeful and inspired to build public or political will in the climate movement?

text:
Deep cuts to fossil fuel finance, unfinished business on clean energy

In 2021, Clean Energy Transition Partnership (CETP) signatories committed to end their international public finance for fossil fuels within a year of joining the partnership and to fully prioritize their support for clean energy. This brief provides the latest progress report on the CETP’s implementation.

Policy Recommendations

CETP signatories should maintain progress in ending international public support for fossil fuels, in the name of climate action, energy security, and affordability. This work should include members using their voice and vote at multilateral development banks and stopping gas finance.

CETP signatories should redouble efforts to engage more countries in the initiative. Major financers such as South Korea, Japan, and China, as well as multiple multilateral development banks, still have not signed on.

CETP signatories should implement commitments to phase out domestic fossil fuel subsidies. The credibility of the CETP depends on all signatories showing climate leadership domestically as well. Many CETP countries continue to provide significant domestic subsidies for fossil fuels.

CETP signatories should materially scale up clean energy finance on fair and just terms, especially for transformative energy democracy and environmental justice priorities.

The brief’s findings include the following:

International fossil fuel finance from signatories continues to drop. Compared with the pre-CETP baseline, in 2025 CETP members dropped their fossil fuel financing to USD 3.3 billion, representing an up to 80% drop. This continued and sustained drop in fossil fuel finance means the CETP is one of the most successful climate leadership coalitions when it comes to implementation.

The 28% increase in clean energy finance in 2025 compared with the pre-CETP baseline does not match the drop in fossil fuel finance. Only 42% of the funding removed from fossil fuels has been redirected into clean energy.

Some countries continue to break the pledge, despite the political and economic rationale for reducing fossil fuel dependencies being stronger than ever. Italy is the biggest fossil fuel financer, followed by Germany and Switzerland.

text:
GENERAL Motors’ decision to close one Michigan manufacturing facility and consider alternative uses for another provides further evidence of a significant retreat from electric and hydrogen vehicle investment in the United States, as the Trump administration continues dismantling policies intended to accelerate automotive electrification.

The latest developments affect two facilities near Detroit, including the Brownstown Battery Assembly plant, which GM will reportedly decommission when its lease expires in mid-2027. The 480,000-square-foot (44,593 square metre) facility has been involved in the production of battery packs and electric drive components for vehicles including the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray and Cadillac Celestiq, while approximately 80,000 square feet of the premises supported the company’s hydrogen fuel-cell joint venture with Honda.

According to US publication Automotive News, the facility’s workforce has declined from approximately 300 employees at its peak to fewer than a dozen, with remaining workers offered positions at nearby GM operations under existing United Auto Workers (UAW) agreements.

GM has also assumed the long-term lease of a separate 300,000-square-foot (27,871 square metre) Detroit facility originally intended to manufacture hydrogen fuel cells through a partnership with automotive supplier Piston Automotive.

That project, announced with a proposed investment of $US55.0 million ($A78.2m), was expected to create approximately 150 jobs before GM abandoned its hydrogen development program.

The company is now evaluating alternative uses for the premises, although no replacement manufacturing activity has been announced. The closures represent another chapter in the restructuring of GM’s alternative-powertrain investments, following a series of production reductions, cancelled manufacturing projects, and substantial financial write-downs.

They also raise questions about the longer-term direction of America’s automotive industry, particularly as manufacturers attempt to balance immediate profitability with the need to remain competitive in an increasingly electrified global market.

GM was previously among the industry’s strongest advocates of electrification, having outlined an ambition to eliminate tailpipe emissions from its new light-duty vehicle portfolio by 2035.

That ambition underpinned billions of dollars in manufacturing and battery technology investment, including new facilities, vehicle platforms, and supply agreements intended to support substantially higher electric vehicle sales.

However, consumer demand has failed to develop at the rate originally anticipated, leaving manufacturers with excess production capacity and investments increasingly difficult to justify. In January, GM disclosed a further $US6.0 billion (A8.5b) in charges associated with reducing its EV investments, including approximately $US4.2 billion ($A6.0b) in supplier settlements and contract-related costs.

Ford has similarly announced $US19.5 billion ($A27.7b) in EV-related charges as it rationalises its electric vehicle strategy, highlighting the financial consequences of production forecasts that have not materialised.

The restructuring coincides with fundamental changes to US automotive policy under President Donald Trump, whose administration has moved decisively away from the regulatory and financial incentives previously supporting electrification.

Federal tax credits worth up to $US7500 ($A10,700) for qualifying new electric vehicles were withdrawn for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, removing a substantial purchase incentive for American consumers.

In February this year, the US Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding and repealed subsequent federal motor vehicle greenhouse gas emissions standards.

The administration has also relaxed Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) requirements, with revised standards published in September substantially reducing the efficiency improvements previously required of manufacturers through the end of the decade.

Under the revised framework, average manufacturer fuel economy requirements for the 2031 model year are projected at approximately 34.9mpg (8.0L/100km), compared with 49.3mpg (5.7L/100km) under the preceding rules. Collectively, the changes reduce regulatory pressure to introduce electric vehicles and improve the commercial case for continued investment in conventional petrol-powered models.

For manufacturers already struggling to achieve profitability from EV production, the policy shift provides additional justification to redirect investment towards vehicles generating stronger immediate returns.

However, attributing GM’s decisions entirely to the Trump administration would overlook significant commercial problems that emerged well before the change of government.

Battery costs, production complexity, charging infrastructure limitations, vehicle affordability, and slower-than-forecast consumer adoption had already undermined the assumptions supporting many American EV investments.

Indeed, GM announced in late 2024 that it would withdraw from a planned $US2.5 billion ($A3.6b) battery manufacturing investment in Lansing, Michigan, before the administration’s latest policy changes took effect.

The Trump administration has therefore accelerated an existing commercial reassessment rather than initiated it.

The distinction is particularly relevant to hydrogen, where GM formally announced the termination of its next-generation Hydrotec fuel-cell development program in October 2025.

At the time, the manufacturer acknowledged that hydrogen retained potential in heavy transport, mining, and stationary power generation, but said high costs and limited infrastructure made sustainable commercial returns difficult to achieve.

GM noted that the United States had only 61 hydrogen refuelling stations, compared with more than 250,000 locations offering Level 2 or faster electric vehicle charging.

The decision subsequently contributed to the winding down of GM’s fuel-cell manufacturing joint venture with Honda, which has confirmed production of the jointly developed system will cease before the end of 2026.

Importantly, Honda has not withdrawn from hydrogen development, instead intending to pursue independently engineered next-generation fuel-cell systems.

As reported by GoAuto News, Toyota, Daimler Truck, and Volvo Group are also continuing their development of hydrogen technologies for heavy commercial vehicles, suggesting the technology’s future may increasingly lie outside mainstream passenger transport.

For General Motors, however, the immediate commercial argument has become increasingly difficult to sustain.

The company’s decision to redirect resources away from hydrogen and reduce EV manufacturing investment reflects a preference for technologies offering more predictable demand and profitability.

Recent US sales figures illustrate the scale of the challenge.

According to Cox Automotive’s latest Kelley Blue Book estimates, Americans purchased 262,649 battery-electric vehicles during the third quarter of 2026, representing a decline of 39.5 per cent against the corresponding period last year (see table below).

Electric vehicles accounted for approximately 6.4 per cent of new light-vehicle sales, compared with more than 10 per cent during the record-setting September quarter of 2025.

However, the year-on-year comparison is distorted by the rush to purchase electric vehicles before federal incentives expired.

Sales actually increased 6.1 per cent against the second quarter of 2026, suggesting the market may be stabilising at a lower level rather than continuing an uninterrupted decline.

The divergence between manufacturers is equally revealing.

Tesla remains the dominant player in the American EV market, while Rivian, Toyota, and Subaru have recorded stronger results, demonstrating that demand continues where products meet customer expectations.

Conversely, EV sales for Chevrolet and Ford have declined sharply, reflecting both changing demand and adjustments to their respective product portfolios.

The broader US market is also showing renewed interest in hybrid vehicles, which offer fuel economy improvements without requiring consumers to adopt external charging infrastructure.

For American manufacturers, that creates an increasingly complicated investment decision.

Conventional petrol and hybrid vehicles may offer the strongest immediate financial returns, particularly under the administration’s revised regulatory framework, yet international competitors continue investing heavily in battery technology, electric platforms, and more efficient manufacturing methods. European and Asian manufacturers are advancing electric vehicle development for markets where emissions requirements remain comparatively stringent, and consumer adoption continues to grow.

Perhaps the greatest long-term consequence of America’s retreat from electrification is the opportunity it presents to Chinese manufacturers, which already dominate global electric vehicle and battery production.

According to the International Energy Agency, China accounted for almost three-quarters of global electric car manufacturing in 2025 and more than 80 per cent of battery cell production, while Chinese manufacturers supplied approximately 60 per cent of electric vehicles sold worldwide.

With American manufacturers scaling back investment and domestic policy increasingly favouring conventional powertrains, China has further opportunity to consolidate its technological and manufacturing advantages.

The implications extend well beyond the United States, particularly in export markets such as Australia, where Chinese manufacturers are expanding rapidly and established brands face increasingly stringent emissions requirements.

While US tariffs may protect American manufacturers domestically, they offer little competitive advantage in international markets, where Chinese companies continue to improve battery technology, reduce production costs and expand their product portfolios.

The concern is that a prolonged reduction in American investment could leave its manufacturers increasingly dependent on technologies developed elsewhere, potentially surrendering ground in an industry they once helped lead.

There are implications for Australia, too.

American-built vehicles sold locally must comply with Australia’s New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (NVES), irrespective of changes to US emissions regulations.

That creates potentially diverging regulatory requirements for manufacturers supplying petrol-powered pick-ups, large SUVs, and other models from North America.

It may also increase the importance of alternative powertrains and emissions-offsetting vehicles within the Australian portfolios of manufacturers heavily dependent on conventional internal combustion engines.

For hydrogen, GM’s withdrawal could leave future Australian heavy commercial vehicle development increasingly dependent on Japanese, Korean, and European manufacturers continuing to invest in fuel-cell technology.

None of this suggests electric or hydrogen propulsion has reached the end of the road.

General Motors continues to develop and sell battery-electric vehicles, while hydrogen remains under investigation for applications in which battery-electric propulsion may be less practical.

Rather, the closure and repurposing of its Detroit-area facilities illustrate the consequences of a fundamental change in manufacturing priorities.

For now, American manufacturers are concentrating on financial returns, rationalising ambitious electrification plans, and extending the commercial life of conventional powertrains.

Whether that strategy ultimately strengthens the US automotive industry or leaves it less competitive against international rivals will depend on how quickly electric vehicle demand develops in the years ahead.

What is increasingly clear is that America’s automotive transition is no longer proceeding according to the timetable once envisaged by its largest manufacturers.
