text:
After bringing hundreds of Chinese specialists to Spain, Stellantis and CATL are now organizing the reverse process. The first Spanish employees of the future battery gigafactory in Figueruelas have been sent to China to learn how to manufacture electric vehicle batteries. This is an important milestone for this 4.1-billion-euro industrial project, which also highlights a reality: Certain skills that are essential for manufacturing LFP batteries are still very rare in Europe.

After Chinese workers in Spain, Spaniards are heading to China

We told you about it last June : The construction of the future Stellantis and CATL battery plant near Zaragoza was expected to employ up to 2,000 Chinese workers. Late July, we learned that 172 Chinese specialists were already on site, with a workforce that was expected to gradually grow to 1,700 people during the most technically demanding phases.

Today, the flow of talent is moving in the opposite direction. The joint venture Contemporary Star Energy (CSE), owned equally by Stellantis and CATL, has just confirmed that its first locally recruited employees are now based in China. More specifically, these professionals have joined CATL’s industrial facilities in Xiamen, in the southeastern part of the country. Their mission? To learn directly from the Chinese teams how to manufacture the battery cells and modules that will roll off the production line at the future Spanish plant in a few months.

Announced in early September, this training program has now entered its practical phase. After a period of familiarizing participants with the facilities, Production and maintenance teams are now working directly on the production lines, alongside CATL employees.

A level of expertise that is virtually nonexistent in Europe

This trip to China is not just a training trip. It addresses a very real industry challenge: Europe still lacks experienced personnel in certain lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery manufacturing processes. Back in September, Paula Marín, director of human resources at Contemporary Star Energy, explained that the main challenge was not only to attract talent but also to develop skills «that are virtually nonexistent in Europe today.».

The manufacturing of LFP cells requires expertise in several highly technical stages, including electrode production, cell assembly, and cell formation—a critical process for preparing the batteries for use. However, these skills cannot be acquired solely in a training room. They require hands-on experience on large-scale production lines. This is precisely what CATL can offer at its Chinese plants, where this technology is already widely industrialized. For Stellantis, the transfer of expertise therefore takes place directly through China, before it can be reproduced in Spain.

These first employees will then be responsible for training their Spanish colleagues

Obviously, the goal is not to send the approximately 4,000 future employees of the gigafactory to China. The first employees currently in training will have a second mission upon their return to Figueruelas: to pass on the knowledge they have acquired to the new Spanish recruits.

Contemporary Star Energy thus aims to gradually build its own production and maintenance teams, capable of operating the plant without relying on specialists sent by CATL in the long term. In its press release dated October 22, the joint venture also noted that this immersion program includes shared cultural activities designed to strengthen relations between the Chinese and Spanish teams.

In parallel, Recruitment is already underway in Spain. Contemporary Star Energy is currently posting job openings for maintenance engineers, quality managers, and specialists in training, compliance, and risk prevention. Administrative, IT, and finance positions are also available in Zaragoza and Figueruelas. The project is therefore no longer limited to the construction of the buildings: the organization of the future plant is also beginning to take shape.

A €4.1 billion plant that is strategic for future electric Fiats

As a reminder, the Figueruelas Gigafactory represents an announced investment of 4.1 billion euros, with a production capacity of up to 50 GWh per year. The facility is set to become one of Europe’s leading manufacturing centers for LFP batteries, a technology that is less expensive than NMC batteries and particularly promising for reducing the price of electric cars.

title: How trade policy could help finance the energy transition

Within carefully defined limits, high-integrity international carbon credits could provide an additional source of transition finance.
Carbon finance can improve the economic viability of investments that reduce emissions but remain difficult to fund through conventional sources alone.

text:
By Damilola Ogunbiyi, CEO and Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Sustainable Energy for All, and Margaret Kim, CEO of Gold Standard

Climate change does not stop at national borders. A tonne of emissions avoided in one country has the same value to the atmosphere as a tonne avoided anywhere else. That simple fact should shape the way governments approach climate-related trade measures.

The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, known as CBAM, has a legitimate purpose. It seeks to ensure that European producers acting on emissions are not placed at a disadvantage against imports made under less stringent carbon rules. It is also intended to prevent high-emitting production from simply moving beyond Europe’s borders.

Its success, however, will depend on what it achieves beyond Europe.

For exporters in developing economies, the barriers to lower-carbon production are often practical and financial. Clean electricity may be limited or unreliable. Investment capital can be expensive. Industrial facilities may need modernisation, while systems for measuring and reporting emissions are still developing. These are difficult conditions in which to absorb new compliance costs.

If CBAM is seen only as the price of entering the European market, it risks being treated as a tariff under another name. That would create friction between trading partners and do little to speed up the wider transition that climate action requires.

There is a more useful direction available. CBAM could help mobilise investment in cleaner production, rather than simply collecting payment at the border.

The EU recently recognised a role for high-quality international credits in meeting its post-2030 climate objectives. The next question is how those credits should be integrated in a way that supports both environmental integrity and sustainable development.

Within carefully defined limits, high-integrity international carbon credits could provide an additional source of transition finance. Carbon finance can improve the economic viability of investments that reduce emissions but remain difficult to fund through conventional sources alone. It can help exporters and their European customers support verified emissions reductions while investments in cleaner factories, supply chains, energy systems and enabling infrastructure are put in place.

Article 6 of the Paris Agreement provides an important framework for this cooperation. It enables countries to authorise and transparently account for emissions reductions transferred internationally, helping to prevent double counting while aligning carbon finance with national climate priorities. Used effectively, Article 6 can create a bridge between international demand for high-integrity credits and the investment needs of developing economies.

This would require firm guardrails. Direct reductions from industrial processes and electricity use must remain central to the transition. Carbon credits should not replace companies’ own decarbonisation efforts. Any credits recognised under CBAM or the EU’s wider climate framework should represent genuine and additional emissions reductions; be independently verified and transparently tracked; avoid double counting; and meet robust social and environmental safeguards.

The detailed criteria for eligible international credits have not yet been defined. This creates an opportunity to develop practical rules that maintain the highest standards of environmental integrity while enabling carbon finance to reach the countries and sectors where the transition is hardest to fund.

Done well, this approach could channel private capital into areas central to long-term decarbonisation: renewable power, energy efficiency, cleaner industrial processes, distributed energy and stronger electricity networks. It could also help countries build the institutional capacity, emissions data and project pipelines required to participate effectively in international carbon markets.

The wider development context matters. Nearly 600 million people in Africa still lack access to electricity. Countries need to lower emissions while also expanding access to reliable, affordable energy and creating the industrial base on which jobs and prosperity depend. These aims should reinforce one another.

Europe has an opportunity to show that climate-linked trade measures can support that shared agenda. A CBAM that recognises genuine action, supports investment and creates credible pathways for exporters to decarbonise would be stronger climate policy. It would also be more likely to earn the cooperation needed for it to work.

As the EU develops detailed rules for the use of high-quality international credits within its wider climate framework, there is an opportunity to ensure those rules strengthen both industrial competitiveness and sustainable development.

Trade policy cannot solve the energy transition by itself. It can, though, help direct finance towards the places where cleaner growth is hardest to fund and most urgently needed.

USC is built and ready: the Satellite Ion Exchange ("IX") Plant and first production wellfield are constructed and already expensed. Uranium extraction is expected to begin shortly after receipt of the PAA, supplying uranium-loaded resin feed to the Company's fully licensed Rosita Central Processing Plant ("CPP").

Alta Mesa PAA-8 and PAA-3 extension continue to work their way through TCEQ technical review and the wellfields remain on schedule as announced in our Q2 report with final permitting expected by the end of the year for PAA3 Extension and early in the new year for PAA8. Together, these three production areas are expected to renew enCore's extraction growth profile into 2027.

We are prepared to initiate injection and recovery operations at Upper Spring Creek as soon as the final permit is received. At Upper Spring Creek, the initial designed capacity of the plant and first wellfield are constructed with a large majority of these expenses now behind us. All that is remaining now is a final review process of the permit along with the approval of our disposal well completion report. PAA-8 and the PAA-3 Extension at Alta Mesa are following the same path. These are the wellfields that support our improved extraction outlook for 2027, and we look forward to bringing them online."

Upper Spring Creek PAA-1: Final Authorization Expected Within Weeks

A PAA is the TCEQ authorization that permits ISR uranium extraction within a defined wellfield area. Receipt of USC PAA-1 will allow enCore to begin ISR operations at Upper Spring Creek, the largest satellite facility the Company has built to date. The USC PAA-1 application was submitted in May 2025 and progressed through the TCEQ's administrative review, a technical review that included seven revision cycles, and two public notice periods. Key milestones are summarized below:

Following the close of the notice period, the permit requires a final authorization signature from the TCEQ. Upon receipt, the Company expects to commence uranium extraction from the first USC wellfield, with loaded resin trucked to the Rosita CPP for processing into yellowcake.

To support optimal production, the USC project also requires TCEQ operational approval of its Waste Disposal Well ("WDW"), which will handle the bleed stream from ISR production operations. The WDW has been constructed and is in final testing and TCEQ review.

The 100% Company-owned Project consists of a Satellite IX Plant and wellfield and is a key component of enCore's larger South Texas Uranium Project. This satellite facility will operate in conjunction with multiple future potential production units within the historic Clay West uranium district. The Project was previously held by Signal Equities LLC, which previously had licensed and permitted the property including the aquifer exemption as an ISR uranium project prior to 2020. The Company acquired the Project in December 2020. The uranium-mineralized sands at the Project lie within the Oakville Formation at depths typically between 300 and 450 feet below surface, allowing for efficient and economical uranium recovery with ISR methods.

text:
Experiencing exceptionally warm weather influences voting behaviour across Europe, with hot days heightening climate concerns and resulting in more votes for Green parties, according to a study by the Austria-based International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), published in the scientific journal PNAS.

The authors analysed data from the European Social Survey, across 25 European countries between 2012 and 2022. They found a link between the number of unusually warm days voters experience before an election and an increased sense of responsibility for climate change, worries about its effects and support for Green parties as well as those parties willing to enter coalitions with them.

Polls show that climate change is currently not a top concern among the EU population, but researchers have generally found no broad rejection of climate action among European voters – though how costs are distributed shapes support.

“Our analysis shows that firsthand experiences of extreme temperatures can shift attitudes and voting behaviour, particularly among groups that are generally less concerned about climate change,” said author Jonas Peisker.

Men with lower levels of education show the greatest shift in voting behaviour following heatwaves, although women and people with higher education remain more likely overall to hold pro-environmental views and vote Green, IIASA said. Workers in the services sector adjusted their voting behaviour more than those in agriculture or manufacturing. Meanwhile, in regions where decarbonisation could worsen economic inequalities, such as those with greenhouse-gas intensive industries, the effect was much weaker.

“The study makes an important contribution to the question of whether, and to what extent, people respond politically to their direct experience of extreme weather events,” Franziska Quoß, a research associate at the Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, told the Science Media Center Germany.

The authors called for policies to support regions that are relatively disadvantaged in the transition away from fossil fuels, with communication highlighting the real-world impacts of climate change and focused on groups that are less engaged. “Exacerbating economic inequalities across and within regions in the process of decarbonisation is likely to further alienate people from a pro-environmental agenda,” said author Roman Hoffmann.

title: US renewables are outpacing total electricity growth, according to EIA data
description:
On October 23, 2026, the EIA published its monthly Electric Power Monthly report, which covers data through August 2026.
In the year-to-date cumulative figures since January, output from coal-fired plants is falling sharply, while output from gas-fired and nuclear plants is rising only slightly.
Capacity additions concentrated in renewables On installed capacity, the analysis highlights the gap between renewable capacity additions and the net change in fossil and nuclear plants over the past year.
Coal capacity is falling, gas capacity is rising and nuclear capacity is unchanged.
The ratio between renewable additions and the net change in fossil and nuclear plants therefore concerns installed power, not electricity delivered.
text:
Renewable energy is growing in the US power system far faster than total generation, according to an analysis by the SUN DAY Campaign based on statistics from the Energy Information Administration (EIA), the statistical agency of the Department of Energy. On October 23, 2026, the EIA published its monthly Electric Power Monthly report, which covers data through August 2026. In the year-to-date cumulative figures since January, output from coal-fired plants is falling sharply, while output from gas-fired and nuclear plants is rising only slightly. Battery storage power is also increasing, as shown by battery commissioning in Australia or the storage deployment by Madison with CORE Electric Cooperative, but it returns electricity without producing it.

A year-to-date total, not a summer snapshot

These results should be read as a cumulative total since the start of the year. From one monthly edition to the next, the renewable share of cumulative generation was higher in the first half than at the end of August. Annual growth in renewable generation peaked at mid-year before easing.

The decline in coal-fired output also eased over the same period. The reasons for these movements are not documented. The end-of-August value is therefore neither a record nor a decline for renewables.

Capacity additions concentrated in renewables

On installed capacity, the analysis highlights the gap between renewable capacity additions and the net change in fossil and nuclear plants over the past year. Renewables, led by utility-scale solar, account for most of the additions. Coal capacity is falling, gas capacity is rising and nuclear capacity is unchanged.

According to data that were not re-checked against the primary tables, utility-scale solar grew more slowly over the recent period than in the previous year. Wind, by contrast, accelerated markedly. The Department of Energy has also issued emergency orders that delayed coal plant closures.

Comparing capacity is not the same as comparing energy. A solar or wind plant runs at full power only a fraction of the time, whereas nuclear, gas or coal plants can operate at high output for much longer. The ratio between renewable additions and the net change in fossil and nuclear plants therefore concerns installed power, not electricity delivered.

EIA projections and the SUN DAY Campaign's assumption

One-year projections for large installations, of at least 1 megawatt (MW), come from the EIA. They rest on plans declared by developers and operators. The agency publishes no projection for small-scale solar, whose capacity is estimated rather than measured.

The SUN DAY Campaign, a nonprofit founded in 1992 and led by Ken Bossong, made an assumption to fill that gap. The assumption produces the analysis's most striking totals, including a projected overtaking of gas-fired plants by renewables by August 2027. The organization advocates a rapid transition to sustainable energy, which calls for distinguishing its extrapolations from the data published by the EIA, led since September 25, 2025 by Tristan Abbey.

title: GM plant closures expose US electrification retreat - GoAutoNews Premium

Indeed, GM announced in late 2024 that it would withdraw from a planned $US2.5 billion ($A3.6b) battery manufacturing investment in Lansing, Michigan, before the administration’s latest policy changes took effect.
Electric vehicles accounted for approximately 6.4 per cent of new light-vehicle sales, compared with more than 10 per cent during the record-setting September quarter of 2025.

text:
GENERAL Motors’ decision to close one Michigan manufacturing facility and consider alternative uses for another provides further evidence of a significant retreat from electric and hydrogen vehicle investment in the United States, as the Trump administration continues dismantling policies intended to accelerate automotive electrification.

The latest developments affect two facilities near Detroit, including the Brownstown Battery Assembly plant, which GM will reportedly decommission when its lease expires in mid-2027. The 480,000-square-foot (44,593 square metre) facility has been involved in the production of battery packs and electric drive components for vehicles including the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray and Cadillac Celestiq, while approximately 80,000 square feet of the premises supported the company’s hydrogen fuel-cell joint venture with Honda.

According to US publication Automotive News, the facility’s workforce has declined from approximately 300 employees at its peak to fewer than a dozen, with remaining workers offered positions at nearby GM operations under existing United Auto Workers (UAW) agreements.

GM has also assumed the long-term lease of a separate 300,000-square-foot (27,871 square metre) Detroit facility originally intended to manufacture hydrogen fuel cells through a partnership with automotive supplier Piston Automotive.

That project, announced with a proposed investment of $US55.0 million ($A78.2m), was expected to create approximately 150 jobs before GM abandoned its hydrogen development program.

The company is now evaluating alternative uses for the premises, although no replacement manufacturing activity has been announced. The closures represent another chapter in the restructuring of GM’s alternative-powertrain investments, following a series of production reductions, cancelled manufacturing projects, and substantial financial write-downs.

They also raise questions about the longer-term direction of America’s automotive industry, particularly as manufacturers attempt to balance immediate profitability with the need to remain competitive in an increasingly electrified global market.

GM was previously among the industry’s strongest advocates of electrification, having outlined an ambition to eliminate tailpipe emissions from its new light-duty vehicle portfolio by 2035.

That ambition underpinned billions of dollars in manufacturing and battery technology investment, including new facilities, vehicle platforms, and supply agreements intended to support substantially higher electric vehicle sales.

However, consumer demand has failed to develop at the rate originally anticipated, leaving manufacturers with excess production capacity and investments increasingly difficult to justify. In January, GM disclosed a further $US6.0 billion (A8.5b) in charges associated with reducing its EV investments, including approximately $US4.2 billion ($A6.0b) in supplier settlements and contract-related costs.

Ford has similarly announced $US19.5 billion ($A27.7b) in EV-related charges as it rationalises its electric vehicle strategy, highlighting the financial consequences of production forecasts that have not materialised.

The restructuring coincides with fundamental changes to US automotive policy under President Donald Trump, whose administration has moved decisively away from the regulatory and financial incentives previously supporting electrification.

Federal tax credits worth up to $US7500 ($A10,700) for qualifying new electric vehicles were withdrawn for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, removing a substantial purchase incentive for American consumers.

In February this year, the US Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding and repealed subsequent federal motor vehicle greenhouse gas emissions standards.

The administration has also relaxed Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) requirements, with revised standards published in September substantially reducing the efficiency improvements previously required of manufacturers through the end of the decade.

Under the revised framework, average manufacturer fuel economy requirements for the 2031 model year are projected at approximately 34.9mpg (8.0L/100km), compared with 49.3mpg (5.7L/100km) under the preceding rules. Collectively, the changes reduce regulatory pressure to introduce electric vehicles and improve the commercial case for continued investment in conventional petrol-powered models.

For manufacturers already struggling to achieve profitability from EV production, the policy shift provides additional justification to redirect investment towards vehicles generating stronger immediate returns.

However, attributing GM’s decisions entirely to the Trump administration would overlook significant commercial problems that emerged well before the change of government.

Battery costs, production complexity, charging infrastructure limitations, vehicle affordability, and slower-than-forecast consumer adoption had already undermined the assumptions supporting many American EV investments.

Indeed, GM announced in late 2024 that it would withdraw from a planned $US2.5 billion ($A3.6b) battery manufacturing investment in Lansing, Michigan, before the administration’s latest policy changes took effect.

The Trump administration has therefore accelerated an existing commercial reassessment rather than initiated it.

The distinction is particularly relevant to hydrogen, where GM formally announced the termination of its next-generation Hydrotec fuel-cell development program in October 2025.

At the time, the manufacturer acknowledged that hydrogen retained potential in heavy transport, mining, and stationary power generation, but said high costs and limited infrastructure made sustainable commercial returns difficult to achieve.

GM noted that the United States had only 61 hydrogen refuelling stations, compared with more than 250,000 locations offering Level 2 or faster electric vehicle charging.

The decision subsequently contributed to the winding down of GM’s fuel-cell manufacturing joint venture with Honda, which has confirmed production of the jointly developed system will cease before the end of 2026.

Importantly, Honda has not withdrawn from hydrogen development, instead intending to pursue independently engineered next-generation fuel-cell systems.

As reported by GoAuto News, Toyota, Daimler Truck, and Volvo Group are also continuing their development of hydrogen technologies for heavy commercial vehicles, suggesting the technology’s future may increasingly lie outside mainstream passenger transport.

For General Motors, however, the immediate commercial argument has become increasingly difficult to sustain.

The company’s decision to redirect resources away from hydrogen and reduce EV manufacturing investment reflects a preference for technologies offering more predictable demand and profitability.

Recent US sales figures illustrate the scale of the challenge.

According to Cox Automotive’s latest Kelley Blue Book estimates, Americans purchased 262,649 battery-electric vehicles during the third quarter of 2026, representing a decline of 39.5 per cent against the corresponding period last year (see table below).

Electric vehicles accounted for approximately 6.4 per cent of new light-vehicle sales, compared with more than 10 per cent during the record-setting September quarter of 2025.

However, the year-on-year comparison is distorted by the rush to purchase electric vehicles before federal incentives expired.

Sales actually increased 6.1 per cent against the second quarter of 2026, suggesting the market may be stabilising at a lower level rather than continuing an uninterrupted decline.

The divergence between manufacturers is equally revealing.

Tesla remains the dominant player in the American EV market, while Rivian, Toyota, and Subaru have recorded stronger results, demonstrating that demand continues where products meet customer expectations.

Conversely, EV sales for Chevrolet and Ford have declined sharply, reflecting both changing demand and adjustments to their respective product portfolios.

The broader US market is also showing renewed interest in hybrid vehicles, which offer fuel economy improvements without requiring consumers to adopt external charging infrastructure.

For American manufacturers, that creates an increasingly complicated investment decision.

Conventional petrol and hybrid vehicles may offer the strongest immediate financial returns, particularly under the administration’s revised regulatory framework, yet international competitors continue investing heavily in battery technology, electric platforms, and more efficient manufacturing methods. European and Asian manufacturers are advancing electric vehicle development for markets where emissions requirements remain comparatively stringent, and consumer adoption continues to grow.

Perhaps the greatest long-term consequence of America’s retreat from electrification is the opportunity it presents to Chinese manufacturers, which already dominate global electric vehicle and battery production.

According to the International Energy Agency, China accounted for almost three-quarters of global electric car manufacturing in 2025 and more than 80 per cent of battery cell production, while Chinese manufacturers supplied approximately 60 per cent of electric vehicles sold worldwide.

With American manufacturers scaling back investment and domestic policy increasingly favouring conventional powertrains, China has further opportunity to consolidate its technological and manufacturing advantages.

The implications extend well beyond the United States, particularly in export markets such as Australia, where Chinese manufacturers are expanding rapidly and established brands face increasingly stringent emissions requirements.

While US tariffs may protect American manufacturers domestically, they offer little competitive advantage in international markets, where Chinese companies continue to improve battery technology, reduce production costs and expand their product portfolios.

The concern is that a prolonged reduction in American investment could leave its manufacturers increasingly dependent on technologies developed elsewhere, potentially surrendering ground in an industry they once helped lead.

There are implications for Australia, too.

American-built vehicles sold locally must comply with Australia’s New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (NVES), irrespective of changes to US emissions regulations.

That creates potentially diverging regulatory requirements for manufacturers supplying petrol-powered pick-ups, large SUVs, and other models from North America.

It may also increase the importance of alternative powertrains and emissions-offsetting vehicles within the Australian portfolios of manufacturers heavily dependent on conventional internal combustion engines.

For hydrogen, GM’s withdrawal could leave future Australian heavy commercial vehicle development increasingly dependent on Japanese, Korean, and European manufacturers continuing to invest in fuel-cell technology.

None of this suggests electric or hydrogen propulsion has reached the end of the road.

General Motors continues to develop and sell battery-electric vehicles, while hydrogen remains under investigation for applications in which battery-electric propulsion may be less practical.

Rather, the closure and repurposing of its Detroit-area facilities illustrate the consequences of a fundamental change in manufacturing priorities.

For now, American manufacturers are concentrating on financial returns, rationalising ambitious electrification plans, and extending the commercial life of conventional powertrains.

Whether that strategy ultimately strengthens the US automotive industry or leaves it less competitive against international rivals will depend on how quickly electric vehicle demand develops in the years ahead.

What is increasingly clear is that America’s automotive transition is no longer proceeding according to the timetable once envisaged by its largest manufacturers.

text:
The Trump Administration is set to announce easing of the federal methane regulations for oil and gas production in a bid to boost U.S. domestic energy production and lower costs for producers and consumers.

President Donald Trump is set to unveil the proposal at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, America’s biggest-oil producing state.

The top U.S. oil industry lobby, the American Petroleum Institute (API), and many oil and gas companies have long called for changes to the Biden administration’s 2024 methane emissions standards, arguing that the rules impose excessive compliance costs on producers.

The new rule would provide regulatory relief to small marginal wells producing below 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day, after many small producers have complained that the regulatory burden for complying with the methane rule is busting their economic rationale to keep producing from many of these marginal wells.

As much as 79% of all oil and gas wells in the United States are considered marginal, according to Bloomberg.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is also expected to scrap the so-called Methane Super Emitter Program, an Administration official told Bloomberg ahead of the official announcement of the new methane rule.

The program, which the EPA had already halted last year, encouraged government-approved third-party groups to help find and report large methane releases.

Earlier this month, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the Trump EPA would soon propose the next part of the agency’s comprehensive reconsideration of the Biden Administration’s 2024 oil and natural gas rules.

EPA is looking to address “widespread concerns from American energy producers and operators that the 2024 Rule is unworkable and is holding back American energy dominance,” the agency said.

“This proposal takes on many of the problems American producers and operators have raised with us. That includes the burden on marginal wells and oil and gas operators in general, the Super Emitter Program, associated gas, and control device requirements,” Zeldin said.

“Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work. They can’t do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens.”

text:
Korean battery and power equipment stocks are getting a rare lift after a long slump, as investors bet on a “blue wave” in next week’s U.S. midterm elections, a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress that could revive the clean-energy incentives the Donald Trump administration rolled back.

Shares of Samsung SDI, one of the three largest battery makers in Korea, jumped 5.07 percent to close at 508,000 won ($384) on Tuesday, far outpacing the Kospi’s 3.09 percent gain. LG Energy Solution rose 2 percent to 382,500 won and SK Innovation inched up 1.09 percent to 138,500 won.

Power equipment maker LS Electric rose 3.4 percent, and HD Hyundai Electric edged up 0.67 percent.

The rally builds on a surge on Oct. 19, when Samsung SDI jumped 11.7 percent and LG Energy Solution and SK Innovation each gained more than 7 percent as midterm hopes combined with reports that Chinese energy storage makers, squeezed by Trump-era tariffs, had effectively pulled out of the U.S. market.

Expectations have shifted sharply since September. On Polymarket, the odds of a Democratic sweep stood at about 62 percent this week, up from 50.5 percent on Sept. 1. As of Oct. 26, traders put the chance of a Democratic Senate at 65 percent, up from just 41.5 percent at the end of June, while a Democratic House, at 92 percent, seems all but certain.

On Kalshi, another prediction market, traders put the odds of a Democratic sweep at 64 percent, a split Congress at 29 percent and full Republican control at 10 percent as of Oct. 26.

A Democratic Congress would likely push to restore the repealed $7,500 EV tax credit along with credits for wind and solar power. With AI data centers driving up electricity bills, power costs have become a campaign issue, and Democrats are pitching renewables as the answer.

Morgan Stanley favors renewable energy, consumer staples and pharmaceuticals, while JPMorgan expects health insurers and clean-energy companies to benefit in a blue-wave scenario.

“In their May energy agenda, Democratic leaders pledged to restore the Inflation Reduction Act, clean-energy tax credits that Trump scaled back, simplify permitting for clean-energy projects and expand investment in transmission and energy storage,” said Kim Jae-seung, an analyst at Hyundai Motor Securities, who expects clean energy and energy storage to rebound most sharply.

“With U.S. trade barriers on Chinese goods still in place, Korean solar, green-energy and energy storage companies with U.S. production bases stand to gain the most from a Democratic sweep.”

The data center boom is already fueling North America’s energy storage market. LG Energy Solution plans to expand its North American storage capacity to 50 gigawatt-hours by the end of the year, while Samsung SDI has converted part of its U.S. production to lithium iron phosphate batteries for storage.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration expects electricity consumption to hit records for two straight years, climbing from 4.2 trillion kilowatt-hours last year to 4.3 trillion this year and 4.4 trillion next year.

Hana Securities projects battery makers’ net profit will jump 129.1 percent next year, outpacing the chip sector’s 35.6 percent.

Power equipment makers also stand to benefit as senators from both parties agreed on a bill to speed federal permitting for transmission lines, renewable projects and data centers on Sept. 30.

A Democratic Congress is expected to press for tougher rules requiring tech firms to share the cost of the power their data centers consume, which is pushing up household bills. That would be a burden for U.S. tech companies but an opportunity for Korean suppliers.

To sidestep regulation and grid-connection delays, tech companies are likely to accelerate the construction of their own substations and independent grids, lifting demand for extra-high-voltage transformers. HD Hyundai Electric, Hyosung Heavy Industries and LS Electric are Korea’s biggest suppliers of such equipment to the United States.

“With electricity prices at the center of the midterms, bipartisan permitting reform will ease the bottleneck in transmission construction,” said Julie Cho, a U.S. strategy researcher at NH Investment & Securities.

“Power equipment such as extra-high-voltage transformers is the most direct beneficiary of grid expansion, which is an opportunity for Korean manufacturers, the largest source of U.S. large-transformer imports.”

BY SARAH CHEA [chea.sarah@joongang.co.kr]

text:
Electric vehicles are starting to pull double duty. Beyond transportation, they’re being tested as flexible energy assets that can support both households and grid operations. A new pilot in Washington state offers a closer look at how utilities and automakers are exploring this shift, with early signals pointing to a broader rethink of how distributed energy resources are defined.

Led by Puget Sound Energy in collaboration with ChargeScape and several automakers, the project centers on vehicle-to-home (V2H) capabilities. The goal is straightforward: assess whether EV batteries can reliably step in during outages, ease peak demand, and give customers more control over energy costs—all without requiring major new infrastructure.

EV Batteries Move Into Distributed Energy Strategy

At the center of the pilot is bidirectional charging, which allows energy to flow both to and from the vehicle. Participants, including PSE employees using models like the Ford F-150 Lightning and Kia EV9, can draw power from their vehicles when grid conditions tighten or outages occur.

That setup effectively turns EVs into mobile storage units. For customers, the value shows up in resilience and potential cost savings—charging during lower-priced periods and using stored energy when rates spike. For utilities, the upside is different but just as relevant: a growing pool of distributed, dispatchable resources that can be tapped during peak demand.

The program also incorporates demand response elements, enabling the utility to signal when participating vehicles should reduce load or supply energy back. It marks a shift in how end users interact with the grid, moving from passive consumption toward a more active, responsive role.

A Test Case for Grid Pressure and Sector Convergence

This kind of pilot isn’t happening in a vacuum. Utilities are dealing with rising peak loads, more frequent extreme weather disruptions, and the ongoing challenge of balancing intermittent renewable generation. EV-based storage presents a potential workaround—one that builds on assets already being deployed at scale.

Rather than relying solely on centralized infrastructure, the approach leans into decentralization. If enough vehicles participate, aggregated battery capacity could function as a meaningful grid resource. The Washington project is designed to test exactly that, with a focus on real-world variables like customer behavior, interconnection processes, and billing impacts.

The involvement of ChargeScape highlights another layer: coordination between automakers and utilities. Its platform aims to standardize how EVs connect to grid programs, smoothing what has historically been a fragmented integration process.

For automakers, this opens a path to extend EV value beyond driving. Energy services—like backup power or optimized charging—become part of the offering. Utilities, meanwhile, gain access to distributed storage without owning or maintaining the hardware.

The pilot remains early-stage, but it reflects a clear directional shift. As EV adoption grows, so does their potential role in grid operations. The open question is less about technical feasibility and more about timing—how quickly regulatory frameworks, customer adoption, and interoperability standards can catch up.

text:
Taiwan’s Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) has partnered with California-based eJoule Inc. to develop mid- and high-nickel nickel-manganese-cobalt (NCM) batteries for drones, electric vehicles (EVs), autonomous robots and energy storage systems.

The collaboration combines eJoule’s single-crystal NCM cathode materials with ITRI’s expertise in electrode manufacturing and battery cell engineering. The work focuses on translating cathode material properties into cell-level performance, including rate capability, cycle life and capacity retention.

Jeffrey Kuo-Chan Chiou, ITRI’s vice president and general director of Material and Chemical Research Laboratories, said the two organizations are combining their research capabilities in battery materials and cell technologies. ITRI will tailor cell specifications and capacity to optimize electrochemical performance.

According to the partners, testing has shown that eJoule’s single-crystal NCM cathode materials maintain cycling stability and capacity retention after extended charge-discharge cycles. Their cycle life is approaching that of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, the companies said.

The development targets a key requirement for high-nickel NCM batteries: combining high energy density with longer service life and improved safety compared with conventional NCM materials. These characteristics are relevant to applications such as drones and EVs, where battery weight, operating range and durability affect system design.

eJoule operates in the United States and Taiwan. Its proprietary Dynamic Crystallization Process (DCP) produces single-crystal cathode active materials directly from solution droplets, without the conventional precursor (pCAM) stage.

The company says the process simplifies manufacturing and eliminates waste associated with precursor processing. It also allows control over chemical composition, dopant distribution and particle crystallinity. Based on this process, eJoule has developed mid- and high-nickel NCM cathode materials for high-performance battery applications.

“This collaboration brings together eJoule’s cathode material capabilities with ITRI’s expertise in electrode fabrication, cell development, and battery integration,” said Dr. Minduan Liu, vice president of eJoule Inc. “Together, we can integrate development from powder through electrode to cell, accelerating the path toward commercially viable, high-performance batteries.”

The partners plan to extend their work from material research and cell development to battery manufacturing and commercial deployment, with the aim of strengthening Taiwan’s battery supply chain and expanding access to global markets.

text:
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has identified a water dependency inside Kenya's steadiest power source. In its National Climate Resilience Assessment for Kenya, published September 25, the agency reports that four Olkaria-based geothermal plants, together holding nearly half of the country's geothermal capacity, draw cooling water from Lake Naivasha in Nakuru County. Geothermal supplied 43% of Kenya's electricity in 2024.

Energy managers weighing East African supply usually judge a geothermal project by its reservoir, which can deliver steam for decades. The cooling water is a separate matter. At Olkaria it comes from a lake shared with flower farms, towns and wildlife. In parts of East Africa, weak grid capacity already limits where factories can expand, so any strain on dependable generation carries weight beyond the plant fence.

Wet Cooling Towers Keep Kenyan Geothermal Output Steady but Tie It to Water

Most Kenyan geothermal plants cool with wet towers, according to the IEA. The design holds output steady when air temperatures swing, and it makes generation dependent on water supply. Air cooling removes most of that draw but brings its own penalty. The IEA notes that air-cooled plants such as Olkaria III can lose up to 50% of output when temperatures climb above 86°F (30°C).

That estimate traces to a 2002 conference paper from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), which modeled an air-cooled plant in the western United States and tested four ways to add limited evaporative cooling. Spraying water directly onto condenser tubes paid back fastest. The authors also warned that the method invites scaling and corrosion. The study modeled one American plant and says nothing specific about Kenya. Still, the tradeoff it describes is common to thermal generation, where the choice of technology largely decides how much water a power system consumes.

Lake Naivasha Water Use Has Been a Planning Issue Since at Least 2000

Competition for the lake is long documented. An August 2000 environmental impact assessment for Olkaria III, published by the World Bank Group's Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), named horticulture, tourism, fishing, livestock and power generation among its users. It estimated that the ten largest abstractors drew about 60 million cubic meters a year and called for the project to meter its lake water. Those findings are 26 years old and say nothing about current lake levels.

Environmental assessments cited by the IEA recommend that operators prepare contingency plans for alternative water sources and work with the lake management committee on abstraction. Neither requires new technology. Industrial operators elsewhere are reaching similar conclusions, and water supply now ranks alongside power and labor in site selection for many of them.

Geothermal Output Rose 46% in Early 2023 as Kenyan Hydropower Fell

During the last drought, the fleet proved its value. Geothermal generation climbed 46% in the first months of 2023 to offset lost hydroelectricity, the IEA reports. First-quarter figures published by trade outlet ThinkGeoEnergy put geothermal generation at about 1,506 gigawatt-hours (GWh), up from roughly 1,025 GWh a year earlier, while hydropower fell about 47%.

text:
Cook Labor Government to put downward pressure on electricity prices with Plan for Affordable Energy

Plan backed by modelling showing if government does not take action, industrial electricity costs could rise by 89 per cent

Initiatives include Renewable Energy Target of 75 per cent by 2030-31 and recently launched $150 million Made in WA Energy Affordability Investment Program

The Cook Labor Government has released its Plan for Affordable Energy, outlining how it will deliver affordable, reliable, and lower-carbon energy for business while supporting jobs, investment, and economic growth.

Developed in response to industry feedback from the government's Productivity Roundtable, the plan tackles the growing cost pressures facing Western Australia from ageing coal-fired power stations and changing energy markets.

It also responds to calls from an alliance of industry, investors, unions, and advocacy bodies for a strong Renewable Energy Target as a signal of the State's intent. Investor groups have indicated a target will help mobilise private sector investment in the projects needed to unlock new sources of affordable energy.

The plan is centred on delivering more renewable energy, backed by battery storage and flexible WA gas, to lower energy costs, strengthen the State's competitiveness, and support the industries and jobs of the future.

A key initiative is the $150 million Made in WA Energy Affordability Investment Program, which is open for applications from today and will provide low-interest loans of up to $15 million to help manufacturers install solar and battery systems and upgrade equipment to take advantage of cheaper energy.

The plan also includes:

a target of 75 per cent renewable energy generation on the South West Interconnected System by the 2030-31 financial year;

ongoing support for household solar, batteries, and electric vehicles;

continued support for WA's domestic gas reservation policy and a future gas security strategy; and

transitional measures to ensure consumers do not overpay for reserve capacity.

Modelling undertaken by the Department of Energy and Economic Diversification and assured by Boston Consulting Group demonstrates that without the initiatives outlined, energy prices paid by industry could increase by 89 per cent by 2032.

The Cook Labor Government is already delivering WA's energy transition, having increased renewables from 14 per cent of the State's energy mix in 2017 to 40 per cent in 2025, invested $2.5 billion in Clean Energy Link transmission infrastructure, and delivered more than 1,400 megawatts of grid-scale battery storage.

As WA progresses the retirement of State-owned coal-fired power generation by 2030, the plan will help avoid the increasing costs associated with operating ageing coal assets while ensuring households and businesses continue to have access to affordable and reliable power.

Comments attributed to Premier Roger Cook:

"Every Western Australian with rooftop solar knows that renewable energy is the cheapest form of energy.

"Our Plan for Affordable Energy is about getting more renewables onto the grid, so that all Western Australians can benefit from secure, more affordable energy.

"Our plan is about delivering affordable, reliable, Made in WA energy that will power the next generation of economic growth and job creation.

"By delivering more renewable energy backed by battery storage and flexible WA gas, we're building a State of Energy and putting downward pressure on power prices.

"In addition to getting more renewables into the system for the long-term, my government is building on our Residential Battery Scheme by providing low-interest loans to WA manufacturing businesses, so they can access solar, batteries, and energy-efficient equipment to keep their energy costs down in the meantime.

"Keeping energy affordable for WA manufacturers is about creating WA manufacturing jobs, but it is also about making WA-made goods including food more affordable and helping WA families with the cost of living."

Comments attributed to Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson:

"Our Plan for Affordable Energy is about backing WA jobs and WA businesses.

"We know that renewables, backed by storage and gas, is the cheapest and most reliable energy mix for Western Australia.

"That's why we're powering ahead with our support for the energy opportunities of the future and encouraging businesses to invest in WA."

text:
The Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI) has urged the National Assembly to expedite legislation and expand support for the "domestic production tax credit," which reduces taxes for domestic production of strategic export products such as semiconductors and secondary batteries. While the government plans to implement the policy in January next year, related bills remain pending in the legislature.

The KCCI announced on the 27th that it had submitted to the National Assembly the "KCCI Report on Legislative Issues," which includes 31 legislative tasks across five key sectors and 100 detailed improvement proposals. The report, published annually since 2016, aims to convey the economic sector’s legislative recommendations ahead of regular parliamentary bill reviews.

The KCCI emphasized the need for swift introduction of the domestic production tax credit and expansion of eligible items. While the government’s proposal designates six key sectors—including semiconductors, secondary batteries, and AI robot components—as beneficiaries, the KCCI argued that tax benefits should extend to finished products and components across the entire supply chain linked to these sectors. For example, it proposed including electric vehicles and low-carbon steel.

The KCCI also requested easing restrictions on overlapping tax deductions. Under the government’s plan, companies that receive a "facility investment" tax credit for building factories cannot additionally claim a "production" tax credit for products made using the same facilities. The KCCI advocated for allowing both supports while deducting only the overlapping portion.

Additionally, the KCCI proposed improvements to the "super-wide special zones" initiative, which aims to relax regulations and attract large-scale investments by grouping multiple local governments into a single economic zone. It noted that facilities requiring massive power and water, such as AI data centers, face delays due to the high costs and time needed to secure power grids and water pipelines. The KCCI called for state support in building such infrastructure and simultaneous reviews of permits, which are currently processed sequentially, to reduce project initiation times.

Other legislative recommendations included codifying the "business judgment rule" to prevent reasonable managerial decisions from being penalized as breach of trust and strengthening penalties for overseas leakage of advanced technologies.

Samsung SDI has signed another supply agreement with U.S. energy storage developer and power producer Alpha Omega Power (AOP). The agreement covers battery storage systems with a capacity of one gigawatt-hour. Combined with a contract signed in late 2025, the total agreed capacity reaches 1.5 GWh. U.S.-Made Battery Storage Systems

Under the new agreement, Samsung SDI will supply its integrated Samsung Battery Box (SBB) 1.7 energy storage system. All cells and modules are to be manufactured at the StarPlus Energy plant in Kokomo, Indiana. According to Samsung SDI, delivery is scheduled by the end of 2026.

Artificial intelligence algorithms are intended to detect anomalies early and predict battery life. For fire protection, Samsung SDI also uses technology that injects fire-extinguishing agents directly into individual battery modules.

description: LG Energy Solution is speeding up its push into the North American ESS (energy storage system) market.
text:
LG Energy Solution is speeding up its push into the North American ESS (energy storage system) market. After establishing five production hubs to expand local manufacturing capacity, the company has also recently secured new orders.
LG Energy Solution JF2 AC Link product joins Nvidia DSX Ready. /Courtesy of LG Energy Solution
According to the battery industry on the 27th, LG Energy Solution signed a contract on the 30th of the previous month to supply BESS (battery energy storage system) to Canadian ESS systems integration (SI) firm e-Zinc. Under the deal, LG Energy Solution plans to supply e-Zinc with its high-capacity LFP (lithium iron phosphate)-based "JF2 DC Link" product.
JF2 DC Link is a product that enhances efficiency and safety with capacity of up to 5.1 MWh (megawatt-hours), a modular design, and a liquid-cooling thermal management system. It integrates battery cells, modules, and racks with management, cooling, and safety equipment into a single container-type system, and it features greater convenience by allowing customers to use it by linking their preferred power conversion system (PCS).
LG Energy Solution recently became the only domestic battery company to join Nvidia's "DSX Ready" as a BESS company. DSX Ready is a qualification program that Nvidia operates for partner products and solutions that meet the relevant requirements to integrate and optimize AI factories from design to construction and operation. Only three companies worldwide have been named Nvidia BESS partners.
In the battery industry, the move is seen as showing not only battery manufacturing capability but also the advanced power control and systems integration (SI) capabilities required by AI data centers. Many interpret it as significant recognition of overwhelming technological prowess and local business capabilities in the North American AI data center market.
In August, LG Energy Solution held an opening ceremony for its plant in Lansing, Michigan, signaling full-scale operations and establishing "five major ESS production hubs in North America."
The Lansing plant is a complex manufacturing hub that produces LFP batteries for ESS and NCM (nickel, cobalt, manganese) batteries for electric vehicles, with annual cell production capacity of more than 35 GWh (gigawatt-hours). It began producing pouch-type batteries for ESS this year and plans to start mass production of prismatic LFP batteries next year.
Through three standalone production hubs in Lansing and Holland, Michigan, and the NextStar Energy plant in Ontario, Canada, as well as two joint-venture plants—L-H Battery Company in Ohio with Honda and Ultium Cells in Tennessee with GM—LG Energy Solution has built a production network capable of responding to surging ESS demand across North America. By the end of this year, it plans to secure more than 50 GWh of production capacity in North America, equal to 80% of its global ESS production capacity.
As of the end of last year, LG Energy Solution had an ESS order backlog of about 140 GWh. In the first half of this year, it also secured more than 3 trillion won in new ESS orders. It signed a series of contracts with Tesla, Terragen, Excelsior Energy Capital, EG4, and Qcells. In May, following a contract with U.S. utility DTE Energy—handling Oracle's AI data center project—for the supply of ESS batteries totaling 6 GWh, in July it also announced plans to supply batteries for the solar and ESS project of Google and Cypress Creek Renewables.
An LG Energy Solution official said, "Based on our differentiated North American local production capacity, stable supply chain, and systems integration capabilities, we will continue to secure new order opportunities in the rapidly growing North American ESS market."

text:
A solar energy facility at Toray Resin Company's Shelbyville campus has begun operations. The new facility, from Duke Energy Indiana, can generate up to 900 kilowatts of electricity to help power the plastics manufacturer's operations while offsetting carbon emissions.

The solar project is the first to come from a Duke Energy pilot program that aims to make it easier for businesses, schools and nonprofits to incorporate renewable energy sources into their energy mix.

Under Duke Energy's solar services pilot program, eligible Indiana customers can lease an on-site solar system for a period of up to 20 years. Duke Energy installs, operates, owns and maintains the system, while customers receive all of the kilowatt-hour (kWh) and solar renewable energy credit (SREC) output. Initial program capacity is limited to a total of 10 megawatts (MW) for eligible commercial and industrial customers within the Duke Energy Indiana service territory.

Duke Energy will own, operate and maintain the Blue River Solar Facility on Toray Resin's Shelbyville campus for a monthly service fee. The program provides Toray Resin with the advantages of clean energy to help power their operations, while minimizing upfront costs and maintenance obligations.

Construction on the 8-acre, ground-mounted solar project began in October 2021. The facility consists of 2,487 solar panels and is located on the east side of Toray Resin's campus.

Duke Energy also provides virtual power purchase agreements (VPPAs) — renewable energy contracts that do not involve the physical delivery of energy from the vendor to the customer.

text:
KARACHI: Pakistan’s military-owned Margalla Heavy Industries Limited (MHIL) has signed an agreement with Chinese partners and local investors to set up a $2.25 billion lithium-ion battery manufacturing plant in Rawalpindi, an official said on Monday, with production expected to begin within months of the government approving a policy for the sector, reports Arab News.

The development comes as the South Asian country seeks to reduce its reliance on imported energy technologies and develop local manufacturing capacity amid growing demand for energy storage, electric vehicles and renewable energy.

Lithium-ion batteries are central to storing electricity generated by solar and wind power and powering electric mobility, making domestic production a potential avenue for reducing import costs and attracting foreign investment.

The gigafactory’s feasibility studies have been completed and the project is awaiting approval before it could start manufacturing, according to Hamad Ali Mansoor, CEO of the Engineering Development Board (EDB), an apex government body entrusted to strengthen the engineering base in Pakistan.

“The building is ready, the machines are installed, so after the policy comes, the production will start within six to eight months,” Mansoor told Arab News, adding that Islamabad was working with Chinese and local stakeholders to invest in the multibillion-dollar project.

“They are investing $2.25 billion in Pakistan.”Located at Heavy Industries Taxila in Rawalpindi district, MHIL manufactures defence equipment, including battle tanks, armoured vehicles, unmanned drones, protective gear, compact battery energy storage system and EV buses and two-wheelers.

Arab News reached out to MHIL’s general manager for digital media, Muhammad Ameen, but he was not immediately available for comment.The development comes days after Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif approved the Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-2031, which awaits IMF approval over proposed tax incentives for Pakistan’s Electric Vehicles industry and their potential revenue implications.

After the new EV-based auto policy takes effect, EDB estimates that Pakistan’s demand for battery energy storage systems (BESS) could reach as much as to 100,000 megawatts (MW) by June 2030.

Building a local plant to manufacture lithium-ion batteries would be crucial for the cash-strapped country, which aims to shift its petrol-powered vehicles to EVs to save billions of dollars it spends every year to import fuel.

Mansoor said the battery gigafactory project was signed in July with a Chinese company he described as one of the “top-tier manufacturers in China” alongside a local private-sector investor. He would not name the Chinese and local investors now.

“They are manufacturing lithium-ion cells,” he said, adding that the facility would produce lithium-ion cells having a capacity of more than 1,000MW annually.EDB has estimated that grid stabilization alone could require 3,000-5,000MW of battery storage and that meeting the projected demand would require four to five gigafactories, each costing around $1 billion to $1.25 billion.

“In our industry, we will have up to 100,000 megawatts of battery energy storage systems. This is a very large capacity. For this, we need four to five gigafactories,” the EDB CEO said.The first factory will initially produce around 200-300 MW before reaching its planned capacity of 1,000 megawatts, according to Mansoor.

“If our economy grows by 5.0 per cent or more than 5.0 per cent of GDP (gross domestic product), then by June 2030, our demand will be up to 100,000MW,” he said.“And if our GDP grows by less than 3 percent, then our demand will be up to 80,000MW.”

Mansoor said the demand would come from households, commercial buildings, industry and electric vehicles, including two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses and trucks.The government has prepared a lithium battery manufacturing policy that was submitted to the Ministry of Industries in March and is awaiting approval, according to the official.

The plan includes four major factories, three in Punjab’s Lahore, Faisalabad and Rawalpindi divisions and one in southern city of Karachi, aimed at building domestic capacity for batteries used in electric vehicles and energy storage.

The policy would require manufacturers to export a specified percentage of production, although Mansoor declined to provide the target before the policy’s approval.“We will manufacture it in Pakistan and export it,” he said, adding that the policy incorporates international safety and performance standards.

Pakistan currently assembles around 3,000-4,000MW of batteries as well as parts like motors, controllers and chargers, but needs to move toward domestic manufacturing to avoid costly imports, according to Mansoor.“All these parts we [will] start manufacturing 100 per cent in Pakistan by next year,” he added.

text:
MANAUS, Brazil (AP) — Environmentalists, Indigenous groups and climate scientists are celebrating the reelection in Brazil of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, which brings the prospect of a continued focus on stopping the illegal cutting of the Amazon, the largest rainforest in the world.

But supporters also warned that a Congress increasingly dominated by the far right and the agribusiness caucus could undermine those efforts to protect the forest and combat climate change.

Lula defeated Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro, in Sunday’s runoff with 51.78% of the vote to 48.21%. After trailing in the first round, Lula staged a comeback to win by 4.4 million votes.

“The Amazon can breathe a sigh of relief!” said David Lapola, a Brazilian scientist and lead author of a chapter on so-called tipping points in an upcoming United Nations climate report. Scientists debate the threshold beyond which the dense, humid Amazon rainforest could shift to a drier ecosystem, with irreversible consequences for biodiversity and the climate. The forest absorbs vast amounts of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that drives global warming. About 60% of the Amazon lies in Brazil.

Flávio Bolsonaro contests the loss

Lula’s victory reflected shifts in voter support and higher turnout nationwide. In the Amazon, Indigenous communities and advocacy groups mobilized voters and, aided by court rulings last week, helped secure government transportation for those living in remote areas.

The Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil, known as APIB, was among the organizations that went to court to secure Indigenous voters’ access to the polls. Lula’s victory reflected the “strength of grassroots mobilization in defense of democracy, life and Indigenous peoples’ rights,” it said in a statement.

Flávio Bolsonaro refused to concede Monday and said he would ask the electoral court to nullify the results. He faces a high hurdle: presenting evidence of fraud sufficient to overturn Lula’s winning margin and persuading the court before the results are certified Dec. 18. Early signals from Brazil’s institutions and regional leaders, including conservative presidents who oppose Lula, suggest the outcome will be accepted at home and abroad.

Flávio Bolsonaro had pledged to pursue policies aligned with those of his father, who governed from 2019 through 2022. Deforestation surged under Jair Bolsonaro as his administration weakened environmental enforcement agencies and loosened regulations. Lula’s government last week announced the lowest Amazon deforestation rate on record.

Environmentalists express concern despite a Lula win

Lula is expected to continue efforts to curb deforestation and finance a sustainable economy through international donations as well as public and private funding. While he was the clear favorite for environmentalists, climate scientists and others who want to protect the Amazon, Lula has put forward policies that have drawn criticism. Most recently, he has supported efforts to drill for oil in offshore waters near the Amazon.

Still, Flávio Bolsonaro presented a stark choice that for many environmentalists felt would put the Amazon and Brazil’s overall environmental protections at risk. He had denied climate change while casting himself as an environmental defender. However, he offered few details on forest protection or financing, calling for “modernizing” environmental laws and giving Amazon landowners more decision-making power — proposals environmentalists warned could weaken safeguards and accelerate deforestation.

Brazil’s Climate Observatory, a nonprofit coalition of 172 organizations, welcomed Lula’s reelection but said seven in 10 incoming lawmakers oppose the climate and environmental agenda. It cited recent measures weakening pesticide rules, Indigenous land rights and environmental licensing, and urged Lula to broaden his alliances and strengthen ties with Congress.

“The goal of ending deforestation across Brazil’s biomes must be pursued relentlessly,” the group said.

Amazon Watch, a nonprofit focused on environmental protection and Indigenous rights, also welcomed Lula’s victory while warning of legislative obstacles.

“A Congress strengthened by forces seeking to open Indigenous lands to mining and weaken environmental protections remains a serious threat,” said Ana Alfinito, an Amazon Watch legal adviser.

WWF Brazil said the country’s vast biodiversity and share of the Amazon give it a strategic role in addressing climate change. It credited Lula with strengthening Brazil’s leadership through international cooperation.

“Maintaining this leadership is essential to mobilizing other countries, raising the ambition of global commitments and turning agreements into concrete action,” the organization said.

Election results bring money for forest protection

Claudio Angelo, the Climate Observatory’s head of international policy, said Lula’s reelection had already delivered a result: a $500 million pledge Monday from the Netherlands to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a Brazil-backed fund launched at last year’s U.N. climate summit in Brazil.

The initiative pays developing countries to keep forests standing but has struggled to secure an initial $10 billion by year’s end. The Dutch pledge brings commitments to $7.8 billion.

Angelo said prospective donors had put plans on hold pending the election results, calling the Dutch pledge a vote of confidence in Lula’s victory.

“There was justified concern that a Flávio Bolsonaro victory could derail the TFFF, that Brazil would pull out and the fund would miss its $10 billion target,” Angelo said.

text:
Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said.

The PM has suggested that rebuilding the UK’s industrial capacity will be central to meeting his pledge to bring “good growth in every postcode”.

John Healey, who will deliver his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, used his speech at Labour’s conference last month to promise a “new age of industrialisation”.

However, in a briefing paper seen by the Guardian, the backbenchers warn that decades of deindustrialisation and deregulation mean the government no longer has the detailed understanding of industry needed to make such a plan work.

“The state has lost capacity and has acquired a worrying set of behaviours which will inhibit reindustrialisation. The state has become less knowledgable about the state of the economy and our businesses, unable to comprehensively plan and slow to make decisions,” the paper says.

The MPs are calling on Burnham to pass a new Reindustrialisation Act, to set clear targets for creating jobs by rebuilding the country’s manufacturing capacity, and to ensure ministers are held to account against them. “If we do not plan for reindustrialisation, we cannot achieve it,” the group argues.

The briefing paper urges the PM to give the job of overseeing reindustrialisation to the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and base it at No 10 North, the Manchester outpost he established in July, which has already taken on some responsibility for growth policy.

And the paper argues that the National Wealth Fund – the arm’s length body that invests in promising businesses – should be transformed into a Reindustrialisation Development Corporation, whose primary job is to provide capital for rebuilding UK industry.

Andy MacNae, the MP for Rossendale and Darwen, who chairs the group, said: “I’ve got absolutely no doubt about Andy or John’s commitment to this, but there is a kind of inertia in government, within the civil service, within economic orthodoxy, that still says that growth policy is about cities – it’s about the places that are already doing well.”

Instead, he said, reindustrialisation must be about “delivering jobs to the places that need them most.” He added: “It’s about making things again, and it’s about making the things that give us national resilience in a turbulent world.”

He cited the government’s recent decision to nationalise British Steel, adding that reindustrialisation involved policies across government, from procurement to education.

Steve Yemm, the MP for the former mining constituency of Mansfield, said: “Countries around the world are reindustrialising, yet too many in Whitehall still treat industrial policy as dangerous nostalgia. We need the prime minister’s full backing to challenge those outdated assumptions.”

A third member of the group, Lorraine Beavers, the MP for Blackpool North and Fleetwood, said she was enthusiastic about the promise of reindustrialisation for constituencies like hers, but said: “If I have learned anything since becoming an MP two years ago, it’s that Whitehall doesn’t fix a problem unless it is told to.”

In its industrial strategy, published while Keir Starmer was prime minister, Labour identified eight sectors ripe for growth, including advanced manufacturing, clean energy and defence.

description:
The air is crisp and invigorating, apples and pumpkins are everywhere, and North Carolina is as beautiful as ever.
Just like here in North Carolina, cooperatives are powerful engines of economic growth for our whole nation.

Robert Hosford is the USDA Rural Development North Carolina state director.
text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

I love October. The air is crisp and invigorating, apples and pumpkins are everywhere, and North Carolina is as beautiful as ever.

But October isn’t just a pretty month. It’s also National Co-op Month and as the Rural Development North Carolina state director, I’m proud to shine a light on the incredible work cooperatives do in our neck of the woods.

For example, in Oxford, Piedmont Electric Membership Corporation helps provide modern equipment that will strengthen emergency response capabilities and improve quality of life for residents across rural communities in central North Carolina.

Earlier this month, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins proclaimed the 62nd anniversary of National Cooperative Month. The theme this year is “Built for this Moment,” as chosen by the National Cooperative Business Association. This theme acknowledges the electric co-ops delivering essential infrastructure to rural America, the food co-ops that support local farmers and agricultural producers, the housing co-ops creating lasting affordability and the worker co-ops preserving local businesses. It also highlights co-ops as resilient networks, working hard every day to care for communities.

Just like here in North Carolina, cooperatives are powerful engines of economic growth for our whole nation. Across the U.S., more than 30,000 cooperatives — including food, grocery, worker, retail, purchasing, utility, housing and financial cooperatives — support over 2.5 million jobs and generate roughly $650 billion in annual revenue.

Given this far-reaching impact, it is no surprise that co-ops are central to President Trump’s America First agenda to strengthen our economy and empower communities. Since the start of the Trump-Vance administration and under the leadership of Secretary Rollins, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has invested more than $18.1 billion in loans and grants to support 242 cooperatives. These investments are spurring economic development, supporting critical electric and broadband infrastructure, and paving the way for unprecedented prosperity through rural cooperatives supported by USDA Rural Development’s programs.

In our state alone, USDA has supported 10 co-ops, investing $22 million in rural communities since the beginning of this administration. In fact, in western North Carolina, Blue Ridge Electric Cooperative is partnering with Rural Development through USDA’s Rural Economic Development Loan and Grant programs, which provide funding for rural projects through local utility organizations.

Supporting cooperatives strengthens farmer profitability, expands market access and creates jobs in rural communities. It also encourages innovation and reinforces America’s leadership role in agriculture, food production and farm security. At USDA Rural Development, we will be celebrating the co-ops we support throughout the month of October, because they work so hard on behalf of people in rural communities across North Carolina. We invite you to join our celebration on social media @RDNorthCarolina.

USDA Rural Development offers a variety of financial assistance and services to assist rural businesses, including cooperatives and agricultural producers. For more information on cooperatives, visit USDA Rural Development Cooperative Services.

Robert Hosford is the USDA Rural Development North Carolina state director.
