text:
A pair of solar carports, a battery storage system and an electric vehicle charging station will increase the renewable energy capacity of Rhode Island’s Capitol Hill campus to 1 megawatt in total, the state Office of Energy Resources announced Monday.

The $9.3 million project is funded through a $4.5 million federal earmark and will be matched with state funds through revenue from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, said Robert Beadle, a spokesperson for the energy department.

The state has also secured an immediate federal tax credit deduction equal to 5% of the project costs, with the promise of additional federal tax credits equal to between 30% and 40% of total costs in tax year 2028.

“By leveraging federal funding and tax credits, we’re bringing innovative solar, battery storage and electric vehicle charging technologies to state facilities while making smart investments in Rhode Island’s energy future,” Gov. Dan McKee said in a statement.

Construction is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The parking lot solar panels, battery storage and charging station must be operational by the end of the year to secure the federal tax credits administered through the Internal Revenue Service. Once complete, the projects, together with existing rooftop solar panels on state buildings, will provide enough solar-powered electricity to power roughly 190 homes per year while helping meet state decarbonization mandates.

“This is a forward-looking project that is both economically and environmentally responsible,” said U.S. Sen. Jack Reed, who secured the $4.5 million federal earmark.

The projects also advance the state’s Lead by Example program, which aims to spur private investments in renewable energy infrastructure by starting with solar panels, battery storage, and charging stations on state and municipal-owned buildings and public schools. Since the 2015 executive order establishing the state-led program, the Office of Energy Resources has invested more than $48 million into 185 projects, said Chris Kearns, the state’s acting energy commissioner.

Kearns hailed the upcoming projects for the parking lots of the Rhode Island Department of Administration and Department of Health as among the largest to date. The work will also help to reduce energy costs, Kearn said in a statement.

There are already 900 rooftop solar panel on Smith Hill buildings, including on the departments of transportation, health and administration buildings, as well as energy-efficient lighting upgrades at the State House and Department of Transportation buildings.

Rising energy bills remain a top concern among residents, despite seasonal bill credits meant to offset the seasonal spike in electricity prices. Two of the three gubernatorial candidates, independent Ken Block and Republican Aaron Guckian, have called for delaying the deadlines for state climate change mandates to reduce costs for customers, a move which Gov. Dan McKee tried unsuccessfully to incorporate in the state’s fiscal 2027 budget.

Democrat Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who defeated McKee in the Sept. 9 primary, has insisted the state should “lean in” to renewables as a more stable and cost-effective energy solution, without changing decarbonization deadlines in state law.

The new Capitol Hill project is expected to save $3.3 million in avoided energy costs, reducing carbon emissions by 12,700 metric tons over the lifetime of the project, according to state analysis.

Since 2021, state agencies have produced or purchased credits to offset 100% of electricity needs across state facilities.

Maryland Governor Wes Moore has introduced a program to help residents lower electricity costs by increasing clean energy generation efforts in the state.

"Megawatts for Maryland" is a $200 million project developed and administrated by the Maryland Energy Administration (MEA), said a press release issued by the governor's office.

"We're using every tool at our disposal to bring Marylanders relief as energy costs skyrocket in our region and across the country," said Governor Moore. "This program will tackle rising electricity demand with cleaner, cheaper, in-state energy generation that will drive down costs for the long-term."

The program will give grants to energy and storage developers. Grants will help with costs relating to the development and construction of grid-scale renewable energy and energy storage projects. The Moore administration says the initiative will help fill gaps left when the Trump administration canceled investment tax credits from the Inflation Reduction Act.

"Megawatts for Maryland" includes a two-stage process for determining eligible applications. In stage 1, an applicant can submit a preliminary application to see if they are eligible. If they are accepted, they then move to stage 2, where they can submit a bid price with additional documentation, the release said.

The application deadline for stage 1 is Nov. 30, while the one for stage 2 is Jan. 22, 2027. Only eligible stage 1 applicants may submit a bid for stage 2.

"Maryland families and businesses need reliable electricity at prices they can afford," said Maryland House of Delegates Speaker Joseline A. Peña-Melnyk. "That's why we made increasing our state's energy supply a central part of the Utility RELIEF Act."

The Moore-Miller administration issued an executive order on responsible data center development in Maryland in September that guaranteed that ratepayers are protected from energy price hikes caused by data centers.

"Lowering costs for Maryland families remains our top priority," said Senate President Bill Ferguson.

description: Five decades ago, he charted two paths for energy use in the US. His soft path rightly emphasized efficiency and renewables but underestimated the importance of electricity.
text:
(HOUSTON, TEXAS) Hurricane Belle was barreling toward New England in August 1976 when an editor from Foreign Affairs called. Physicist Amory Lovins took the call on a payphone in a shack in the Maine woods, where he spent summers as a camp guide.
“If it happened to hit that area, the wires would be down with trees on them for weeks, so we’d miss the press date,” Lovins told me in a 2025 interview. The lines held up as he and the editor worked through final edits on a 14-hour phone call.
Published in October 1976 in the wake of the 1973 oil crisis, “
Energy Strategy: The Road Not Taken?
” drew more reprint requests
than any Foreign Affairs article in decades
.

Two U.S. Senate committees called on the 29-year-old
Lovins to testify about his ideas that December
. The following year, Lovins met with President Jimmy Carter and his top energy advisers in the Oval Office and expanded his article into a book, “
Soft Energy Paths: Toward a Durable Peace
.” The New York Times chronicled the “raging debate” sparked by Lovins, noting that “
even his critics concede that he is something of a genius
.”
Amory Lovins, left, shakes hands with then-President Jimmy Carter in the Oval Office in 1977.
Rocky Mountain Institute
The article charted two paths for the future of energy. One, which Lovins called the “hard” path, required ever more energy supply to meet inexorably rising demand. With U.S. oil production
in decline since 1970
, coal and uranium would supply most growth by generating electricity at large, remote facilities.
Lovins instead championed a “soft” path that put people’s wants ahead of supplies. “
People do not want electricity or oil
… but rather comfortable rooms, light, vehicular motion … and other real things,” he wrote.
The soft path would meet those wants with a diverse array of renewable energy resources, sourced locally where possible. Heating would come from solar collectors and waste heat. Vehicles would be made more efficient and run on biofuels. Wind power would be used to compress air to drive machinery. Oil and gas would be reserved for making chemicals. Lovins hoped that matching form with function could enable U.S. energy use to plateau and then decline so that it could be supplied renewably by 2025.
When Lovins wrote his article, most electricity was generated inefficiently from fossil fuels or uranium, while wind and solar power remained prohibitively expensive. “Photovoltaics were out of bounds intellectually; that gets you laughed out of the room, and I didn’t actually think they would get cheap enough,” Lovins told me in 2025.
Burning or fissioning a fuel to generate electricity inefficiently, transmitting it far away, and turning it back into low-grade heat for homes was “
like cutting butter with a chainsaw
,” Lovins wrote. Thus, his soft path included only a narrowing lane for electricity, steering it toward essential purposes such as electronics, subways, lighting and smelting. Lovins posited that “
an affluent industrial economy
could advantageously operate with no central power stations at all,” though he did not advocate going that far.
The road taken
They were paths, not predictions, and neither path foretold the road actually taken in the 50 years since. Unlike most forecasts from the era, which projected ever-rising demand, the soft path foresaw that
total U.S. energy use
could plateau, and
it almost exactly matched the actual level in 2000
. However, Lovins and his contemporaries failed to foresee the drilling advances that have kept oil and gas dominant.
As an
environmental engineer
completing a book about the visions that are shaping energy realities and opportunities around the world, I think Lovins got it half right about how to secure sustainable energy. Efficiency and renewable energy are indeed essential, but clean electricity and electrification are proving far more important than Lovins expected.
Critics argued
that Lovins underestimated the costs of clean technologies and overstated what they could achieve. In fact, opportunities for clean energy have been transformed by unanticipated plunges in the costs of
wind and solar electricity
,
battery storage
and
LED lighting
.
For example, the price per watt of solar panels tumbled from
around US$100 in current dollars in 1976
to
around 10 cents in global markets today
and a President Donald Trump-set minimum price of
38 cents for panels imported to the United States
.
The soft path goes electric
Modern technologies turn the chainsaw analogy on its head by making electrification the soft path to reducing energy use.
Heat pumps
supply several times as much heat as the electricity they consume.
Induction stoves
cook food far more efficiently than gas flames. And
electric vehicles
are a few times more efficient than gasoline ones.
Powered by renewable electricity, from local resources like the solar panels on Lovins’ roof and mine, or from larger solar, wind and geothermal facilities, these technologies can slash fossil fuel use. A diversity of resources blended with high-voltage transmission and storage can make
clean electricity available around the clock
.

It was the induction stove that he showed off first, boiling water at lightning speed, then the batteries in the utility room. Two electric cars were charging outside. The wood stoves had been retired.
Former colleagues of Lovins now advocate an “
electrotech revolution
” centered on renewable electricity and increased electrification. Lovins told me he embraces their work but is pushing them to add integrative design — optimizing efficiency by redesigning whole systems — a
subject he teaches at Stanford
.
I believe Lovins was right to focus on matching resources with people’s actual needs. Renewable electrification and efficiency provide the softest path to doing so for the next 50 years.

description: Five decades ago, he charted two paths for energy use in the US. His soft path rightly emphasized efficiency and renewables but underestimated the importance of electricity.
text:
(HOUSTON, TEXAS) Hurricane Belle was barreling toward New England in August 1976 when an editor from Foreign Affairs called. Physicist Amory Lovins took the call on a payphone in a shack in the Maine woods, where he spent summers as a camp guide.
“If it happened to hit that area, the wires would be down with trees on them for weeks, so we’d miss the press date,” Lovins told me in a 2025 interview. The lines held up as he and the editor worked through final edits on a 14-hour phone call.
Published in October 1976 in the wake of the 1973 oil crisis, “
Energy Strategy: The Road Not Taken?
” drew more reprint requests
than any Foreign Affairs article in decades
.

Two U.S. Senate committees called on the 29-year-old
Lovins to testify about his ideas that December
. The following year, Lovins met with President Jimmy Carter and his top energy advisers in the Oval Office and expanded his article into a book, “
Soft Energy Paths: Toward a Durable Peace
.” The New York Times chronicled the “raging debate” sparked by Lovins, noting that “
even his critics concede that he is something of a genius
.”
Amory Lovins, left, shakes hands with then-President Jimmy Carter in the Oval Office in 1977.
Rocky Mountain Institute
The article charted two paths for the future of energy. One, which Lovins called the “hard” path, required ever more energy supply to meet inexorably rising demand. With U.S. oil production
in decline since 1970
, coal and uranium would supply most growth by generating electricity at large, remote facilities.
Lovins instead championed a “soft” path that put people’s wants ahead of supplies. “
People do not want electricity or oil
… but rather comfortable rooms, light, vehicular motion … and other real things,” he wrote.
The soft path would meet those wants with a diverse array of renewable energy resources, sourced locally where possible. Heating would come from solar collectors and waste heat. Vehicles would be made more efficient and run on biofuels. Wind power would be used to compress air to drive machinery. Oil and gas would be reserved for making chemicals. Lovins hoped that matching form with function could enable U.S. energy use to plateau and then decline so that it could be supplied renewably by 2025.
When Lovins wrote his article, most electricity was generated inefficiently from fossil fuels or uranium, while wind and solar power remained prohibitively expensive. “Photovoltaics were out of bounds intellectually; that gets you laughed out of the room, and I didn’t actually think they would get cheap enough,” Lovins told me in 2025.
Burning or fissioning a fuel to generate electricity inefficiently, transmitting it far away, and turning it back into low-grade heat for homes was “
like cutting butter with a chainsaw
,” Lovins wrote. Thus, his soft path included only a narrowing lane for electricity, steering it toward essential purposes such as electronics, subways, lighting and smelting. Lovins posited that “
an affluent industrial economy
could advantageously operate with no central power stations at all,” though he did not advocate going that far.
The road taken
They were paths, not predictions, and neither path foretold the road actually taken in the 50 years since. Unlike most forecasts from the era, which projected ever-rising demand, the soft path foresaw that
total U.S. energy use
could plateau, and
it almost exactly matched the actual level in 2000
. However, Lovins and his contemporaries failed to foresee the drilling advances that have kept oil and gas dominant.
As an
environmental engineer
completing a book about the visions that are shaping energy realities and opportunities around the world, I think Lovins got it half right about how to secure sustainable energy. Efficiency and renewable energy are indeed essential, but clean electricity and electrification are proving far more important than Lovins expected.
Critics argued
that Lovins underestimated the costs of clean technologies and overstated what they could achieve. In fact, opportunities for clean energy have been transformed by unanticipated plunges in the costs of
wind and solar electricity
,
battery storage
and
LED lighting
.
For example, the price per watt of solar panels tumbled from
around US$100 in current dollars in 1976
to
around 10 cents in global markets today
and a President Donald Trump-set minimum price of
38 cents for panels imported to the United States
.
The soft path goes electric
Modern technologies turn the chainsaw analogy on its head by making electrification the soft path to reducing energy use.
Heat pumps
supply several times as much heat as the electricity they consume.
Induction stoves
cook food far more efficiently than gas flames. And
electric vehicles
are a few times more efficient than gasoline ones.
Powered by renewable electricity, from local resources like the solar panels on Lovins’ roof and mine, or from larger solar, wind and geothermal facilities, these technologies can slash fossil fuel use. A diversity of resources blended with high-voltage transmission and storage can make
clean electricity available around the clock
.
When I visited Lovins’ ultra-efficient, solar-powered Colorado home in 2025, electrification took center stage. It was the induction stove that he showed off first, boiling water at lightning speed, then the batteries in the utility room. Two electric cars were charging outside. The wood stoves had been retired.
Former colleagues of Lovins now advocate an “
electrotech revolution
” centered on renewable electricity and increased electrification. Lovins told me he embraces their work but is pushing them to add integrative design — optimizing efficiency by redesigning whole systems — a
subject he teaches at Stanford
.
I believe Lovins was right to focus on matching resources with people’s actual needs. Renewable electrification and efficiency provide the softest path to doing so for the next 50 years.

text:
The U.S. zero-emission bus (ZEB) market is continuing to expand, with adoption spreading well beyond the early coastal markets that initially drove deployment.

New data from CALSTART’s Zeroing in on ZEBs market update shows transit agencies across the country increasing orders for battery-electric and hydrogen fuel cell buses as part of broader fleet modernization and emissions reduction strategies.

As of July 2025, the national pipeline includes 8,116 full-size zero-emission buses that are funded, ordered, delivered, or already operating. That figure represents a 16% increase compared with July 2024, despite ongoing procurement challenges and long manufacturing lead times.

Adoption Expands Across the U.S. Transit Landscape

California remains the largest market for zero-emission buses, but adoption is becoming more geographically diverse as transit agencies across the country begin integrating the technology into long-term fleet planning.

According to the report, California currently has 1,933 battery-electric buses and 690 hydrogen fuel cell buses either deployed or in the procurement pipeline. Several other states are also building sizable fleets.

New York ranks second nationally with 829 zero-emission buses, followed by Washington with 521. Adoption is also growing in the Southeast, with Florida reaching 519 buses, while Massachusetts has 292 vehicles in its pipeline.

Year-over-year growth has been particularly strong in several Midwestern and Western states, including Indiana, Wisconsin, Illinois, Washington, and California. The broader geographic spread suggests zero-emission buses are increasingly becoming part of mainstream fleet planning rather than limited pilot deployments.

Battery-Electric Buses Lead While Hydrogen Deployment Grows

Battery-electric buses continue to represent the majority of the zero-emission market. Nationwide, 7,261 battery-electric buses have been funded, ordered, delivered, or deployed, reflecting a 13% increase year over year.

Transit agencies cite improvements in battery technology, expanding charging infrastructure, and the relative maturity of the platform as key factors supporting continued growth.

Hydrogen fuel cell buses remain a smaller segment of the market but are expanding more rapidly. The report shows 855 fuel cell buses nationwide, marking a 49% increase during the latest reporting period.

California continues to lead hydrogen deployment, though other states are beginning to establish smaller fleets. Nevada currently operates 52 fuel cell buses, while New York has 15 and both Illinois and Ohio have 14 each.

Many transit agencies are evaluating hydrogen as a complementary option for routes with longer distances, heavier duty cycles, or operational constraints that may limit charging opportunities.

Federal funding programs remain a major driver of adoption. Grants from the Federal Transit Administration — including the Low or No Emission (Low-No) Program and the Grants for Buses and Bus Facilities Program created under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act — have helped transit agencies finance both vehicles and charging infrastructure.

However, industry stakeholders continue to point to several structural challenges that could affect deployment timelines. Supply chain disruptions, limited domestic manufacturing capacity, and extended vehicle lead times remain persistent issues.

text:
Texas-based startup Natura Resources LLC has cleared two of the biggest hurdles in advanced nuclear development: regulatory approval and access to high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU). The company, in partnership with Abilene Christian University, is building the MSR-1 molten salt reactor, which recently received a first-of-its-kind construction permit from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). This marks the first regulatory approval for a commercial-scale, liquid-fueled reactor in the U.S.

The NRC decision followed extensive safety assessments of the reactor's unique design, which uses liquid fuel and operates at low pressure. These features allow passive safety mechanisms—such as fuel drainage into cooling tanks—to reduce risk in emergency situations. With the permit in hand, Natura has finalized its reactor design and is now moving into the procurement phase, anticipating accelerated construction over the coming year.

The Department of Energy’s decision to allocate HALEU fuel for MSR-1 addresses a critical supply challenge facing the next generation of reactors. HALEU remains in short supply due to limited domestic enrichment capacity, making this allocation a significant step toward commercial readiness. Federal support in this form signals increasing confidence in molten salt reactor technology as part of a decarbonized energy mix.

Texas Investment Underscores State-Level Confidence in Advanced Nuclear

The state of Texas is backing the MSR-1 project with a $120 million allocation through Texas Tech University—an unusual but significant move that reflects growing policy interest in advanced nuclear technologies. The funding aims to position Texas as a leader in next-generation reactor deployment, leveraging the state’s deregulated electricity market and growing demand from industrial users.

Texas has become an increasingly favorable environment for advanced nuclear projects, combining regulatory flexibility with high energy consumption from sectors like manufacturing, data centers, and petrochemicals. Natura’s MSR-1 fits into this energy landscape by promising not only clean electricity but also co-benefits like isotope production and desalination—features designed to appeal to both utilities and industrial customers.

text:
The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) terminated its environmental impact statement (EIS) on revising seven western energy corridors in a notice published Oct. 23 in the Federal Register. The agency also rescinded its plan to amend the land use plans tied to those corridors, effective immediately.

The review began with a notice of intent on Dec. 1, 2023. It covered about 673 miles of designated Section 368 corridors on BLM land and would have amended 19 land use plans in Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming, according to the project's EIS page.

The Agency Had Found Segments Poorly Placed for Wind and Solar

BLM's own planning record said some corridor segments sat in the wrong places for newer wind and solar supply. It also cited changes in sensitive resources that limited use, plus nonfederal land and physical pinch points. A regional review had suggested changes could improve east to west transmission connectivity. The corridors under study crossed California and Nevada, Arizona and New Mexico, and Nevada and Utah, and included a proposed addition near Wamsutter linking Colorado and Wyoming.

The corridor network dates to records of decision issued Jan. 14, 2009, under Section 368 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005. BLM designated about 5,000 miles across 11 western states and the U.S. Forest Service about 990 miles, according to the program's frequently asked questions page. A lawsuit filed July 7, 2009 was dismissed under a settlement agreement on July 11, 2012.

BLM Says Updated Tools Make the Review Unnecessary

In the notice, BLM said updated processing methods and tools now let siting and review of linear energy infrastructure proceed without the EIS. The notice does not say whether the seven corridors will be revised through another process, and it names no replacement action.

Corridor use is optional for developers. Projects that use them can get a defined set of agency actions, a single federal point of contact and incorporation by reference from the earlier programmatic review, which can shorten authorization. BLM has announced other energy policy shifts on public land and has used faster paths for individual linear projects, including when it fast-tracked an Arizona pipeline under emergency rules. Changes to the underlying permitting statutes rest with Congress, which Ohio House members have urged to reform federal energy permitting.

For transmission and pipeline developers working in the seven states, the corridors as currently designated remain the reference for route planning on BLM land. BLM's analysis of the management situation, the planning document meant to anchor the alternatives, stands as the last published product of the review.

text:
A new $200 million Maryland grant program aims to finance clean energy development and boost generation on the region’s stressed power grid.

The grants, announced Monday, are part of a broader push by Maryland leaders to address the state’s dwindling power generation, surging electricity demands from data centers and climbing consumer energy prices.

Officials with the Maryland Energy Administration believe the funding will help finance “several hundred megawatts” of energy, or enough to power around 150,000 homes. The program targets battery storage projects and renewable sources, which the state considers to be solar arrays, wind farms, geothermal power, and some types of biofuels.

“This is simple economics,” said Maryland Energy Administration Director Kelly Speakes-Backman. “When high demand sends prices up, we need to bring more supply online.”

Called “Megawatts for Maryland,” the program was authorized earlier this year by Democratic leadership in the General Assembly through a sweeping energy law, the Utility RELIEF Act. Energy officials framed the grants Monday as a way to fill financing holes created by Trump administration’s cuts to federal clean energy tax credits.

Grants will be administered over two years and draw on appropriations from the state’s clean energy fund. That fund has ballooned, thanks to compliance payments from utility companies, and lawmakers and Gov. Wes Moore’s administration have nearly exhausted it in recent years to finance energy rebates and clean energy projects as well as to balance the budget.

Clean energy projects, including wind farms, solar arrays and batteries, have frequently encountered local opposition around the state, hampering the expansion of renewable power.

MEA spokesperson Erin Dempsey said eligible projects must meet criteria for financial solvency and public engagement — including through plans for potential community benefits agreements — but under state law, awards at auction must go to projects offering the lowest energy prices.

Recipients also must have applied for state permits and connections to the regional power grid.

While Maryland leaders have searched for ways to amp up energy output, the state has slipped well behind the pace on its goal to zero out its contributions to climate change. Maryland has struggled to replace large coal and natural gas plants with renewable power sources, an effort that has seen further setbacks because of President Donald Trump’s attacks on offshore wind projects.

The state’s money can only do so much to counteract federal policy, Speakes-Backman acknowledged.

“We are one state within the entire nation,” she said. “But I don’t think it’s a drop in the bucket, either.”

Siemens unveiled its advanced on-site microgrid at its Wendell, North Carolina facility today with an official “power on” ceremony. Integrated into the company’s U.S. Electrification and Automation headquarters, the 1.25-megawatt microgrid combines a solar photovoltaic carport array paired with a 3.9-megawatt-hour battery energy storage system. The microgrid, together with other campus-wide energy saving initiatives, enabled the Wendell site to achieve fully carbon-neutral operations while reducing the overall grid energy consumption by 2.5 MWh annually. According to the press release, the project underscores Siemens' unwavering commitment to achieving a net-zero carbon footprint by 2030 and represents a significant advancement for sustainable manufacturing in the United States.

The Wendell microgrid significantly improves operational resilience, helping protect the factory from grid outages that threaten production of vital medium-voltage power equipment. As one of the largest solar + storage industrial microgrids interconnected with Duke Energy’s distribution network in the Carolinas, the system can participate in net energy metering, exporting excess electricity back to the grid to support other customers. This capability not only strengthens energy reliability at the Wendell campus but also contributes to broader grid stability for the surrounding community.

“There is no question that we must do more to lower energy costs for North Carolinians and strengthen the resilience of our electric grid,” said Congresswoman Ross. “I’m grateful to see Siemens stepping up in Wendell with innovative investments that will expand clean, reliable energy. In Congress, I will keep working to advance commonsense solutions that drive down costs and accelerate North Carolina’s clean energy future.”

Built using Siemens products, the microgrid solution consists of the company’s SICAM A8000 Microgrid Controller, fire protection solutions, low-voltage switchboards, low-voltage bolted pressure switches, KACO string inverters, SIPROTEC universal relays, among other hardware solutions. From the software side, Siemens’ Desigo building management system and Electrification X cloud analytics enable seamless communication between the microgrid and the facility’s building management systems. On-site Siemens VersiCharge electric vehicle chargers are also connected into the microgrid, enabling EVs to be charged via self-generated solar energy while showcasing real-time charging statuses and dynamic load management as part of the site’s Customer Experience Center.

“The microgrid that we’ve integrated here at our Wendell campus is one of the more advanced microgrids installed in the market today,” said Brian Dula, Siemens USA’s President of Electrification and Automation. “It’s a true showcase of Siemens’ end-to-end portfolio of products, from generation to consumption and demonstrates not only how we’re making our own operations more efficient but also displays what we can do for our customers.”

Stated in the release, Siemens is advancing energy resilience and sustainability not only within its own operations, but for industry and infrastructure customers across the U.S., and alongside partners like Wake Technical Community College. Together, Siemens and Wake Tech are developing a future on-campus microgrid that will support reliable, efficient energy while creating new opportunities for students and workforce training.

“Given the strong growth we’re experiencing across the regions we serve, protecting customer reliability in a cost-effective manner is a core focus of Duke Energy’s grid modernization efforts,” said Venu Ghanta, Duke Energy’s vice president of North Carolina regulatory affairs and policy. “We’ve had a tremendous partnership for decades with Siemens, and we appreciate their focus on delivering solutions that improve grid resiliency.”

In addition to the on-site microgrid, the Wendell headquarters recently opened its interactive Customer Experience Center, workforce training Power Academy classrooms, conference center, and expanded manufacturing lines. The facility has added hundreds of new roles over the past several years and plans to continue expanding its workforce through 2028 and beyond.

name: Clean Energy
title: The loudest voices against the Eugene Clean Energy Fund have it wrong. Here's why I'm voting no.
authors: Ethan Clevenger, Letters to the Editor, Lillian Schrock-Clevenger, Leo Heffron, SHAYLA ESCUDERO, Lincoln Chronicle, Jaime Adame, Ashli Blow
description:
But the Eugene Clean Energy Fund ballot measure misses the mark.
Whether the Eugene Clean Energy Fund’s cost becomes a line-item or is bundled into the price, it will be passed on to consumers.
On such goods, this fee will be calculated, and passed on, regardless of the income of who makes the purchase.
Those local, boutique transactions and purchases outside our jurisdiction will not bear the cost of the fee and won’t contribute to the clean energy fund.
It would reward businesses of all sizes that invest in our community and align with our values through internal, cost-effective clean energy projects, better wages and expanded workforces.
text:
Let me start by saying I’m an “eat the rich” kind of guy.

But the Eugene Clean Energy Fund ballot measure misses the mark.

Most opposition collateral is designed to scare you with hallucinated receipts and exaggerations. But the more realistic impacts are concerning enough to vote no.

Measure 20-388 is a progressive cause with regressive funding that will be passed onto consumers. Look no further than credit card transaction fees on many of your receipts and local surcharges at the end of your cell phone bill. If you argued — rightly — that Donald Trump’s tariffs on international goods would increase consumers’ costs, this is no different. Whether the Eugene Clean Energy Fund’s cost becomes a line-item or is bundled into the price, it will be passed on to consumers. Digital price tags at box stores make this increasingly easy to do in specific localities.

We all purchase roughly similar amounts of staple, nonexempt goods like socks, body wash, cellphone service. On such goods, this fee will be calculated, and passed on, regardless of the income of who makes the purchase. This is the core of regressive tax policy.

But further, the selective application of this fee further disproportionately places its burden on the working poor.

Many well-intentioned voters — perhaps even you, dear reader! — recognize they could pay more into the system, and are happy to bear the passed-on costs. But voters that can afford higher costs are more likely to already shop at local, boutique, exempt stores (my fellow boutique-store owners and I thank you!).

Such voters are more likely to travel outside Eugene for luxury purchases and take shopping trips to, say, the Woodburn Outlets. Those local, boutique transactions and purchases outside our jurisdiction will not bear the cost of the fee and won’t contribute to the clean energy fund.

But the working poor don’t trek to the Woodburn Premium Outlets. They’ll pay the fee on clothes at Walmart. Someone who has to save every penny they can at WinCo will continue to shop there, because the cost will not increase enough to make local shops more competitive.

Goods will still be cheaper at the big box store. Costs will only increase enough to be a bigger burden on already over-burdened households. I lose no sleep over the future of the Walton family, but we can’t deny that the poorest households are dependent on their stores’ more affordable goods.

I’ll save talk about lack of clarity and inequitable outcomes by industry, as the regressive impacts are concerning enough to make the point. Opposition collateral doesn’t present alternatives, but here is mine.

I want Jeff Bezos to pay for our solar panels, but I don’t have standing to send him the bill. Eugene cannot tax billionaires and reclaim the wealth they’ve extracted, like California and New York City are attempting to do. They don’t live here. Trying to bill them via their local business operations gives us inequitable, manipulate-able solutions like this fee.

And let’s face it — Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and billionaires like them extract wealth from every facet of our lives and are destroying not just our environment, but our housing, roads, schools, local businesses and the very fabric of our communities. The dollars we scrape together and claw back are needed for more than strictly climate initiatives.

A truly progressive solution within Eugene’s borders would recognize what we can and can’t effectively accomplish as but one 170,000-person city. It would start with those locally who can afford to pay more, and give us the flexibility to use the funds on everything the billionaire class is destroying.

It would reward businesses of all sizes that invest in our community and align with our values through internal, cost-effective clean energy projects, better wages and expanded workforces.

We all want green jobs with good wages, a reduced carbon footprint and energy-efficient improvements to the homes of our most housing-burdened. But people already pinching nickels shouldn’t bear the cost. This measure will make life immediately harder for working class people in Eugene with a hope that as-of-yet-undetermined projects will roundabout put that money back into their pockets.

I plan to vote no. I look forward to collaborating on, and supporting, truly progressive solutions to climate change and income inequality locally and in this country.

text:
The Trump administration has continued to hand out illegal Clean Air Act exemptions allowing industrial facilities to ignore vital clean air protections

Records recently obtained by Environmental Defense Fund show a close degree of collaboration between EPA political appointees and the White House in facilitating companies’ exemption requests

President Trump has also continued to grant exemptions to companies that asked for them after EPA’s deadline

WASHINGTON – The Trump administration has continued to hand out expansive, illegal Clean Air Act exemptions allowing industrial sources to ignore vital limits to protect public health from hazardous air pollutants, including mercury and cancer-causing ethylene oxide, according to records recently obtained by Environmental Defense Fund.

The records, obtained through the Freedom of Information Act, show that political officials in the Trump EPA with previous ties to regulated industries asked the agency’s enforcement office not to enforce certain Clean Air Act standards for highly potent cancer-causing ethylene oxide pollution. President Trump has also continued to grant exemptions to companies that asked for them after EPA’s deadline.

While EPA has insisted it played no role in the process, the records show a close degree of collaboration between EPA political appointees and the White House in facilitating companies’ exemption requests. A former White House official, when asked about the exemptions, offered a political official within EPA as “the best person to talk to,” according to this weekend’s New York Times investigation into how the Trump administration has abused these exemptions to give a free pass to some of the country’s worst polluters.

“The Trump administration is continuing to operate behind closed doors to help large industrial emitters evade vital limits on the most toxic pollution,” said Erin Murphy, Lead Counsel and Director, Clean Air and Energy Markets at Environmental Defense Fund. “Giving companies a pass to delay long-needed, commonsense pollution controls puts more Americans in harm’s way. We will continue to shine a bright light on how this administration is working behind the scenes to tear down lifesaving limits on toxic pollution.”

Key findings from the latest set of records include:

Companies have continued to submit requests for exemptions long after EPA’s deadline: Industry had advance knowledge of upcoming new rounds of presidential exemptions and assumed their exemptions would ultimately be granted, despite missing the application deadline.

In addition to the presidential exemptions, the Trump EPA has also explored other ways to help companies evade pollution limits: Former EPA Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo, a political appointee and former lobbyist for the energy and sterilizer industries, requested a nationwide non-enforcement guarantee for some key air pollution standards for sterilization facilities while EPA pursued a rollback of the relevant pollution limits. It is not clear whether the enforcement office acted on this request, which only became public as a result of EDF’s request for agency records.

EPA has undersold its involvement in the exemptions process: EPA political appointees regularly assert that the White House is handling any presidential exemption requests. However, EPA continues to be extensively involved in processing the exemption applications and in interfacing with exemption applicants.

The National Energy Dominance Council has taken the lead on Clean Air Act exemptions for the White House, alongside EPA: EPA staff indicated that the National Energy Dominance Council led the presidential exemption process within the White House, specifically directing industry to John Reiten, NEDC Deputy Executive Director, as the “best contact.”

Industry representatives continued to meet with political appointees at EPA: At least 14 meetings occurred between industry representatives and Trump EPA political officials about the presidential exemptions or the underlying pollution regulations since March 2025.

A detailed explanation of the records is available in this fact sheet. The full set of records is available here.

Note that Environmental Defense Fund has redacted, in blue, the names and identifying information of EPA career staffers from the records obtained via FOIA. Civil servants are under unprecedented attack by the Trump Administration.

Background:

President Trump has made expansive use of an obscure Clean Air Act provision that allows the president to temporarily exempt sources of pollution from air quality standards in narrow circumstances carefully delineated by the plain terms of the law: when the technology to implement a standard is not available and when doing so would protect national security interests. But in a series of presidential proclamations, President Trump has repeatedly invoked this authority – which no previous president had ever used – to grant roughly 200 industrial facilities sweeping waivers from Clean Air Act protections against highly toxic pollutants.

Through the Freedom of Information Act, Environmental Defense Fund has obtained over 5,000 pages of records related to the Trump EPA’s actions to provide industry with presidential exemptions. Records previously released by Environmental Defense Fund show how Trump EPA political appointees with ties to industry scrambled to set up the exemption application process in March of 2025 and that the administration ultimately granted pollution exemptions for coal-fired power plants that were even more sweeping than what the companies had requested.

text:
Should Louisiana be selected as the site of the new U.S. Department of Energy nuclear life cycle innovation campus, it could potentially create 25,000 additional jobs, Louisiana Illuminator reports. The state is one of four others competing for the campus.

State officials outlined the proposal to lawmakers last week, describing a multi-parish approach that could involve small modular reactors in northwest Louisiana, uranium enrichment and testing at Entergy’s River Bend nuclear plant and LSU, and potential nuclear waste disposal in offshore salt domes near Port Fourchon.

Federal officials expect to select three states by late 2026 or early 2027, with the possibility of additional selections later. Louisiana’s pitch emphasizes recycling spent nuclear fuel to recover unused uranium rather than simply storing waste from other states or countries. State officials said the initial focus would be reprocessing fuel from River Bend, Waterford 3 in St. Charles Parish and Mississippi’s Grand Gulf plant, which together store approximately 1,600 tons of spent fuel.

Industry experts caution that new utility-scale nuclear plants remain prohibitively expensive, pointing to two Georgia reactors that cost nearly $37 billion and came online years behind schedule. Small modular reactors could offer a more practical path, although none are operating in the U.S. yet.

Louisiana Economic Development officials say the state’s finalist status is already generating interest from nuclear manufacturers and suppliers, including plans by Turner Industries to add 500 jobs at its Port Allen and New Iberia facilities.

However, moving forward would require changes to state laws restricting nuclear waste imports and salt dome evaluations, as well as federal legislation permitting a permanent waste repository outside Nevada’s stalled Yucca Mountain project.

WEST PALM BEACH, FL / ACCESS Newswire / October 26, 2026 / Exploring a Potential Domestic Lithium Opportunity

With investors watching technology and resource markets for fresh opportunities, ELEKTROS Inc. ELEK, a publicly traded company, is evaluating a prospective lithium property in upstate New York, near the Canadian border but on the United States side. The Company sees strategic appeal in exploring an American source of lithium for domestic battery and industrial supply chains. No acquisition agreement has been signed, and the presence, quantity, quality or commercial recoverability of lithium at the property has not been independently established.

Made in America: A Potential Logistics Advantage

For a company examining international lithium logistics, a viable U.S. property could potentially reduce reliance on ocean freight, container scheduling, port handling, customs procedures and import documentation. Domestic sourcing would not automatically remove taxes, duties on imported equipment, permitting obligations or inland transportation costs. If supported by technical and economic studies, a U.S.-based source might simplify some steps between extraction and American processors or battery manufacturers. ELEKTROS believes this possibility warrants further evaluation.

Why Lithium Matters to America

Lithium is an important material in rechargeable batteries used in electric vehicles, grid storage and portable electronics, as well as in some aerospace and defense applications. Battery-grade material requires specialized processing and customer qualification; raw ore from a prospective property cannot be presumed to meet those specifications. Government and private-sector attention has increasingly focused on domestic supply chains spanning exploration, extraction, refining and battery manufacturing. If a commercially viable project were ultimately established, ELEKTROS could explore potential relationships in automotive, energy-storage and appropriately qualified defense-related markets. The Company has announced no military supply contract.

Bloomberg, Reuters and Benzinga Highlight the National Opportunity

Bloomberg News reported on June 25, 2026, that the U.S. Army had reached arrangements with companies including EnergyX and ioneer for mineral-processing facilities associated with military installations, with lithium among the materials involved. Separately, Bloomberg reported that a Defense Logistics Agency lithium purchase solicitation worth up to $300 million was later canceled in August 2026; that canceled tender is not an active purchase commitment. Reuters reported on September 12, 2023, that Albemarle received a $90 million Pentagon grant for its planned Kings Mountain lithium mine reopening in North Carolina. More recently, Reuters reported on August 7, 2026, a broad U.S. investment initiative for mineral and battery projects, including a conditional defense-related loan for battery-materials company Sila Nanotechnologies. Benzinga reported on October 22, 2026, on the substantial capital requirements for new lithium mines, Albemarle's U.S. position and the domestic supply-chain opportunity. These are independent industry examples, not contracts, endorsements or funding commitments involving ELEKTROS.

An Exploratory Property-Not Yet an Acquisition

The Company's review may include property title and mineral rights, geological information, independent sampling, possible resource estimates, environmental matters, permits, infrastructure access, funding requirements and potential processing partners. Any transaction would be subject to satisfactory due diligence, mutually agreed terms and available financing. There can be no assurance that ELEKTROS will acquire the property, confirm a mineral resource, develop a mine or produce or sell lithium.

Beyond Lithium: Patented EV Charging Technology

The Company seeks to engage qualified engineering, development and commercial partners. The existence of a patent alone does not establish a functioning commercial prototype, a particular charging rate, regulatory approval or market acceptance.

As ELEKTROS considers a possible role in the domestic lithium landscape, the Company recognizes the growing attention on American critical-mineral supply chains. title: Louisiana axes limits on noneconomic damages involving carbon capture and storage
description:
Before the change, state law generally capped noneconomic damages at $250,000 per person, with a $500,000 limit for specified severe injuries and wrongful death.
Noneconomic damages can include compensation for pain and suffering, emotional distress and loss of enjoyment of life, while economic damages cover measurable losses such as medical expenses and lost wages.
Supporters of the bill argued that carbon capture companies should not receive liability advantages unavailable to most other industries.
The legislation’s bipartisan support signaled a willingness among lawmakers to reconsider the industry’s special legal protections, even as other proposals restricting carbon capture development faced opposition.

text:
A newly enacted Louisiana law marks a significant change in how companies in the emerging carbon capture industry could be held financially accountable for injuries or losses. House Bill 79 (now Act 614) took effect Aug. 1, removing special damages caps that previously applied to certain carbon dioxide storage facilities, transmission pipelines and related operations.

Before the change, state law generally capped noneconomic damages at $250,000 per person, with a $500,000 limit for specified severe injuries and wrongful death. A separate provision established a $1 million fallback limit if the original cap were found unconstitutional or otherwise invalid. Noneconomic damages can include compensation for pain and suffering, emotional distress and loss of enjoyment of life, while economic damages cover measurable losses such as medical expenses and lost wages.

By removing those limits, Act 614 allows potential noneconomic damage awards to exceed the previous statutory thresholds when supported by the evidence. Previously, even if a jury determined that a person’s noneconomic losses were worth more than the applicable cap, the special statutory limit restricted the amount recoverable. The change removes that restriction for claims governed by the amended law, potentially increasing companies’ financial exposure following an accident.

The legislation follows a contentious debate at the State Capitol over how Louisiana should regulate carbon capture, a technology promoted as a tool for reducing industrial emissions but criticized by some landowners and residents concerned about pipeline safety, property rights and long-term environmental risks.

Supporters of the bill argued that carbon capture companies should not receive liability advantages unavailable to most other industries. Rep. Mike Johnson, R-Pineville, previously questioned the rationale for the caps, arguing that limiting damages could weaken incentives for companies to prioritize safety. The legislation’s bipartisan support signaled a willingness among lawmakers to reconsider the industry’s special legal protections, even as other proposals restricting carbon capture development faced opposition.

However, Stephen Babcock of Babcock Louisiana Injury Lawyers cautions that removing the damages caps does not eliminate every legal protection for storage operators.

His analysis states that Act 614 leaves intact separate provisions governing the transfer of completed storage projects to the state and the release of certain future obligations and liabilities after a certificate of completion is issued. Operators must meet specific conditions for that process, and exceptions remain for certain circumstances, including pre-certificate noncompliance and intentional concealment or misrepresentation of material facts.

The state also does not automatically assume financial responsibility simply by taking ownership of a storage site, and removing the caps does not establish fault or guarantee compensation in an individual case.

For businesses, landowners and communities near proposed projects, the practical consequences will depend on the circumstances of a claim, the timing of an incident and the financial protections available for a specific facility. Act 614 changes the potential scale of noneconomic damage awards, but questions of liability, causation and applicable legal defenses remain central to any dispute.

title: Op-Ed: EPA's Carbon Repeal Saves Billions, Protects Energy Supplies | Opinion
description: In April 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) gave America’s coal and gas plants an ultimatum: capture most of your carbon dioxide emissions or close. On Sept. 14, the
text:
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin speaks at a MAHA Commission meeting to release the 'Make Our Children Healthy Again' strategy report. Photo: Morgan Sweeney / The Center Square

In April 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) gave America’s coal and gas plants an ultimatum: capture most of your carbon dioxide emissions or close. On Sept. 14, the agency withdrew the order. The repeal corrects one of the most reckless regulatory actions of the past decade.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the decision at a G20 “energy abundance” meeting in Houston. He scrapped most of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards and proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse gas standard for power plants.

The Government Accountability Office's review of the repeal shows that EPA calculated savings of $95 billion to $160 billion . Utilities would have sunk that money into machinery never shown to be effective in the real world, and the cost would have landed on monthly electricity bills.

The purpose was obvious from the start: Set a bar plants could not clear and force them to go out of business. The Supreme Court had already rebuked the agency in West Virginia v. EPA for trying to redraw the nation’s fuel mix through the Clean Air Act. The Biden administration simply tried again by another route.

PJM, which runs the grid for 67 million people in 13 states and Washington, D.C., had warned that 40 gigawatts of generation could retire by 2030, with 25 gigawatts of that driven by policy. In addition, replacement capacity is arriving too slowly, according to the grid operator. The current administration’s EPA now acknowledges that the old standards required technology that was not adequately demonstrated .

Defenders of the old rule now cite $370 billion in climate and health benefits through 2047 . But that number is highly suspect. Most of the health gains come from cutting soot, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that separate EPA programs already regulate . Regulators borrowed those benefits to prop up a carbon rule that could not justify itself on carbon alone. If any of those pollutants need a tighter limit, EPA can write one directly. Counting the same benefit twice is fraudulent.

The climate half of the ledger fares worse. It depends on the so-called social cost of carbon, a figure generated by computer models that project damages decades ahead and had long leaned on worst-case emission scenarios that many climate researchers themselves now call implausible .

The rule’s champions rarely say how much warming the regulation would avoid because the honest figure is a sliver of a degree too small for any thermometer to register. According to a 2022 EPA estimate, power plants produce roughly a quarter of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, which account for a shrinking share of the global total. China and India, meanwhile, keep approving coal plants to lift hundreds of millions of people out of poverty. Charging Americans $160 billion for a temperature effect no one can measure is green ideology’s virtue signaling billed to ratepayers.

The deeper error is treating carbon dioxide like soot. It is a trace gas that plants need to grow, and rising concentrations have coincided with record global harvests and satellite-observed greening across much of the planet. A regulator that classifies the molecule feeding the world’s crops as a danger to public welfare is disconnected from basic biology.

Twenty-one states led by New York have sued to stop the EPA repeal, and environmental groups have filed their own challenges. Courts will rule. But notice who is suing. Many plaintiff states already charge some of the highest electricity rates in the country, and New York residents watched their rates climb 14% in the past year. Those states remain free to impose their own climate policies on their own voters. What they want from the courts is permission for a federal agency to impose those costs on you, without any clear instruction from Congress.

Watch three things next. Will utilities use the relief to postpone planned coal retirements and keep gas units running? Will developers break ground on new gas plants faster now that a carbon-capture mandate no longer threatens a 30-year investment? And will your state utility commission pass the savings to you or let them disappear into corporate balance sheets?

For too long, regulators justified punishing mandates with scenarios of catastrophe based on the flawed outputs of computer models. The practice should end with the demise of the carbon rule. The next time a bureaucrat promises to save the planet, demand two numbers: the measurable effect of the rule, whether temperature or some other metric, and the name of the power plant that will keep your lights on.

Vijay Jayaraj is a Science and Research Associate at the CO2 Coalition , Fairfax, Virginia. He holds an M.S. in environmental sciences from the University of East Anglia and a postgraduate degree in energy management from Robert Gordon University, both in the U.K., and a bachelor’s in engineering from Anna University, India. He served as a research associate with the Changing Oceans Research Unit at University of British Columbia, Canada.

text:
German automaker Audi took a historic step toward American manufacturing on Saturday when President Donald Trump revealed the company's plans to build its first-ever assembly facility on U.S. soil. Standing alongside Audi CEO Gernot Döllner at a packed campaign rally in Perry, Georgia — just a short drive from the designated site — Trump framed the project as proof that his tariff-driven trade strategy is reshaping global industry. Döllner took the microphone to confirm the commitment directly: "We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia."

A Mega-Plant in Georgia's Heartland

The facility will be built at the 1,474-acre Middle Georgia Megasite in Peach County, along Georgia Highway 96 near Interstate 75, roughly ten minutes from the city of Perry. The greenfield project is designed to produce large premium SUVs — specifically the Q7, Q8, and the newly launched Q9 — tailored to North American buyers. Those three models are the ones a U.S. government official disclosed to Reuters; Audi's own official announcement describes the output as particularly large and upmarket SUVs without specifying a final model lineup. At full capacity, the plant is expected to roll out roughly 200,000 vehicles annually. Audi confirmed the project will generate approximately 4,500 direct jobs, with additional positions expected at suppliers and logistics providers throughout the region.

Reuters and Bloomberg reported the total investment as approximately $4 billion. Georgia Governor Brian Kemp hailed the investment as the largest economic deal in state history.

Groundbreaking Is Still a Year Away

There is a clear gap between Trump's characterization of the timeline and Audi's own communications. At the rally, the president implied construction would begin within weeks. Audi's official press release, however, states that site grading is scheduled to begin in 2027, with series production not expected until the early 2030s. Georgia state officials have pointed to 2031 as the target year for full-scale output.

Tariffs as the Engine Behind the Decision

The announcement is inseparable from the trade environment Audi has navigated since Trump's return to office. Unlike BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Volkswagen's core brand, Audi currently has no factory anywhere in the United States, importing every vehicle sold in the American market from plants in Europe or Mexico. The White House originally imposed a 25% tariff on imported vehicles, a rate the EU negotiated down to 15% under the July 2025 Turnberry Agreement — though that figure has since been the subject of repeated diplomatic friction, with Trump threatening to push it back to 25% as recently as May 2026. Even at 15%, the levy dealt Audi more than a €1 billion blow in a single year, according to Reuters reporting.

A Strategic Move, Not a Political Concession

Döllner has been careful to frame the Georgia project in strategic rather than reactive terms, emphasizing that the decision reflects a long-term belief in the American market and not a capitulation to political demands. "This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market," he told the Perry crowd. That framing aligns with the company's broader North America growth strategy, though the tariff timeline makes it difficult to fully separate commercial reasoning from political urgency.

The timing of Saturday's event was anything but coincidental. Trump made the announcement in the closing stretch of the midterm cycle, using it as a political showcase days before the November 3 elections, with Georgia hosting competitive races for both the U.S. Senate and the governor's mansion. Ohio Republican Senator Bernie Moreno, who appeared at the Perry event, made the political subtext explicit — crediting the plant's arrival to tariffs, regulatory rollbacks, and the elimination of California's authority over federal fuel economy standards.

A State Already Deep in Auto Manufacturing

Georgia's selection was no political accident. The state already anchors a major slice of Southern automotive output, including a Kia plant in West Point and a large Hyundai facility near Savannah. The Peach County announcement also complements a broader Volkswagen Group expansion underway across the region: Scout Motors, a Volkswagen-backed electric vehicle brand, is constructing a $2 billion plant near Columbia, South Carolina. Together, the two projects extend the Southeast's automotive manufacturing corridor deeper into the mid-Atlantic and signal the region's growing dominance over legacy Rust Belt production centers.

text:
Introduction

With the rapid growth in data centers and the transition to a more electrified economy,1 electricity demand patterns are shifting across the United States. This shift is creating an urgent need to manage loads to maintain grid reliability and minimize escalating utility bills for customers. This places new pressures on electricity systems that were not designed for this rapid transition, and as a result, utilities and their regulators are increasingly focused on strategies that can reduce peak demand and improve overall system utilization.

In cold-climate states such as Pennsylvania and Massachusetts, these trends are expected to fundamentally reshape seasonal demand patterns. Historically, electricity demand has peaked in the summer in these states. However, with increased electrification of space heating, they are likely to see electricity demand peak in winter. The future winter electricity peak will be driven largely by building space heating loads, making effective management of winter demand critical to maintaining grid reliability and containing utility infrastructure costs.

In warm-climate states like Texas, the challenge takes a different but equally pressing form. Rapid growth of data centers, alongside continued electrification of buildings and transportation, is intensifying already high summer peak demand driven by space cooling. In these regions, addressing cooling demand from buildings is essential to reducing grid strain and mitigating the required capital investment for electricity system expansion.

This report provides summaries highlighting how the utility system value of ground-source heat pumps differs across climates, building sectors, and future electricity demand scenarios, focusing on Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, and Texas. There are also links to the full analysis for each state. Together, these analyses demonstrate that GHPs can consistently reduce peak demand and improve grid utilization, while illustrating the state-specific opportunities for utilities and policymakers to better capture these benefits through planning, regulation, and customer programs.

Geothermal Heat Pumps

Geothermal heat pumps (GHP), or ground source heat pumps, offer a compelling but underutilized solution for both climates. Compared to conventional air conditioners and air-source heat pumps, GHPs deliver higher efficiency on average, with even greater performance advantages during extreme temperatures due to the relatively stable ground temperature that provides the heat source (during heating) and sink (during cooling). This makes them particularly well-suited to addressing both winter heating peaks in cold climates and summer cooling peaks in warm climates.

GHPs can be deployed as individual systems serving a single building or as thermal energy networks (TENs), where multiple buildings share a common underground geothermal loop to provide heating and cooling across the network. However, adoption has been constrained by high up-front costs and a limited pool of experienced contractors, especially those with the specialized drilling expertise required for installation. These challenges create a significant barrier to wider adoption despite the technology’s strong operational savings and potential for peak demand reduction.

Against this backdrop, the goal of this analysis is to assess the practical potential of geothermal heating and cooling to deliver value to the utility system by shaving peak demand and reducing annual energy consumption. It also examines whether this value is appropriately being captured in utility bill savings, and identifies policy and regulatory levers that could better translate these benefits into financial incentives to support broader deployment of GHPs.

Analysis Overview

This analysis evaluates the system impacts of GHP adoption across climates, states, building types, and timeframes. The analysis focuses on three representative states: Massachusetts and Pennsylvania in cold climates, and Texas in a warm climate.

In the cold-climate states, the analysis centers on residential buildings, including both single-family and multifamily homes, where space heating demand plays a significant role in shaping electricity use. For Massachusetts, the analysis also considers the benefits of serving residential buildings through TENs in mixed-use settings, where residential and commercial load diversity can improve system efficiency.

In contrast, the warm-climate analysis focuses on commercial buildings, where consistent cooling demand throughout the year and relatively higher energy use per site make these buildings strong candidates for near-term GHP deployment. Within this sector, office buildings and retail stores are the primary focus of the core scenarios as they represent the largest contributors to commercial cooling energy use,2 while hotel and warehouse buildings are included in an additional scenario to capture the incremental impacts of expanding GHP adoption to a broader set of commercial building types.

Building on the 2023 Oak Ridge National Laboratory study, Grid Cost and Total Emissions Reductions Through Mass Deployment of Geothermal Heat Pumps for Building Heating and Cooling Electrification in the United States,3 which evaluated the national-scale impacts of deploying GHPs to all applicable building floor space by 2050, this analysis focuses on regionally relevant, near- and mid-term deployment pathways that could help drive practical adoption. The study assesses the impacts of GHP adoption across different scales of deployment through four adoption scenarios:

Low: 2% of single-family and multifamily dwelling units or office and retail buildings

Medium: 10% of single-family and multifamily dwelling units or office and retail buildings

High: 20% of single-family and multifamily dwelling units or office and retail buildings

Very High: 50% of office and retail buildings and 20% of hotel and warehouse buildings

Today (2025): Representing current load profiles and predominantly summer-peaking systems across all three states.

Electrified Future (2040): Reflecting increased electrification across buildings,4 transportation, and industry, resulting in higher overall electricity demand. Remains summer-peaking system in warm climate and flips to winter peaking in cold climate.
