text:
Highlights

American Electric Power joined Amazon and X-energy on an advanced nuclear development plan in Indiana.

The regulated electricity group prepared to release its third-quarter figures late in October.

Surging data-center demand continued to shape the company's grid and generation planning.

American Electric Power (NASDAQ:AEP) Utilities American Electric Power Co Inc (NASDAQ:AEP) 129.80 USD +0.110 ↑ 0.085% stepped into fresh attention this week after confirming a joint development plan with Amazon and X-energy to explore advanced nuclear generation in Indiana. The arrangement, described by the company as a way to serve rising electricity demand without lifting costs for existing customers, landed just days before the group was set to share its third-quarter figures late in October. The pairing of a high-profile technology partnership with an imminent earnings date gave the week an unusually busy tone for a name often seen as steady and slow-moving. The stock remains one of the more closely followed names among Utility Stocks.

The timing stitched together two threads that market watchers have tracked all year. One thread is the scramble among large technology buyers to lock up firm, carbon-free electricity for data centers. The other is the steady build-out of regulated grid assets across the broad sweep of states the company serves, from the industrial Midwest down through parts of the South. By placing itself in the middle of both stories at once, the company signaled that it means to ride the demand wave rather than watch it pass.

Why The Spotlight Gathered This Week

Several strands converged to lift the profile of the stock. The advanced nuclear plan arrived alongside a separate step tied to Bloom fuel cells arranged to serve a large Google electricity load, and a freshly declared quarterly cash distribution on common stock. Each item on its own would draw notice; together they framed a company leaning hard into the demand surge created by computing and cloud growth. The sheer clustering of announcements in a single stretch of days stood out against the usually measured cadence of a regulated electricity group.

Market observers also kept one eye on the calendar. With the third-quarter release due in the final stretch of October, the agreements offered a preview of the kind of large, long-horizon projects that regulated electricity groups are now weaving into capital plans. The combination of fresh partnerships and an imminent earnings update encouraged a closer look at how the company intends to fund and sequence the generation and transmission it has lined up across its footprint.

How American Electric Power Keeps The Lights On

At its core, the company operates one of the largest electricity transmission networks in the United States, moving power across tens of thousands of circuit miles and serving millions of homes and businesses. The business spans regulated distribution utilities in multiple states, each overseen by a state commission that sets the rate framework under which the company recovers the cost of poles, wires, substations and generation. That patchwork of jurisdictions gives the enterprise both scale and a built-in diversity of regulatory relationships.

Because so much of the enterprise sits inside regulated structures, earnings tend to track the pace of approved capital spending rather than swinging with wholesale commodity prices. That design gives the group a relatively stable base of revenue, which it then channels into grid hardening, cleaner generation and the expanding web of connections that new large customers require. The result is a business whose growth is paced less by the market cycle and more by the steady rhythm of rate cases and commission decisions.

Reading The Broader Landscape

For readers scanning the wider space, this name sits squarely within the family of Utility Stocks that anchor many conservative portfolios because of dependable cash distributions and regulated revenue streams. Membership in that group means the company is often weighed against peers on metrics such as approved spending programs, rate-case progress and the pace at which demand is climbing across its footprint. Those comparisons shape how the market frames the name against a long list of regional electricity operators.

That peer comparison matters because the current environment is anything but static. Demand that was flat for the better part of a decade has turned sharply upward, and every regulated operator is racing to line up generation and transmission to match. The company's Indiana step is one visible example of how that race is playing out across the country, as utilities compete to secure the large new loads that computing and electrification are creating.

Data-Center Demand Reshapes The Grid

The single largest force behind the week's announcements is the explosion of electricity demand from data centers and artificial-intelligence computing. These facilities draw enormous, around-the-clock power, and the buyers behind them increasingly want that electricity to be firm and low-carbon rather than intermittent. That preference pushes utilities toward nuclear, long-duration storage and advanced generation, reshaping how new capacity is planned and financed across the country.

American Electric Power has positioned itself as a willing partner for those buyers. By pairing with Amazon and X-energy on an advanced nuclear plan, the company signaled that it intends to meet hyperscale demand with new generation designed inside the regulated framework, where costs and benefits are weighed by state commissions and spread fairly across the customer base. Landing such relationships can anchor decades of demand and justify the heavy spending that expands the regulated base.

The scale of these loads is reshaping how utilities think about generation. A single large campus can draw as much power as a sizable town, and the clustering of several such projects in one region can strain a grid that was planned for far gentler growth, pushing operators to line up firm supply well in advance of the demand actually arriving.

The Nuclear And Fuel-Cell Threads

The Indiana plan centers on advanced nuclear technology, a category that promises firm output from a compact footprint and that has drawn growing interest from large electricity buyers seeking dependable carbon-free supply. The joint development arrangement sets out a path to study siting, engineering and the sequence of regulatory steps that any new generation of this kind must clear before a single unit delivers power to the grid.

Running in parallel, the company advanced a separate solution built around Bloom fuel cells to serve a sizable Google electricity requirement. Taken together, the two moves show a willingness to blend several generation technologies at once, matching the specific needs of each large customer rather than relying on a single approach across the whole system. That flexibility has become a selling point as hyperscale buyers shop for tailored, reliable supply arrangements.

A Regulated Business Model Explained

Understanding the stock means understanding how a regulated utility earns revenue. State commissions allow the company to recover prudently spent capital plus an authorized rate of return on that capital. The more the company directs funds into approved grid and generation projects, the larger the base on which it earns, provided regulators agree the spending genuinely serves customers rather than merely enlarging the company's asset base.

This structure explains why large, long-horizon projects such as advanced nuclear matter so much. Each approved program adds to the regulated base and supports steady earnings growth over many years. It also explains why rate cases, settlement talks and commission decisions draw such close attention from those tracking the name, since the pace of approvals effectively sets the ceiling on how quickly the business can grow.

The Market Environment For Regulated Names

Regulated electricity groups have moved through a shifting backdrop as borrowing costs, demand trends and clean-energy mandates all evolve. Because these companies carry heavy debt loads to fund long-lived assets, the cost of capital feeds directly into planning. When borrowing costs ease, large capital programs become less expensive to finance; when they climb, the math grows tighter and management must weigh the pace of spending against the cost of funding it.

Against that backdrop, the steady membership of these names in the S&P 500 keeps them visible to a wide audience of market participants who prize dependable cash distributions. Inclusion in the Nasdaq Composite and the Russell 1000 gives the stock added visibility among index trackers and fund managers. The group's defensive reputation tends to draw attention during periods of broader market uncertainty, when steady demand for electricity offers a measure of stability that more cyclical corners of the market cannot match.

Capital Spending And Grid Modernization

Much of the company's story in recent years has been about the sheer scale of spending. The group has laid out multi-year capital programs aimed at hardening the grid against storms, expanding transmission to connect new load, and modernizing aging equipment. The surge in data-center demand has only sharpened the need for that spending, pulling forward projects that might once have sat further down the queue.

Grid modernization is not glamorous, yet it sits at the heart of the business. Replacing worn conductors, adding substations and building the high-voltage lines that carry power across state borders all expand the regulated base while making the system more resilient. The week's partnerships feed directly into that broader program of reinvestment, tying marquee generation projects to the unglamorous wires work that actually delivers the electricity.

Interstate transmission has drawn particular emphasis, as moving power between regions helps balance supply and demand across a continent-spanning grid. The company's position within several regional markets gives it a role in that broader build-out, tying its own spending to the wider effort to knit the national system together into a more resilient whole.

Dividend Mechanics And Steady Cash Distributions

This week the board declared a regular quarterly cash distribution on common stock, nudging the per-share amount higher than the prior period. Dependable, rising cash distributions are a central reason many market participants gravitate toward regulated electricity names, and the company has long positioned steady payouts as a defining feature of owning the stock through varied economic conditions.

The ability to keep lifting distributions rests on the same regulated earnings engine that funds capital spending. As the approved base grows and demand climbs, the company aims to balance reinvestment against cash paid out, a balance that commissions and lenders both watch closely. Straying too far in either direction can strain the credit standing that keeps the whole capital program affordable to finance.

Headwinds And Uncertainties

No regulated operator is free of uncertainty. Rate cases can land below what a company requests, weather can swing demand and restoration costs, and the price of financing heavy capital programs can shift with broader markets. Each of these headwinds can nudge reported earnings in either direction from quarter to quarter, which is why the market reads quarterly commentary so closely for signs of how the pressures are balancing out.

Large new projects add their own uncertainties. Advanced nuclear, for all its appeal, must clear engineering, licensing and siting hurdles that stretch across many years. The company has framed the Indiana plan as a study-and-develop step rather than a committed build, a careful wording that acknowledges how much work remains before any such facility delivers power to customers.

The Competitive Map Across Regions

The company competes for capital, talent and large customers against a field of other regulated electricity groups, each with its own service territory and regulatory relationships. Because service areas rarely overlap, the competition is less about head-to-head customer battles and more about which operator can most efficiently deploy capital and secure the big new loads reshaping demand across the country.

On that measure, the week's agreements with Amazon, X-energy and Google place the company among the operators actively courting hyperscale buyers. Winning those relationships can lock in decades of demand and justify the large generation and transmission projects that expand the regulated base, giving the company a visible edge in the race to serve the computing boom.

Where The Third-Quarter Report Fits

All of this sets the stage for the third-quarter earnings release due late in October. Market participants will read the figures for signs of how demand growth, capital spending and rate-case progress are translating into reported results, and for any refreshed guidance on the pace of the company's multi-year program across its many jurisdictions.

The partnerships announced in the days before the report give the update added context. Rather than a routine quarter, the release arrives amid visible momentum around data-center load, advanced generation and a steadily growing distribution, all themes that the figures and accompanying commentary are likely to touch. The market will be listening closely for how management frames the demand wave against the cost of meeting it.

Beyond the headline figures, the commentary around the report often carries the most weight. How management describes demand trends, the pace of approvals and the progress of marquee projects can shape the market's read of the company well beyond the single quarter the numbers cover, setting the tone for how the name is discussed into the close of the year.

Broader Market Relevance

Beyond the single name, the week's developments speak to a larger shift reshaping the American electricity system. The marriage of regulated utilities and hyperscale technology buyers is rewriting how new generation gets planned, financed and built, and American Electric Power has placed itself near the center of that change with a string of visible agreements.

For anyone tracking how the demand wave from computing meets the steady machinery of regulated power, the company offers a clear case study. The Indiana nuclear plan, the Google fuel-cell step and the imminent earnings update together sketch a business leaning into growth while keeping the dependable, regulated structure that defines the broader group of American electricity names.

text:
Informa Markets in India has brought together industry leaders at the Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo and The Battery Show India (TBSI) to discuss opportunities in battery manufacturing, critical mineral supplies, technology partnerships and supply chain resilience, with implications for India’s electric vehicle (EV) industry.

At the event held on October 23, industry leaders highlighted opportunities to combine India’s manufacturing capabilities with international expertise in battery technology, energy storage and critical minerals. Discussions also emphasised the importance of building domestic capabilities as India expands its clean energy infrastructure.

For the automotive industry, access to battery technologies and critical minerals remains an important consideration as manufacturers develop electric mobility solutions. Australia, which has significant lithium, cobalt and rare earth resources, identified battery manufacturing and EVs as key areas for cooperation with India.

Philip Green, Australia’s High Commissioner to India, said the two countries could combine Australia’s engineering expertise and mineral resources with India’s manufacturing strength and integration into global supply chains.

Green also highlighted Australia’s mineral resources, stating that the country produces more than 50 per cent of the world’s lithium and holds the world’s second-largest cobalt reserves. He added that Australia ranks second or third globally in rare earth resources.

Australia has 20 companies and 32 exhibitors participating in the expo, showcasing technologies across energy storage, grid infrastructure, green hydrogen and renewable energy integration.

Yogesh Mudras, Managing Director of Informa Markets in India, highlighted the need for renewable energy generation and grid storage to expand together as India advances its energy transition. According to Mudras, India’s renewable energy market is projected to reach 486 GW by 2030, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15 per cent. The country’s battery storage sector is projected to exceed USD 8.5 billion by 2031, with a CAGR of 33 per cent.

The three-day event, organised by Informa Markets in India, brings together more than 1,080 exhibitors, 1,400 brands and over 54,000 professionals. The co-location of REI Expo and The Battery Show India brings renewable energy developers, battery manufacturers, investors and policymakers together to discuss developments across the sector.

Beyond Australia, India is also looking to international partnerships to strengthen its clean energy technology base. Anandi Iyer, Director of Fraunhofer Office in India, highlighted opportunities for India and Germany to collaborate in battery research, power electronics, advanced engineering and industrial automation.

Iyer cited global renewable energy capacity additions of approximately 800 GW in 2025 and global battery storage deployment of 108 GW, an increase of 40 per cent from the previous year. She also highlighted the importance of trusted partnerships and supply chains in translating research into commercially viable solutions, noting that technological self-reliance did not mean working in isolation.

Scotland’s First Minister John Swinney also highlighted opportunities to combine Scottish technological expertise with India’s manufacturing scale, talent and market potential.

The broader clean energy transition is also being shaped by falling technology costs and economies of scale. Manu Srivastav, Additional Chief Secretary in Madhya Pradesh’s Power and Renewable Energy Department, said renewable energy was becoming increasingly competitive with conventional power as costs declined. He pointed to opportunities for wider adoption over the next two to five years.

Jai Asundi, Executive Director of the Centre for Study of Science, Technology & Policy (CSTEP), highlighted the need for continued investment in manufacturing, energy storage, grid infrastructure, research and skilled talent to build a resilient clean energy ecosystem.

For India’s EV industry, the discussions highlighted the importance of strengthening access to battery-related technologies and materials and developing domestic manufacturing capabilities. The discussions at the expo did not specify new investments or agreements involving individual EV manufacturers.

title: Innovative approaches to scaling EV charging infrastructure - World Economic Forum
authors: Vince Wong Co-Founder, Tiya Gordon Co-Founder, Chief Executive Officer, it's electric
description:
This raises an important question: how can innovative approaches help close the gaps in public EV charging and make electric mobility accessible to more people?
The access gap: EV charging for people without private parking For drivers with a garage or driveway, charging is as simple as plugging in overnight.
The power gap: fast EV charging where the grid is constrained For long trips, ride-hail drivers and delivery fleets, fast charging remains essential.
Rethinking what public charging can look like These examples point to a broader lesson: there is no single best charging model.
Closing the EV charging gap will take a mix of approaches, each matched to the community it serves.
text:
EV adoption is rapidly scaling worldwide, but this expansion needs to be accompanied by infrastructure that is available in the right places and suited to different patterns of use.

The growth of the electric vehicle (EV) market is accelerating globally. However, the expansion of electrified transport is increasingly dependent on infrastructure readiness.

The United States illustrates the scale of the challenge. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), there were approximately 32 electric light-duty vehicles for every public charging point in 2024. Under the IEA’s stated-policies scenario, the country’s public charging network would need to grow from nearly 200,000 points in 2024 to more than 500,000 by 2030, requiring the installation of roughly 58,000 new points each year.

Yet expanding the network will not be equally straightforward everywhere. Dense cities face limited curb space, complex permitting and expensive grid connections, while rural areas may face lower utilization rates, longer distances and weaker investment incentives. Conventional charging models might therefore lack sufficient economic and physical adaptability to suit every scenario.

Access to EV charging remains a top barrier to adoption. As EV adoption expands beyond households with access to private parking and home charging, the challenge will not only be to build more infrastructure, but to ensure that it is available in the right places and suited to different patterns of use.

This raises an important question: how can innovative approaches help close the gaps in public EV charging and make electric mobility accessible to more people?

The access gap: EV charging for people without private parking

For drivers with a garage or driveway, charging is as simple as plugging in overnight. For many others, it is not.

Research by Energy Innovation finds that up to 94% of US EV drivers in detached single-family homes have access to home charging, compared with about half of those living in apartments. Nearly one-third of US households live in multifamily housing.

A 2022 survey also found that Black and Latino drivers are more likely to rely on public or on-street parking, making accessible public charging a question of fairness as well as convenience.

These portable power banks deliver fast EV charging where the grid falls short

02:10

Charging therefore needs to fit into daily routines, where cars already park overnight. About half of New York City residents park on the street, and the city has set a goal of 40,000 public Level 2 chargers and 6,000 fast chargers by 2030, including 10,000 at the curb. Yet curb space is scarce, permitting is slow and new grid connections are costly.

One response is to draw on spare electrical capacity in nearby buildings instead of building a new grid connection, with property owners sharing in the revenue. The approach was first deployed by It's Electric in Boston, where the mayor set a goal of a public charger within a five-minute walk of every resident, and has since been taken up in more than 10 additional US cities.

Viability matters as much as technology: cities and property owners are more likely to say yes when they take on little upfront cost, while operators need enough regular users to cover costs.

The power gap: fast EV charging where the grid is constrained

For long trips, ride-hail drivers and delivery fleets, fast charging remains essential. However, this requires substantial power capacity, particularly at locations serving many vehicles or supporting long-distance travel.

Grids often need to be sized for peak demand even though it is only needed briefly. Upgrades add cost and delay, putting rural corridors, older urban districts and smaller commercial sites out of reach.

Battery-integrated chargers take a different approach; rather than upgrade a site’s grid to match the charger’s power levels, battery-integrated solutions leverage the site’s spare grid capacity by integrating energy storage directly inside the charger to make up the difference.

Have you read?

The battery fills slowly from a modest grid connection, then releases energy quickly when a car plugs in. This is what the utility industry calls a non-wires alternative, which defers the need for costly distribution grid upgrades, facilitating deployment and reducing lead times.

US National Renewable Energy Laboratory analysis shows that well-sized systems can cut the grid capacity a fast-charging station needs by roughly 50–80%, with no difference for drivers. Operational and economical reliability within the local grid constraints is key.

By integrating intelligent demand management software, battery-integrated charging can also lower electricity consumption costs, provide resilient backup power and monetize grid services alongside its charging operations.

In Detroit, the City's Office of Mobility Innovation deployed an ElectricFish charger at Eastern Market, able to deliver up to 400 kilowatts while drawing about 30 kilowatts from the grid. The model suits places where drivers already stop for brief periods, such as fuel stations, convenience stores, fleet depots and rural highway stops.

Rethinking what public charging can look like

These examples point to a broader lesson: there is no single best charging model. Future networks will likely combine different technologies under different ownership models based on location, user dynamics and local constraints.

Three principles can guide this:

Start with the use case: Speed, location and ownership should fit how people use a place. No technology is an end in itself.

Make charging dependable and easy: Reliability, transparent pricing and the ability to use any network matter as much as raw speed.

Plan charging alongside everything else: Charging should be built into urban, transport and electricity-system planning, so that cities, utilities and operators work from the same map, including where the grid has room to spare.

Policy-makers can support all three through clear guidelines, practical roadmaps, streamlined permitting and better coordination between the authorities that manage streets and those that manage the grid. Cities can also test ideas at a small scale first, as San Francisco and Detroit have done with It's Electric curbside chargers. Without these steps, even well-designed solutions can stall before they reach the street.

Closing the EV charging gap will take a mix of approaches, each matched to the community it serves. Done well, charging can create value for drivers, cities, property owners, utilities and operators alike, and bring electric mobility to far more people.

text:
Newport Beach, CA, Oct. 26, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Bimergen Energy Corporation (NYSE American: BESS), a developer, owner, and operator of utility-scale and distributed battery energy storage systems, today announced that its wholly owned subsidiary, Emergen Commodities LLC, has filed an application with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) for an Option 2 Retail Electric Provider (REP) certificate. The application represents a step toward adding retail electricity capabilities to Bimergen’s energy infrastructure business. Subject to regulatory approval and applicable market requirements, the certification would enable Bimergen, through Emergen Commodities, to supply electricity directly to qualifying data center customers in Texas.

“Pursuing retail electric provider certification is a step toward broadening Bimergen’s capabilities in the Texas energy market,” said Cole Johnson, Co-CEO of Bimergen Energy. “The substantial electricity requirements of large data centers present a compelling commercial opportunity. By building on our energy infrastructure expertise and adding retail electricity supply capabilities, we believe we can position Bimergen to participate in this growing market and create additional opportunities for long-term value.”

Supplying electricity to large data center customers could generate substantial revenue for Emergen Commodities and its parent company, Bimergen Energy. The significant and ongoing electricity requirements of these facilities present an opportunity to establish recurring revenue streams through customer supply agreements.

Texas’ Option 2 certification provides a pathway to serve specifically identified customers contracting for at least one megawatt of capacity. Subject to regulatory approval and applicable market requirements, the certification would establish a foundation for Emergen Commodities to participate in this segment of the Texas retail electricity market.

In parallel with the regulatory process, Bimergen is working with multiple counterparties to provide credit support for large data center loads. These efforts are intended to support the electricity supply arrangements needed to serve customers with substantial power requirements and advance Bimergen’s proposed retail electricity business.

Bimergen’s broader strategy focuses on advancing battery energy storage projects through development, technology partnerships, and collaboration with capital providers. The proposed retail electricity capability would complement that strategy by expanding the ways Bimergen participates in the energy market and connects its infrastructure expertise with electricity needs.

“We are focused on translating this opportunity into a commercially viable business that can contribute meaningfully to Bimergen's long-term growth,” said Bob Brilon, Co-CEO of Bimergen Energy. “Our work to establish the necessary credit support and advance the regulatory process reflects a disciplined approach to entering this market. We see the potential for substantial revenue from serving large electricity customers while continuing to advance our core battery energy storage business.”

Emergen Commodities filed its application with the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) on October 5, 2026, under Docket No. 60368. The application is currently under regulatory review and remains subject to PUCT approval.

text:
A battery developer and manufacturer has begun production at its new Webster facility, which leaders there say will help the company with its goals to expand the use of long-duration energy storage in New York.

Ashlawn Energy LLC marked the start of manufacturing for its VanCharg vanadium redox flow batteries at an Oct. 15 event at the company’s 10,000-square-foot site on the Xerox Webster campus. The facility opened earlier this year and is expected to bring 20 jobs to the region.

The company manufactures and assembles its proprietary battery systems at the Webster location, combining production operations under one roof as it works to scale its technology for stationary energy storage.

“Watching Ashlawn Energy go from concept to actualization has been a long time coming and it is a proud moment for me to see production begin,” said Norma Byron, the company’s president and founder.

New York has ambitious climate goals, Byron said, and the company believes its technology can help advance those efforts.

The production launch marks a step toward bringing the company’s battery systems to a broader market as utilities, businesses and communities look for ways to store renewable energy, manage peak electricity demand and strengthen grid reliability.

VanCharg batteries store electricity generated by sources such as wind and solar, as well as the electrical grid, and release it when needed. The systems can provide backup power for hundreds of homes and help support electricity transmission and distribution.

The batteries also can help customers reduce electricity costs and carbon emissions by storing power when demand and prices are lower, then using it during peak-demand periods.

Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, VanCharg systems use a water-based electrolyte and are nonflammable, according to the company. Ashlawn says its batteries can operate for up to 30 years and provide four to 14 hours of energy storage, compared with a lifespan of up to seven years and one to four hours of storage for the lithium-ion systems cited by the company.

The technology is designed for stationary applications where extended storage duration, safety and scalability are important considerations.

Greater Rochester’s existing energy and manufacturing capabilities helped attract Ashlawn to the region, said Matt Hurlbutt, president and CEO of Greater Rochester Enterprise.

“Energy innovation is a key industry strength that made Greater Rochester the right location for Ashlawn Energy to establish operations and scale production of its energy storage solutions,” Hurlbutt said.

The company also is drawing on engineering talent and research resources at Rochester Institute of Technology. Its longstanding collaboration with RIT’s Center of Excellence in Advanced and Sustainable Manufacturing focuses on optimizing the battery design and supporting commercial-scale production. Ashlawn also is leveraging resources at RIT’s Golisano Institute for Sustainability.

Founded in 2008, Ashlawn was established by Byron, a former defense contractor who sought to apply her knowledge of hydrogen fuel cells to energy storage. The company was previously based in Vestal, in Broome County.

Its move to Webster was influenced in part by its existing relationship with RIT and the opportunity to advance manufacturing of its VanCharg technology.

The company has also received recognition and funding for its efforts.

text:
Today, the European Commission launched the T-MED Investment Platform, to mobilise large-scale investment in renewable energy and clean technologies across the Mediterranean. The platform is a key component of the Trans-Mediterranean Renewable Energy and Clean Tech Cooperation Initiative (T-MED), a flagship initiative of the Pact for the Mediterranean.

The platform was presented by Commissioner for the Mediterranean Dubravka Šuica during a stakeholder event in Brussels, bringing together European and international financial institutions, private investors and project promoters to identify investment opportunities and projects that could benefit from Commission support.

EU support will include up to €4.5 billion in guarantee capacity under the European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus (EFSD+), helping reduce investment risks, attract private capital and accelerate the implementation of viable renewable energy and clean technology projects across the region. The platform will facilitate cooperation between financial institutions, investors and project promoters, matching promising projects with potential sources of financing and helping turn investment opportunities into concrete projects.

The Mediterranean holds considerable untapped renewable energy potential. The T-MED Investment Platform aims to unlock this potential by supporting investments in renewable electricity generation, renewable hydrogen, electricity transmission and distribution networks, energy storage, cross-border interconnections and clean technology manufacturing.

Beyond financing, the platform will support efforts to improve regulatory frameworks, permitting procedures, grid access and power purchase agreements, while promoting skills development and local clean technology value chains. By addressing these barriers to investment, T-MED will help strengthen energy security, deepen economic cooperation and create new opportunities for sustainable growth across the Mediterranean.

Turning ambition into concrete investments

T-MED is already taking shape through projects that concretely illustrate the initiative's ambitions and objectives:

In Egypt, T-MED is enabling the modernisation and expansion of the national electricity grid, with a total investment value of €1.6 billion. The programme includes the construction of state-of-the-art substations and the installation of advanced transmission lines to integrate solar and wind power generated in the Red Sea and Gulf of Suez regions into the national grid. The investments are expected to reduce transmission losses, improve electricity reliability, strengthen energy security and support sustainable economic development. They will also contribute to regional electricity cooperation and future clean-energy trade and integration across the Mediterranean.

In Ain Sokhna, Egypt, T-MED enabled the first Green Ammonia project in North Africa, a €575 million operation, with a European electrolyser at its heart. The ammonia produced is exported to the EU market.

In Egypt, through an EU guarantee T-MED has enabled the construction of one of the biggest hybrid solar photovoltaic projects in Africa worth around €430 million.

The Niat and Rasgha Wind Projects in Egypt will bring 500 MW of new onshore wind to the Gulf of Suez, strengthening the renewable base for Egypt's future hydrogen production through European wind technology.

In Tunisia, T-MED is supporting the construction of two 100 MW solar photovoltaic plants and their associated transmission infrastructure, amounting to total EU support of about €92 million and €80 million respectively. The projects will back private sector participation in the Tunisian power sector and increase the country's energy security and resilience.

Background

The T-MED Investment Platform reflects the Pact for the Mediterranean's ambition to build a Common Mediterranean Space that is connected, prosperous, resilient and secure. By translating this shared ambition into concrete investment opportunities, the EU and its partners aim to support the diversification of renewable energy systems and supply chains, create new economic opportunities and contribute to the region's long-term prosperity and stability.

By 2035, T-MED aims to mobilise up to €25 billion in expected investments in renewable energy production, electricity grids, interconnections and clean technologies, alongside the training and upskilling of up to 10 000 workers.

T-MED is a flagship initiative of the Pact for the Mediterranean, which was developed by the Commission and the European External Action Service, and adopted by the College in October 2025, ahead of its official launch by EU and Southern Mediterranean partners on 28 November 2025, on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of the Barcelona Declaration. Rooted in the principles of co-creation, co-ownership and shared responsibility, the Pact is the result of an unprecedented, inclusive consultation process, ensuring alignment with the real needs and aspirations of the citizens on both shores of the Mediterranean. It is a joint effort between the EU, its Member States and the Southern Mediterranean partners, to work together on shared priorities for a connected, integrated, prosperous, resilient and secure Common Mediterranean Space.

title: Roads That Charge Your EV While You Drive Are Incredible, But Good Luck Finding One
description:
However, while these so-called "electric roads" actually already exist, it could be a very long time before we see them deployed on a meaningful scale, if ever.
Before deciding if electric roads are worth installing, it's a good idea to look at the cost of building them.
Electric roads may make the most sense on busy freight corridors and around places like ports, where trucks drive along predictable routes.
For electric roads to spread, the technology will need to show that savings from smaller batteries and reduced downtime can outweigh the expense of installing and maintaining the roads.
The future of electric roads may therefore lie not in electrifying every highway, but in targeting the routes where they can deliver the greatest benefit.
text:
There's something wonderfully appealing about the idea of wirelessly charging your electric vehicle (EV) on the very road that you're driving along. The technology could help ease range anxiety and save you time by reducing the need to stop and recharge on longer journeys. However, while these so-called "electric roads" actually already exist, it could be a very long time before we see them deployed on a meaningful scale, if ever. Plus, how do they even work?

The principle is actually pretty simple. Coils buried under the road surface generate an electromagnetic field that transfers electricity to a receiver fitted to the underside of a moving vehicle. This electricity can then charge the battery. Other systems exist, too, using conductive rails embedded in the road, and overhead wires for specially equipped trucks. An important point is that vehicles need to be specially built to receive power from these roads, so you can't just drive any EV onto one and expect the battery to begin charging.

The wireless technology isn't new, either. In 2009, researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) demonstrated charging from equipment embedded beneath a road. By 2013, specially equipped electric buses were operating on a charging route in the South Korean city of Gumi, and since then, trials have taken place in Sweden, Italy, Germany, Japan, and the U.S., with Detroit opening a short stretch of electrified road as part of an ongoing demonstration project in 2023. Recent examples include a 1.5 km stretch of motorway near Paris that was fitted with wireless charging coils in 2025, and in 2026 researchers in Indiana successfully charged an electric heavy-duty truck traveling at highway speeds. Such projects show that the technology works, albeit in limited real-world settings using compatible prototype vehicles.

Before deciding if electric roads are worth installing, it's a good idea to look at the cost of building them. Construction estimates range from $1.8 million to $3.6 million per kilometer, including infrastructure and connection to the electricity grid.

While private motorists with compatible EVs might find electric roads to be extremely convenient, such vehicles aren't yet widely available to consumers, and investing in the infrastructure solely for their benefit would be hard to justify. After all, many EV drivers can charge their vehicles overnight. While those without access to home charging would gain more from the technology, it seems sensible to invest instead in conventional charging infrastructure, avoiding the expense and traffic disruption that would result from installing the technology beneath existing roads. The real benefit might, however, come with commercial vehicles, particularly autonomous trucks like those being tested in Texas. Trucks and human drivers that travel over long distances have expensive downtime, plus large batteries add weight and reduce the amount of the freight they can carry. Charging while moving would potentially allow for a smaller battery, while autonomous trucks would be able to operate for much longer periods, with stops only needed for loading, unloading, and maintenance.

Electric roads may make the most sense on busy freight corridors and around places like ports, where trucks drive along predictable routes. For electric roads to spread, the technology will need to show that savings from smaller batteries and reduced downtime can outweigh the expense of installing and maintaining the roads. The future of electric roads may therefore lie not in electrifying every highway, but in targeting the routes where they can deliver the greatest benefit.

text:
On the second day of early in-person voting for the upcoming midterm elections, Democratic House hopeful Adam Hamawy joined a group of environmental activists to protest a planned data center in South Brunswick.

The campaign stop shows Hamawy, a physician who is hoping to succeed Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman in the 12th Congressional District, recognizes that public anger over data centers is key to energizing Democratic voters hoping to win back control of the House of Representatives.

In an interview last month with the New Jersey Monitor, Hamawy said federal regulations on data center construction are needed because the environmental and energy issues they present cross state lines. He said he does not support a ban on data centers, but backs a temporary pause on construction to study their impact.

“We need to slow down. We are moving too fast,” he said. “It’s uncontrolled.”

The election is Nov. 3. All 12 of New Jersey’s House seats are on the ballot, as is Sen. Cory Booker (D), who is seeking a third full term against Republican Justin Murphy.

New Jersey Democrats say if they take back control of the House next year, moving to rein in data center construction and the artificial intelligence industry is a top priority. They say they want to push bills to make data centers supply their own clean power and call AI executives to testify before Congress.

“I think the entire AI conversation is very high on the priority list,” said Rep. Rob Menendez (D-08), who is running for a third term with no GOP challenger. “We can’t wait another day to have this conversation.”

A new Politico Poll says half of Americans oppose data centers being built within three miles of their home and are more likely to oppose candidates who back data center construction. Democrats are benefiting from the backlash, the poll says.

So far, the fight over data center regulation has played out largely at the local level. In New Jersey, more than 100 of the state’s 564 municipalities have banned or restricted new construction.

There are at least 80 data centers in New Jersey, according to South Jersey Climate News. And while some states are considering moratoriums on data center construction, including neighboring New York, our governor, Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, has resisted calls for such a ban.

In January, Menendez introduced two bills targeting data centers, one that would require them to generate all the electricity they use, with clean energy targets in 2040, and another that would require them to report how much water is used and greenhouse gases emitted every six months. He also pointed to other legislation introduced that would halt construction of AI data centers until the federal government requires approval for new AI models.

“States are sort of in the laboratory now, and they’re thinking about AI regulations, but we very much need a federal framework,” Menendez said.

Hamawy, a surgeon whose chief opponent is Republican Gregg Mele, said he’s used AI in his medical practice to increase efficiency with paperwork, but sees clear downsides of the technology, like the mistakes it makes when used for research or the impact it’s had on children’s reading and writing skills.

“We need to just kind of make sure that we are doing this correctly, and maximizing the good and minimizing the bad,” he said.

Carmen Bucco, a Republican challenging Rep. LaMonica McIver (D) in the 10th District, lives in Kenilworth, about a mile from where the cloud computing company CoreWeave is now building a $1.8 billion data center. So he fully understands the community’s concerns about how much water the facilities use, the noise they make, and the energy they consume.

But he finds some hypocrisy in the revolts now raging in communities around the state, noting that no one protests outside golf courses over their water consumption.

People initially complained about the effects of cell phones and microwaves when they were first introduced too, he said.

“And all these things are here now, and maybe they’re affecting our lives, maybe they’re not. We’ll never know the truth. Science is good, but there’s no 100% in science either,” he said.

Data centers are also a hot issue down in the 2nd District, where Rep. Jeff Van Drew is seeking reelection against Democrat Zack Mullock.

Mullock, the Cape May mayor, regards data centers as an environmental justice issue, pointing to the controversial data center in Vineland that state officials recently fined $1 million for installing dozens of unpermitted power generators. The problems that have arisen since that project broke ground earlier this year prove that policymakers must demand more transparency around data center development before greenlighting anything, he said.

“This is a huge, huge, huge project, and that’s not what it was sold to the public,” Mullock said.

Mullock said he would support a moratorium on data center development until policymakers can learn more about their impacts. He opposes tax breaks for developers, noting the multibillion-dollar price tags of bigger projects.

“I think data centers are a part of our future. But we’re at the genesis. We are at the moment where we can choose our future,” he said. “We the people should shape that future. It shouldn’t be made in backroom deals.”

The CEO of the firm behind construction of the Vineland data center has said Van Drew’s support of the facility was critical. Van Drew has expressed support for data centers but has joined some of his colleagues in pushing for guardrails on the industry.

Earlier this year, he joined Rep. Josh Riley (D-New York) on a bill aimed at stopping data center projects from driving up energy bills.

“Artificial intelligence has the potential to do a lot of good for our country, but that growth must be handled responsibly,” Van Drew said in a statement when that bill was introduced. “Families and small businesses are already paying far too much for electricity, and they should not be hit with even higher bills because major data center projects require massive amounts of energy and new infrastructure.”

Bucco said if elected, he would restrict data center development to rural areas, prioritize bolstering the power grid, and require data center developers to generate their own power and water supply. He opposes tax breaks for them, but said their development is inevitable.

“I understand progress. I might get hated for it, but that’s life. If we don’t progress, we sit in the Stone Age, and AI is going to be here,” he said. “It’s just a matter of what towns want them and what towns don’t.”

text:
India's electric vehicle (EV) industry needs to address battery costs and recycling challenges to make electric mobility more affordable and build a sustainable battery supply chain. While new battery chemistries could create opportunities to reduce costs, an effective recycling ecosystem will be important to recovering valuable materials and returning them to manufacturing.

In an exclusive conversation with Samiksha Choudhary of BW Auto World at the Renewable Energy India Expo 2026 and The Battery Show India, Jai Asundi, Executive Director of the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), discussed the challenges facing India's battery ecosystem. He said emerging chemistries such as sodium-ion could help bring battery prices down, with significant reductions potentially emerging over the next five years.

Asundi also called for a more mission-driven approach to battery recycling, highlighting the need for stronger collection systems, mandatory recycling requirements and better integration between recovered materials and manufacturing. He also discussed how battery storage can support renewable energy availability and how recycling could eventually help automakers reduce electric vehicle costs.

Read the edited excerpts below

Q. What are the biggest factors driving battery costs in India, and when could consumers expect prices to fall enough to narrow the price gap between EVs and petrol vehicles?

I think the material itself is the biggest factor driving battery costs. Most battery chemistries today are related to lithium-ion, but if new chemistries such as sodium-ion become more widely available, they could bring prices down further.

We are usually sceptical in the short run, but we have to be optimistic in the long run. I would say that over the next five years, we could see some significant drops in prices.

Q. How can manufacturers balance battery performance, affordability and longevity?

I think the way to achieve this is by identifying new battery chemistries. Manufacturers need to explore new ideas because the characteristics of traditional chemistries are fairly well understood. New chemistries could open up further possibilities.

Q. How prepared is India to recycle EV batteries, and what needs to change?

I would say we are not very prepared. We need to approach this in a mission-driven manner. There is discussion within the ministry, and people recognise that this is a problem that will emerge in the future, but I think we should be better prepared and start thinking about it more seriously.

Q. Which policy or regulatory changes could make the biggest difference to battery recycling in India?

There needs to be a stronger framework. We currently have extended producer responsibility, under which manufacturers have responsibilities for managing their products at the end of their life. I think mandatory battery recycling requirements, backed by strict enforcement, could make a significant difference.

Q. What are the biggest challenges in building an effective battery recycling ecosystem?

The challenge is collection. That has always been the case with recycling programmes. We need to establish how batteries will be collected and ensure that, once collected, the materials move through the supply chain and return to manufacturing. That is essential for creating a genuine circular economy.

Q. Can battery recycling eventually help automakers reduce costs and make EVs more affordable?

If effective recycling programmes can recover materials and supply them back into battery manufacturing, automakers would certainly look at the opportunity. They are always seeking ways to reduce vehicle costs, and the battery is currently the most expensive component of an electric vehicle.

Batteries used in vehicles may also be considered for power-sector applications after their automotive life. Vehicles require batteries that deliver high power, and once a battery falls below a particular performance threshold, it may no longer meet automotive requirements. This is why some applications focus on using batteries after their first life in vehicles.

Q. Can battery storage make solar and wind power available when generation is low?

Yes, that is the whole idea behind battery storage. You store energy when it is available and supply it when it is needed.

Currently, storage systems typically provide two, four or six hours of storage. Reaching round-the-clock renewable power will take time, but battery storage can already be useful in locations where electricity demand rises during the early evening.

Driverless vehicles are not yet authorized in Illinois. But state Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago, has called for a formal framework, through House Bill 4663, to test and deploy self-driving cars in the state. The bill thus far has been stalled in the General Assembly.

Buckner has also urged the newly founded Northern Illinois Transit Authority to study how autonomous vehicles could work alongside the existing public transport network, if they’re made legal.

Buckner’s bill would create the Autonomous Vehicle Pilot Project Act, which would restrict testing to counties with over a million residents, as well as Sangamon County or the Metro East region of Madison, St. Clair and Monroe counties.

But this legislation will not authorize autonomous vehicles on the streets immediately, Buckner said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“What we're asking for is a very controlled program with a certain number of cars on the road,” said Buckner. “We can actually take that data and figure out what's the best way to implement the policy.”

Buckner also said the legislation aims to determine Illinois' specific needs through research and proper implementation.

“I don't want Illinois to take everybody else's word for it. I want Illinois to actually do the work, to look through the processes and get the political processes in place, and to walk away and say what we did when no other state did, which is study this intensely, intentionally, and figure out what the way forward was,” Buckner said.

Jim Merrell, advocacy director with the Active Transportation Alliance in Chicago, said Illinois should allow local governments to pass regulations on autonomous vehicles beyond what’s in state law. This differs from House Bill 4663, which he said preempts local authority in some ways, meaning state laws override local ones.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"We think that's something that's going to be really important for a city like Chicago to be able to regulate how and where autonomous vehicles are allowed to operate to make sure that they're not interfering with other infrastructure or transit usage like bus stops or bike lanes,” Merrell said.

The Active Transportation Alliance pointed to another stalled piece of legislation in the General Assembly — House Bill 4789 — that would establish the Automated Driving Systems Development Act, which would introduce stronger implementation measures and create a review committee within the Illinois Department of Transportation.

“Waymo is committed to making roads safer, creating stable local careers, and extending mobility to people who need it in the state of Illinois," a spokesperson said in a statement.

Potential impacts

One issue autonomous vehicles can solve in Illinois is the first- and last-mile problem, especially in neighborhoods where the last station of public transport is far from passengers' homes, Buckner said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Merrell said there are more efficient ways to solve this problem, like expanding transit service, improving bus reliability, and creating bike lanes.

“Inside the city, you still would run into that space efficiency issue, while there are plenty of other alternatives that are much more efficient and sustainable that are already working,” Merrell said.

But autonomous vehicles at high-congestion points may worsen traffic, said Dany Robles, senior legislative director at the Illinois Environmental Council.

“It really comes down to, how are they integrated into more congested areas so that we're not continuing to exacerbate those congestions and pollution from other vehicles around them,” said Robles.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

For the Illinois Environmental Council, the approach to analyzing autonomous vehicles includes several angles, Robles said.

“A lot of AVs are electric vehicles — they're pulling resources from renewable energy, but then there's a lot of emerging concerns too surrounding the loss of jobs in the vehicle space or in the shared driver space,” Robles said.

This is the reason why some labor unions have opposed the Autonomous Vehicle Pilot Project Act. Among them is Service Employees International Union Local 1, which serves five Midwestern states.

Bailey Koch-Farwana, a union spokesperson, said that according to their economic analysis, every autonomous vehicles that hits the road replaces four human drivers. This is because autonomous vehicles can operate 24/7 and do not need breaks.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But there are ways to balance this outcome, Koch-Farwana said.

“There’s a just transition that could happen, you know, for every driver that leaves the app, like the Uber or Lyft app, then a (driverless car) can enter the road,” Koch-Farwana said. “Right now, there’s nothing in that legislation that regulates that or even cares about the working people behind it.”

Buckner responded to criticism that autonomous vehicles will take jobs away from rideshare drivers by saying that everyone needs to be part of the conversation as researchers explore how to implement these vehicles efficiently in the future.

On the other hand, Koch-Farwana said labor unions and rideshare drivers, who have been unionized since August, still haven't been invited to the table.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Next steps

Buckner pointed to the Bay Area as a potential model for integrating autonomous vehicles into public transit.

The San Francisco Bay Area has a program that incentivizes autonomous vehicles to solve the first- and last-mile problem. Passengers who use Waymo, a company owned by Google that operates robotaxis, and go on to public transport within two hours get a $2.85 credit for future Waymo trips, according to Streetsblog San Francisco.

Buckner also said the state does not have to follow this exact example of regional planning.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“I am not going into this with my mind made up about what I want. The only thing I want is data,” said Buckner. “I want people to be able to utilize them (AVs) and see if they make sense for them. And I want data for it to come back and then make an informed decision.”

For research on potential autonomous vehicles implementation to begin, House Bill 4663 needs to clear the House Rules Committee, be assigned to a substantive standing committee, like the transportation or executive committee, pass the full House, and repeat the process in the Senate.

When asked whether the push could occur during the November veto session, Buckner said he is respecting the legislative process.

text:
A cabinet split has emerged over whether to approve drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, with the chancellor, John Healey, in favour of the controversial North Sea project.

The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is ultimately in charge of the decision, and the Guardian reported last week that she was leaning towards rejecting it after granting permission for the smaller Jackdaw gasfield.

It is understood, however, that Healey backs approving the licence, which is on hold over concerns about the project’s environmental impact.

The chancellor hinted at his support last week when he told ITV he expected oil and gas revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, suggesting he was anticipating income from Rosebank. The prime minister would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.

No 10 declined to comment on Sunday after the Mail on Sunday reported that Andy Burnham and Healey had agreed to try to push the project through, saying it was a matter for the energy secretary.

Fahnbulleh is responsible, but the views of Burnham and Healey will hold weight in the choice over whether or not to go ahead.

She told the Guardian the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.

“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”

If the Rosebank field is rejected, it would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. A final decision is expected before the end of the year.

Labour MPs said on Wednesday that there would be a big pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessary part of the transition to net zero.

MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent.

Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet made her decision. Rosebank would produce emissions about seven times greater than Jackdaw, and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe it would do less for UK energy security, given that most of the oil would be exported.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “We do not comment on speculation. The North Sea remains a vital national asset, and oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come – alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.

“Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process.”

Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through an energy wealth fund. She said last week that the fund would be given £2bn in the budget.

“When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes.

She could not, however, say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the fund, or how much that may generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.

[SMM PV Flash] South Korea Proposes Extending Renewable Capacity Targets to Public Agencies

South Korea's Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment opened a public comment period on 25 October on a partial amendment to the enforcement decree of the Act on the Promotion of Renewable Energy Development, Use and Deployment, which would bring public agencies into renewable capacity target management. The change follows the complete replacement of the Renewable Portfolio Standard with a fixed-price contract scheme, and would set targets on two metrics — renewable capacity each agency installs directly and idle land it provides to generators — so non-generation entities such as the Korea Expressway Corporation and KORAIL also carry obligations. The proposal supports the government's 100 GW renewable target for 2030 and must complete the legislative process after the comment period before taking effect.
