title: Here are the top 6 trends shaping the energy sector in 2026 - RSM US
description:
Throughout 2026, companies in the energy sector will need to adapt their operations proactively to thrive in an evolving landscape.
The evolving energy mix, shifting energy policies and supply chain dynamics are just some of the factors that businesses in this sector face.
Here are the top six trends RSM has identified for energy companies this year.
Digital transformation and the rise of AI The energy sector faces new pressures and opportunities from the ongoing energy transition and digital transformation, not to mention the surge in energy demand.
Middle market energy companies can benefit from the lessons learned and investments made by early AI adopters—typically larger energy companies—to chart their own AI adoption journey.
text:
This article has been updated from the original, published in 2025, to reflect new events, conditions or research.

Throughout 2026, companies in the energy sector will need to adapt their operations proactively to thrive in an evolving landscape. This need to adapt applies across the energy ecosystem, whether oil and gas, power and utilities or renewable/clean energy companies.

The evolving energy mix, shifting energy policies and supply chain dynamics are just some of the factors that businesses in this sector face. A continued focus on resiliency will be essential for companies to remain competitive.

Here are the top six trends RSM has identified for energy companies this year.

1. Growth across energy sources

The North American energy landscape is experiencing a major transformation. Demand for energy is growing rapidly, including electricity, natural gas, renewables and more. Electricity demand growth is fueled by a combination of factors: increasing data center needs, the reshoring of manufacturing, widespread electrification and electric vehicle adoption.

To meet this rising demand, the sector has adopted an “all-of-the-above" approach to the energy mix—oil, natural gas, renewables, nuclear, geothermal and other emerging technologies—while also working on the underlying infrastructure needed to transport energy and ensure a reliable supply. Unfortunately, in the meantime, supply and demand dynamics combined with investment in grid modernization and resilience are driving up electricity prices for consumers and businesses.

Oil price dynamics continue to influence investment and supply decisions, while liquefied natural gas (LNG) is playing a pivotal role in meeting domestic and global energy needs. Major technology firms and utility providers are increasingly collaborating to address the challenges posed by data center growth and grid reliability, reflecting the industry’s commitment to resilient infrastructure and flexible energy solutions.

While the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) brought changes to incentives for solar and wind projects, the clean energy sector is expected to continue growing, though more slowly than in previous years. Rather than replacing oil and gas, clean energy will complement these sources, with natural gas no longer seen as a “bridge” fuel in the energy transition but a “backbone” fuel for decades to come.

2. Shifting energy policy and market dynamics

In the United States, a higher-for-longer cost of capital has been driving energy companies toward consolidation and streamlining; it is also causing them to preserve cash and to have a more strategic focus on improving enterprise value through margin expansion and additional revenue opportunities. For example, traditional upstream oil and oilfield services companies are even getting into power generation-related projects.

The OBBBA is also reshaping investment strategies, with the sector balancing fossil fuels and renewables amid evolving regulatory incentives. Geopolitical shifts, including changes in LNG export policies and global tensions, add complexity to market dynamics and affect oil price stability.

Nuclear energy has also seen a resurgence in interest in recent years—not only traditional reactors but small modular reactors (SMRs), microreactors and even fusion. Nuclear investment is coming from a wide range of organizations, including technology companies, philanthropists and venture capitalists, with additional support coming from OBBBA incentives.

Canada is shaping its policies to attract investments in priority sectors, such as clean technology, the electric vehicle supply chain and critical minerals exploration. Governments at the federal and provincial levels offer investment tax credits and incentives, funding and grants through various innovation funds and programs, government financing and targeted support negotiated directly with manufacturers. Canada and other global markets also continue to emphasize decarbonization and other environmental, social and governance goals. While U.S. policy has de-emphasized these areas over the past year, the continued focus on these issues elsewhere means U.S. companies doing business globally will need to consider them.

3. Digital transformation and the rise of AI

The energy sector faces new pressures and opportunities from the ongoing energy transition and digital transformation, not to mention the surge in energy demand. To remain competitive and resilient, energy companies are increasing their adoption of cloud solutions, automation and/or AI across business and operational processes, providing improved efficiency, reliability and safety. This will become critical as IT and operational technology networks advance, Internet of Things-enabled facilities proliferate and utilities update the smart-grid infrastructure put in place 15 to 20 years ago to a more modern, advanced metering infrastructure.

Analytical AI technologies, including machine learning, have come front and center as companies digitize their businesses with use cases ranging from the back office and cybersecurity to field operations and process optimization. Middle market energy companies can benefit from the lessons learned and investments made by early AI adopters—typically larger energy companies—to chart their own AI adoption journey. To take full advantage of AI, organizations should understand their existing capabilities, determine how to manage new risks and challenges, and collect and refine their data with intentionality.

Alongside AI, energy companies should explore how digital twin solutions can help them adapt in the current environment. Virtually modeling supply-and-demand scenarios before making costly changes to business operations can help businesses make more informed decisions, and digital twins can help companies in the energy value chain looking to expand their capacity while limiting capital spending.

4. Cybersecurity and resilience

As companies across the energy value chain are increasingly becoming digital-first companies with interconnected systems and automated business and industrial processes, there are more opportunities for cybercriminals to compromise businesses and disrupt critical operations. This has contributed to a shift in view on the value of cybersecurity for energy companies; once a cost center focused largely on reducing risk, mature cybersecurity programs have become a source of competitive advantage.

Energy companies play a key role in global critical infrastructure, providing the fuel that people, companies and countries depend on. But this also makes them the target of nation-state attackers and cyber warfare. As we’ve seen in recent years, successful cyberattacks on critical energy companies can have a ripple effect on other businesses.

According to the 2025 RSM US Middle Market Business Index special report on cybersecurity, nearly one in five (18%) middle market companies experienced a data breach in the previous year, falling from a record-high 28% in the data from the 2024 report. The decline in reported breaches is certainly positive, but 2025’s results are consistent with data from previous years, outside of the spike in 2024. However, with methods becoming more sophisticated, some attacks may go undetected, highlighting the importance of continuously strengthening controls.

Energy companies—and any third parties they work with—need to raise the bar on protecting themselves in this new world where workers, machines, supply chains and organizations are becoming ever more digitally connected.

5. Supply chain shifts

Tariffs and an evolving trade environment will continue to affect organizations' supply chains and investment decisions, with direct impacts ranging from higher prices on key metals like steel and copper, as well as finished goods, to extended lead times for some goods. Rising electricity demand and the surge in data center needs are also causing ripple effects across energy supply chains.

Some U.S. companies are responding by prioritizing the reshoring of key production activities. This shift is driven not only by a desire to reduce tariff exposure but also to capitalize on tax incentives and strengthen domestic supply chains for critical technologies and resources, such as semiconductors and battery components. Addressing these supply chain vulnerabilities is crucial for supporting the rapid growth of the power grid and ensuring reliable access to the materials needed for energy and battery storage solutions.

6. Workforce transformation

As the energy sector navigates the growing influence of technology, particularly AI and emerging energy innovations, and as the nature of energy production/generation sources and the systems managing them change, the impact on its workforce will be profound. Companies must adopt more intentional and innovative approaches to attract and retain talent, especially as employee expectations and demographics continue to evolve.

The rapid advancement of AI and the digitization of operations demand that the current workforce adapt through upskilling and reskilling. Employees must acquire capabilities to manage and maintain new AI-driven tools and energy technologies, while continuing to support legacy systems.

This shift calls for a renewed focus on developing new skill sets that enable employees to leverage analytics in decision making and to collaborate effectively with robotic systems. Energy companies should prioritize comprehensive training and workforce development initiatives, ensuring workers are prepared for roles shaped by AI and digital transformation. Strategic workforce planning will also be vital as organizations determine which functions to develop internally and which to outsource to maximize growth and efficiency.

Ahead of the 33rd APEC Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, U.S. respondents highlighted the need for greater coordination on trade policies and increased attention to energy challenges, amid shifting U.S. trade policies and geopolitical tensions affecting economic cooperation across the Asia-Pacific.

The meeting will take place in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, from November 18 to 19, under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." Leaders from the 21 APEC member economies, which together account for around 60 percent of global GDP and nearly half of global trade, are expected to discuss ways to strengthen regional economic integration, promote open trade and foster shared prosperity across the Asia-Pacific.

China Global Television Network (CGTN) spoke with people in New York City about the challenges facing regional cooperation and the issues they hope APEC leaders will address.

John Smith Riocco, a consultant, said inconsistencies in U.S. trade policies, particularly regarding tariffs, could make trade coordination a key topic at the meeting.

"What's going on in U.S. politics today changed the way that other Asian countries deal with the United States. I think it's fair to say that we have been inconsistent, for example, on our trade policies. If you look at what happened with tariffs in the last 12 to 18 months, for example. So I imagine that would be a very big topic," said Riocco.

Researcher Mercedes Gallego said energy should be a topic at the meeting, citing disruptions caused by geopolitical tensions and China's role in renewable energy.

"This year, the topic of APEC should be energy. The energy sector has been very much affected by the closing of the Strait of Hromuz and the war on Iran. But at the same time, China has the leading renewable products and batteries, solar batteries, and other products that sell very well in Europe but not in America," said Gallego.

title: A weaker ETS puts €90 billion in green investment at risk - The Parliament Magazine
description:
Europe's carbon market is the very foundation of its climate policy.
On top of this, the European Parliament's draft report would weaken the market even further, potentially injecting more uncertainty into the outlook for the carbon price.
A €90 billion shortfall According to a new study by Strategic Perspectives and Veyt, the Commission's proposal would blow a gigantic financial hole in Europe's climate plans.
Industries covered by the ETS would spend €90 billion less on decarbonization technologies by 2040 than under current law, a drop of more than a quarter.
A stable and robust carbon price is non-negotiable for European industrial leadership.
text:
The review of the European Union's Emissions Trading System, or ETS, is now underway to bring the mechanism in line with the EU's new climate target: a 90% cut in net greenhouse emission by 2040 compared with 1990 levels.

Yet that goal appears far off today. The ETS has helped decarbonize the power sector, but the EU urgently needs to drive investments in hard-to-abate sectors, where fossil fuels still dominate.

Europe's carbon market is the very foundation of its climate policy. By putting a price on carbon dioxide, the cap-and-trade system gives industries a steady incentive to invest in alternative production methods, be competitive and reduce emissions.

The ETS also generates large revenues that can fund climate and clean energy projects.

A proven tool

The carbon market cannot transform industry on its own. The right enabling conditions, whether in energy, infrastructure or markets for clean materials and products, are critical.

But it is an essential industrial policy, and not a new one. For two decades, it has guided capital across many sectors. Following the price signal, companies are spending tens of billions of euros to switch to low-carbon or even net-zero processes.

Where is new money going? Increasingly, into decarbonization.

In 2025, large European companies put €313 billion into Taxonomy-aligned activities, and those with credible transition plans added a further €182 billion, according to the latest Report on Monitoring Capital Flows to Sustainable Investments, published by the Platform on Sustainable Finance, an advisory body to the European Commission.

Clean power, green steel and net-zero cement: The future is already taking shaped.

Mixed signals

Despite the carbon market's positive economic and environmental impact, proposals now under negotiation threaten to derail the business models of companies that underpin Europe's long-term competitiveness and jobs.

The Commission has tried to navigate pressures from industries and countries still heavily reliant on expensive and polluting fossil fuels while maintaining momentum toward the green transition.

The aim is to avoid penalizing front-runners that have already invested in decarbonization.

Nonetheless, the proposal includes several technical but far-reaching changes. It lowers the linear reduction factor, the annual rate at which the emissions cap shrinks. It also adds free allowances and creates a role for unproven international credits and carbon removals.

On top of this, the European Parliament's draft report would weaken the market even further, potentially injecting more uncertainty into the outlook for the carbon price.

A €90 billion shortfall

According to a new study by Strategic Perspectives and Veyt, the Commission's proposal would blow a gigantic financial hole in Europe's climate plans.

Industries covered by the ETS would spend €90 billion less on decarbonization technologies by 2040 than under current law, a drop of more than a quarter.

In absolute terms, the Netherlands would be hit hardest, with its total halving to less than €20 billion. Germany would lose €15 billion and Italy €12.5 billion.

The further softening proposed in Parliament's draft report could widen the gap even more. Recent reports by businesses and investors identify predictable price signals and policy coherence as key factors in their decisions.

Europe will require hundreds of billions of euros a year, most of it from businesses and investors willing to commit capital at scale. In energy-intensive sectors such as steel, projects must be planned at least 10 to 15 years ahead.

The jury is in: Diluting the ETS rewards high-emitting competitors and in the end punishes front-runners. A stable and robust carbon price is non-negotiable for European industrial leadership.

Europe needs an agreement on an effective system that drives investment in industry.

title: Trump's DOE Request Cuts Weak Bets And Useful Research - CleanTechnica
description:

text:

There are Department of Energy programs in the Trump administration’s FY2027 budget request that I would cut too. Hydrogen for buses, trucks, building heat and routine electricity storage has consumed years of public funding and attention without overcoming the basic efficiency and cost advantages of using electricity directly. Ending more attempts to force those applications into existence would be progress. The problem is that the administration has wrapped those defensible cuts into a much broader retreat from batteries, electric vehicles, buildings, solar, wind and public energy research while treating several much weaker technological bets far more gently.

Across thirteen selected DOE technology program lines, FY2026 enacted funding totals about $4.288 billion. Trump’s FY2027 request reduces that to $2.618 billion, a decline of roughly 39%. The distribution matters much more than the aggregate. Solar, wind, vehicles and buildings together fall from $1.005 billion to only $40 million, about a 96% reduction. These are selected annual DOE programs, not the entire department or every federal dollar that supports the technologies, and the FY2027 figures are a presidential request rather than enacted appropriations. But budget requests tell Congress what an administration thinks deserves public support, and the pattern is difficult to mistake.

The useful way to judge these programs is not to divide technologies into politically favored and politically disfavored camps. Research, demonstrations and deployment support should face different tests. Early-stage research should answer a credible question that is worth answering. A demonstration should resolve specific technical, operating or commercial uncertainties. Deployment funding should accelerate something with a plausible path to delivering useful services competitively. A technology can justify a bounded experiment while being a terrible candidate for a billion-dollar rollout, and commercial success in a sector does not mean there are no remaining public-interest research questions.

Solar and wind illustrate the latter point. Their DOE program lines go from $220 million and $100 million respectively to zero in the FY2027 request. Neither technology requires the federal government to prove that it can generate electricity at commercial scale. That argument was settled years ago. The remaining public questions concern durability, manufacturing, recycling, materials, grid integration and operating electricity systems with very large shares of variable generation. Firms should fund ordinary product competition, but shared knowledge and system-level research often produce benefits that no single company can capture.

Vehicles fall from $397 million to $20 million, while buildings fall from $288 million to $20 million. That is especially difficult to square with the actual transition. Battery-electric vehicles have already won substantial passenger-vehicle markets and are spreading rapidly into commercial-duty niches where economics align. Heat pumps are a mature technology whose remaining problems increasingly concern installation quality, controls, building integration, flexible demand and how to electrify existing buildings without making unnecessary renovation a prerequisite. Those are exactly the kinds of practical problems that public research can help solve across an industry.

Hydrogen is a different case. The annual hydrogen and fuel-cell line falls from $160 million to zero, and much of its energy mission deserves to disappear. Producing hydrogen, conditioning it, moving it and converting it back into useful work generally adds energy losses, equipment and cost compared with direct electrification. Necessary industrial hydrogen is different because ammonia, methanol and other chemical processes require the molecule itself. A sensible federal portfolio would focus its hydrogen expertise on reducing emissions from hydrogen that industry actually needs while ending serial attempts to create a giant new hydrogen market for applications where electricity already has the advantage.

That does not mean the much larger regional hydrogen hubs have simply been cancelled. The hubs are multiyear awards funded separately from the annual technology-program comparison, and five remained nominally retained after the administration’s review. Retention, however, is not the same thing as a functioning project. Reporting from Pennsylvania continues to describe uncertainty, cautious partners and little evidence of meaningful momentum, while the FY2027 request proposes clawing back unobligated clean-hydrogen funding. The result is less a coherent technology decision than a prolonged “will they or won’t they?” process that makes planning harder for good projects and bad projects alike.

The mixed treatment of other technologies reinforces the point. Critical-minerals funding rises sharply, from $83 million to $364 million, and some of that can be useful if it builds processing, refining and qualified industrial output rather than merely subsidizing extraction. Geothermal remains at $150 million, including substantial support for enhanced-geothermal work whose eventual electricity economics remain uncertain. Civilian nuclear falls only about 9%, from $1.685 billion to $1.534 billion. Existing-fleet work and bounded research can have value without accepting the proposition that new nuclear or SMRs are likely to become the fast, inexpensive backbone of the transition.

The cement awards show why program management matters as much as headline appropriations. Brimstone’s large demonstration award was reinstated while Sublime’s remained unresolved in the October award snapshot. Neither administrative status tells us whether the underlying technology will succeed. Brimstone still has to prove the economics of a rock refinery whose business case depends on several saleable outputs, while Sublime has its own feedstock, energy, qualification and cost questions to answer. A demonstration should purchase evidence about those uncertainties. Reinstatement is not commercial validation, and cancellation is not scientific falsification.

ARPA-E makes the institutional problem clearest. Its total allocation falls from $350 million to $200.3 million, while project funding drops from $310 million to $160.3 million. The purpose of an organization like ARPA-E is not to select a portfolio in which every experiment becomes a company. Some experiments should fail. Some should reveal that an attractive concept does not scale. Some should create knowledge that private firms subsequently exploit. The public value comes from asking useful questions at stages where private capital cannot capture enough of the upside to justify carrying all of the uncertainty.

That requires competent people inside government who can distinguish research from demonstration, negotiate milestones, inspect projects, interpret evidence and stop work that is no longer justified. Hollowing out that capability while cancelling and reinstating awards through broad political sweeps weakens both sides of the process. It becomes harder to kill bad projects intelligently and harder to protect good experiments from indiscriminate cuts.

I would keep the cuts to weak hydrogen-for-energy applications, narrow several other portfolios whose commercial claims have outrun their evidence, and impose much harder tests on new nuclear and speculative geothermal electricity ambitions. I would restore serious capacity around electrification, buildings, industrial conversion, batteries, renewable generation and useful shared research, while supporting mineral processing where it removes real industrial bottlenecks. That is not a defense of every clean-energy grant. It is an argument for judging technologies by the useful work they can perform and judging public programs by the evidence they buy.

A stopped clock can cancel something that deserved to go. It still cannot decide what the United States should build next.

text:
The interest generated by Brazil’s 2026 presidential election extends far beyond its borders. As South America’s largest economy and a major actor in Latin America, the diplomatic and economic posture of Brazil’s next government will shape not only the country’s own trajectory but also define a crucial fulcrum of U.S.-China competition across the region.

For Brasília, the next government’s challenge is not to make a binary choice between Washington and Beijing, but toleverage its ties with both to strengthen Brazil’s bargaining power and preserve room for maneuver. The election is therefore about more than which major power Brazil will move closer to. It is also about how the country will manage its external economic ties with its domestic development objectives. Beneath the ideological differences between the two leading candidates, their platforms share a broad concern: how to strengthen Brazil’s economic sovereignty, expand domestic productive and technological capabilities, and reduce vulnerabilities arising from external dependence. The difference lies in how they believe Brazil should get there.

Based on the campaign platforms submitted by both candidates, Lula’s strategy can be characterized as one of “state-guided diversification.” On the diplomatic front, Lula leans into his traditional posture of reinforcing Mercosur, advancing South American integration, and expanding South-South cooperation. Beijing is firmly embedded in this broader BRICS and Global South framework, making China a key pillar of Brazil’s multi-vector foreign policy. Through BRICS mechanisms, Lula also seeks to promote local-currency settlement and diversify international financial channels, reducing Brazil’s structural dependence on any single currency, particularly the U.S. dollar, and broadening its options within the international financial system while giving the country greater resilience against external financial shocks and geopolitical pressures. Such diversification does not necessarily imply a desire to disengage from the U.S.-led financial system. Rather, it reflects an effort to expand Brazil’s policy options and preserve its ability to respond to external pressures.

On industry and investment, Lula’s primary lever is his flagship Nova Indústria Brasil (NIB) strategy, launched in 2024.[1] By deploying state-guided industrial planning, public capital, and targeted supply chain development, the NIB seeks to channel investment into infrastructure, green energy, digital infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing, aimed at elevating domestic value addition and boosting international competitiveness.[2] This policy direction aligns with Chinese corporate globalization strategies. Companies like BYD, State Grid, and Huawei have established significant commercial and technological presences in Brazil. Should Brazil's push to localize electric vehicles, infrastructure, and manufacturing continue, Chinese capital is well positioned to deepen that role, not simply by exporting into the market, but by building plants locally, expanding domestic production, and deepening supply-chain partnerships, thereby participating further in Brazil's industrial upgrading. But how far this partnership can go ultimately depends on whether foreign investment can genuinely meet Brasília's core demands around local content, technology transfer, job creation, and domestic value capture. In other words, under Lula, Brazil's openness to foreign capital is a "conditional welcome" policy. Investment that embeds itself into local supply chains and forms deep ties with domestic suppliers and labor markets is more likely to secure policy support and easier market access.

For Flávio Bolsonaro, the diplomatic emphasis is on deepening ties with the United States, Argentina, Israel, and other traditional partners. On the economic and industrial front, his platform favors a more market-driven approach: opening markets, attracting private capital and foreign technology, and expanding the role of private enterprise. Rather than relying on the state to direct investment toward strategic sectors, this model seeks to strengthen Brazil’s competitiveness by drawing more international capital.[3]

This combination of market orientation and strategic alignment is particularly visible in critical minerals policy. Flávio’s platform advocates expanding foreign investment and technical partnerships in the development of Brazil’s critical minerals and rare earth resources, while linking these assets to emerging industries such as clean energy, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, and artificial intelligence. The approach dovetails with Washington’s efforts to reduce dependence on China for critical minerals and build alternative supply chains. Flávio himself has publicly presented Brazil’s rare earths as a potential means of helping the United States reduce its reliance on Beijing.[4] Under a Flávio administration, critical minerals could therefore become a primary channel for deeper economic and strategic cooperation with Western partners. Closer cooperation with Washington, however, would not in itself ensure that Brazil captures greater economic value from its mineral resources. If investment focuses primarily on extraction and the export of unprocessed materials, Brazil could become more deeply integrated into Western-oriented supply chains without developing substantial domestic processing or technological capabilities. Brazil’s critical-minerals agenda also provides a concrete test of its ability to translate resource advantages into industrial development. In September 2026, Law No. 15,506 established the National Policy on Critical and Strategic Minerals and created the National Council for the Industrialization of Critical and Strategic Minerals (CIMCE). The framework signals a policy commitment to strengthening domestic processing and higher-value production. The question for the next government is how effectively these measures will be implemented, and whether foreign investment will help develop domestic capabilities rather than primarily expand extraction and exports.

Yet closer strategic alignment with Washington would not necessarily translate into economic disengagement from Beijing. Flávio’s platform explicitly calls for pragmatic engagement with all major economic partners, from China and the European Union to the United States and Asian markets. China is already deeply embedded in Brazil’s trade structure and remains its primary export destination, particularly for commodities such as soybeans, beef, and iron ore. This creates a structural constraint that any Brazilian government seeking to recalibrate relations with Beijing must navigate. Even if a Flávio administration leans further toward Washington politically and diplomatically, a comprehensive economic decoupling from China would be economically costly and difficult to implement. A far more likely scenario is a dual-track strategy: maintaining core agricultural and commodity trade with Beijing while tilting investment priorities and strategic partnerships toward Western allies. For Chinese investment, this could mean greater scrutiny in strategically sensitive sectors. In particular, in telecommunications, digital infrastructure, ports, and critical minerals, investment decisions would be judged not only on their economic value but increasingly through a geopolitical lens.

Whoever takes office in 2027, Brazil can neither afford to disregard China’s pivotal role as a trading partner and increasingly important global power, nor ignore its deep and structural ties with the United States, a geographically proximate power with a longstanding and often dominant role in the Western Hemisphere. The main challenge for Brazil’s next administration will be to expand its bargaining power and policy autonomy, preserving as much strategic room for maneuver as possible amid intensifying U.S.-China competition.

text:
Autoblog and Yahoo may earn commission from links in this article.

Volkswagen has expanded its affordable electric vehicle offering this year with two new models, the ID. Polo subcompact hatchback and the ID. Cross subcompact crossover.

These new models seem to be a big success so far as Volkswagen Group has received almost 150,000 orders for its Electric Urban Car Family, which also includes the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all of which are based on the MEB+ platform.

VW's $22,500 EV May Be Named ID. Up

But there's still room below these models—the ID. Polo starts at €25,000 ($28,000) and the ID. Cross starts at €28,000 ($31,400)—and Volkswagen knows it. That's why a more affordable model is in the works, and it's coming in a few months in Europe.

We're talking about the production version of the ID. Every1 concept city car, which is expected to have a base price of €20,000 (the equivalent of around $22,500 at the current exchange rate).

The new EV was initially expected to adopt the ID.1 badge, but it looks like Volkswagen has had a change of heart and will go for the ID.Up name instead. According to Electrifying, Volkswagen brand boss Thomas Schäfer has confirmed that the production version of the ID. Every1 concept "will not be called the VW ID.1 or VW ID. Every1."

While he stopped short of confirming the car's actual name, he would neither confirm nor deny when Electrifying suggested that it might be called the VW ID. Up. Naming the electric city car like this would be consistent with Volkswagen's recent electric models that received names derived from established ICE models, such as the ID. Polo and ID. Tiguan. The ID. Up name would also establish it as a successor to the e-Up! electric city car.

ID. Up to Bridge the Gap Between the Old e-Up! and New ID. Polo

Schäfer recently said the ID. Every1 coming next year is "the last piece of the puzzle" as the automaker will then offer broad model lineup in the volume segment.

The new ID. Up will help Volkswagen fend off fierce competition from Chinese automakers, which have taken the European market by storm, achieving almost 15% market share in September. It will also enable VW to compete with electric city cars like the Renault Twingo, the new Dacia Spring, and the new BYD Dolphin Surf.

At 153 inches (3,880 mm) long, the ID. Up will bridge the gap between the former e-Up! (142 in) and the new ID. Polo (160 in). Despite its tiny footprint, Volkswagen said the ID. Up would offer space for four passengers and 10.8 cubic feet (305 liters) of cargo space.

A 37-kWh LFP Battery and Rivian Infotainment Software

While the automaker has not revealed any battery details yet, the ID. Up is expected to use the same 37-kilowatt-hour LFP pack as the base ID. Polo and ID. Cross. In the ID. Polo, this battery enables a driving range of up to 207 miles (334 km). For the ID. Up, VW has promised at least 155 miles (250 km) of range and a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor expected to enable a top speed of 80 mph (130 km/h).

The new ID. Up will also be the first Volkswagen to feature Rivian software. Schäfer told Electrifying that the infotainment system's functionality "has been developed with the consumer, to find out what they like, what they need in life, and from that it's translated into functions. It starts with the customer, and so it makes the whole system easier to use."

The system is said to have a simplified setup that uses fewer ECUs and less wiring to achieve the same job, saving money and weight while also allowing for better over-the-air software updates.

The new ID. Up will be built in Portugal, at the Palmela plant near Setubal. The site, which is also known as Autoeuropa, currently builds the T-Roc crossover. As with the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, the ID. Up won't make it to the United States either.

title: TechCrunch Mobility: Blue-green is the color of autonomy
description:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed new lighting requirements for autonomous vehicles that include an option (dare I say a strong suggestion?)
Still, federal regulators are clearly seeking some uniform way of identifying autonomous vehicles.
The proposal establishes equipment specifications, including where the lights are mounted, the color they emit, and how they’re activated.

text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

U.S. federal safety regulators continue to tackle the sticky problem of autonomous vehicles, this time with a proposal that could signal to the public, quite literally, when a vehicle is operating autonomously.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed new lighting requirements for autonomous vehicles that include an option (dare I say a strong suggestion?) to use cyan-colored lights to signal when a vehicle is operating autonomously without a human occupant monitoring the road.

The agency is not proposing a mandate for blue-green lights. Importantly, under the proposal, the lights would be used when an AV is operating in autonomous mode.

Still, federal regulators are clearly seeking some uniform way of identifying autonomous vehicles.

The proposal establishes equipment specifications, including where the lights are mounted, the color they emit, and how they’re activated. It would also remove requirements for manually operated controls for turn signals, high beams, and hazard lights.

Under the proposal, the NHTSA suggests the lights be cyan (blue-green), remain steadily illuminated rather than flash, and be visible from the front, rear, and both sides.

This latest proposal is one piece of a bigger effort to update regulations that help speed up the adoption of AVs while maintaining safety, according to NHTSA administrator Jonathan Morrison.

The agency is already working on a federal automated vehicle framework and is trying to update federal motor vehicle safety standards, which already govern automakers today. For instance, FMVSS rules were not designed for vehicles like the Tesla Cybercab and Zoox robotaxi, which lack traditional, federally required equipment like pedals, steering wheels, and design features like side mirrors and rearview mirrors.

While the feds wrestle over regulating the future of transportation, GM laid out how it plans to be part of it. The automaker held its annual GM Forward event, and a lot of what was announced builds on last year’s push into AI. But now we have more details and dates.

The U.S. automaker is overhauling the electrical and computational guts of its future vehicles in a bid to deliver faster software, more capable automated driving features, and a custom, conversational AI assistant that will change its 30-year-old OnStar service.

This technological overhaul is set to debut in 2028 with the Cadillac Escalade IQ. The company will also roll out an autonomous highway driving feature in 2028 that will allow drivers to have their hands and eyes off the road and without the need to be ready to take over.

GM has also adopted enterprise AI across the company to slash its traditional four- to five-year development timeline in half.

I have been around long enough to remember previous efforts at GM and other legacy automakers, all of which were interpreted as a bid to compete with Tesla. This time, GM seems to be preparing for a bigger fight.

Deals!

AI startups are getting snapped up across industries, including transportation. The latest example is Rivian’s acquisition of Third Dimension, a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds.

This is all about simulation, and specifically the idea of taking driving data and bringing it into a virtual world that matches the physical world. Rivian’s head of autonomy, James Philbin, told me the company knew it needed a technology that could close the “sim-to-real gap,” meaning the data gap between real and simulated environments.

Students of the AV industry will likely shout “Simulation is so 2017!” And yes, that’s true, simulation is a tool AV developers have relied on and continue to do so. The technology behind simulation continues to evolve, and startups like Third Dimension are ripe for the picking.

The terms of the deal weren’t released. There are a few clues for what size of deal this may have been. Third Dimension previously raised a $7 million seed round, and it has about 15 engineers, and Rivian didn’t disclose this in an SEC filing (meaning it didn’t hit the bar for material information).

Other deals that got my attention …

Ride-hailing company inDrive, known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027. The companies have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing robotaxis to inDrive’s platform.

Reliable Robotics, a startup trying to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft, raised $115 million. The Series D extension round included $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round now totals $275 million and has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark.

Notable reads and other tidbits

A group fighting robotaxis has some mysterious origins, the Washington Post reported. This reminds me of another anti-robotaxi group that I dug into earlier this summer called Coalition for Accountability and Road Safety, which was canvassing voters and posting on social media. My reporting discovered that the organization was registered to an employee of a New York lobbying firm that has previously been retained by several labor unions and the New York Black Car Operators’ Injury Compensation Fund.

GM is closing a plant south of Detroit that assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units and battery packs for the plug-in hybrid Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray. The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy but because the lease on the site was nearing its end, according to a GM spokesperson.

Google is upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe shared his vision for how autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the R1S electric pickup truck and R1S and R2 SUVs it makes today. All eyes are on R4.

Tesla and SpaceX reported third-quarter earnings this week, and comments by Elon Musk, who is CEO of both companies, has kicked merger talk into fifth gear. Musk said the boards of each company have formed special committees to review a merger.

Meanwhile, SpaceX’s AI business is booming, generating $7.5 billion in revenue, and now makes up 52% of the company’s income. And Tesla’s revenue, across its segments, was flat, while the company’s expenses grew. The upshot: Profits fell 43% year-over-year. Musk is very much focused on the company’s AI and robotics future, though. Tesla started production of its Optimus humanoid robot, reported rosy FSD subscription growth even as the “unsupervised version” was delayed to Q2 next year, and said it plans to start selling its Cybercab to customers by the end of the year. As senior reporter Sean O’Kane wrote: Tesla is prepping for a Cybercab onslaught.

Waymo keeps expanding within cities it already operates and into new ones. The company said it plans to launch a robotaxi service in Spain, starting with Madrid. It expects to open it up to riders in 2027. Closer to home, Waymo is now shuttling customers to and from the Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas.

One more thing …

TechCrunch Disrupt just wrapped and I am already preparing for another event. This time, it is the Founder Summit — a one-day event in Boston focused on, you guessed it, founders. This event, taking place November 4, is valuable for startup founders, aspiring founders, and investors. Attendees can expect advice-driven talks from VCs and serial founders, plus lots of chances to network.

text:
Gas price spikes helped push one SUV owner to finally swap into an EV — and they estimated the move had drastically cut fuel spending in just two weeks.

Here's what to know

The driver said the decision came after years of discussion at home over when to go electric. In Reddit's r/electricvehicles forum, they described the Kia EV9 as a "basic 1-to-1 replacement" for an aging six-cylinder SUV. They noted "gas price spikes sealed it," and estimated that they had already saved over $200 on fuel.

Local gas prices were around $3.85 a gallon, below the $4.31 national figure. Even with that advantage, their routine still made fuel costs pile up.

Several times a week, the poster said, they drove 40 miles from a smaller city to a larger one. In an SUV that averaged roughly 20 miles per gallon and had an 18-gallon tank, that commute meant filling up twice weekly and spending over $500 a month on gas.

After factoring in fuel, oil changes, belt and brake jobs, and other upkeep, the poster said they expected the EV9 to save them $7,000 annually, even after accounting for a slightly higher monthly vehicle cost and a $2,000 home charger installation.

Commenters added that the experience of driving an electric vehicle is another major strength. "The real long-term benefit for EVs is just how nice they are to drive," one wrote. "They are smooth and powerful and convenient and clean."

More background

Other users echoed that. One said they noticed "a significant difference" after drives of over two hours because "the decibel reduction makes a nice difference," citing a quieter cabin as a quality-of-life improvement that does not always show up in monthly cost comparisons.

Someone else described making a similar switch after gas hit $6 a gallon, saying their household traded a 2011 MDX for a new EV9. They called it "such a better all-around driving experience" and added that "it feels like I'm part of the solution now (getting off fossil fuels)."

That same commenter said the change also connected to home energy resilience. After adding solar and a Level 2 charger, they found it "liberating not being held hostage by PG&E outages and forever wars."

What can be done?

EV savings depend heavily on an individual driver's circumstances. In this case, the original poster's savings came from replacing an SUV that needed frequent fill-ups.

One commenter said they planned to switch for reasons other than money because the numbers did not work in their case. They described having an old gas sedan that got about 25 mpg, apartment charging for $0.25 per kilowatt-hour, and high state property taxes on a new vehicle.

The OP agreed that there is no universal formula, replying, "The economics don't work all the time for everyone, but for me it was definitely worth the investment."

Users focused on comparing gas spending with charging costs, reviewing maintenance history, pricing out home charging, and considering how much driving consists of repetitive commuting.

The OP said their charger setup should pay for itself within four months, while another EV9 owner said pairing the vehicle with solar added another layer of savings and independence.

"The thing drives like a dream. It is quiet and comfortable and solid all-around. This was the right choice," the OP concluded.

Where can I learn more?

For drivers weighing a similar switch, the articles below explore EV savings.

• In the Bay Area, one driver found their EV cost almost eight times less per mile even without home charging.

• Across the U.S., motorists can save nearly $8,000 on average by switching to an EV.

• For many buyers, the long-term math favors electric ownership over gas models.

• Across Reddit, EV owners said "it's so cheap it's stupid" once commuting moved off gas.

text:
The Aurora Pacific Economic Zone and Freeport Authority (APECO) is taking its investment campaign to the United States and Canada, targeting companies in defense, clean energy, digital infrastructure and other strategic industries for projects in Casiguran, Aurora.

APECO President and CEO Usec. Gil G. Taway IV is leading the investment mission to the United States from October 24 to 30, followed by Canada from November 2 to 6. The delegation is scheduled to hold investment briefings, site visits and government-to-business meetings in Texas, Maryland and Washington, D.C., as well as Montreal, Ottawa and Calgary.

The campaign comes as APECO seeks to convert investor interest into actual projects at its 12,923-hectare Pacific-facing economic zone, which the agency is positioning as a potential gateway for businesses seeking access to the Philippines and the broader Indo-Pacific market.

APECO is highlighting the fiscal and non-fiscal incentives available under the CREATE MORE Act, along with the zone’s location, maritime access and potential for large-scale industrial and infrastructure projects.

“As a Pacific-facing ecozone, we can be a reliable investment location for investors looking to establish presence in the Philippines, access the broader region, and take advantage of the two major economies’ multimillion-dollar Indo-Pacific strategies,” Taway said.

“This mission will allow us to meet prospective American and Canadian investors and develop future projects that benefit the strategic but still untapped Aurora,” he added.

In the United States, APECO will follow up on discussions with US companies, including defense supply-chain firm Anglicotech LLC and consulting firm Valent. About 100 business executives and representatives from infrastructure, energy, mining, critical minerals, defense, aerospace, advanced manufacturing, agriculture and logistics are expected to participate in the two Canadian events.

APECO is located on Luzon’s eastern seaboard, facing the Pacific Ocean and providing potential maritime access to markets across the Indo-Pacific, including Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China, Australia and New Zealand.

The market for lithium 4,5-dicyano-2-trifluoromethylimidazole is expected to expand steadily through 2035 as battery makers place greater emphasis on electrolyte performance, purity and long-term cell stability. IndexBox said the compound is gaining relevance in advanced lithium-ion battery formulations, where small additive choices can influence charging efficiency, safety and lifecycle economics.

That shift matters because the battery materials supply chain is becoming more specialised. As electric vehicles, stationary storage systems and consumer electronics continue to push manufacturers towards higher energy density and better thermal control, demand is rising for additives that can improve electrochemical behaviour without compromising consistency. The latest market outlook suggests that this niche chemical could benefit from that broader industry transition.

Why the additive is drawing attentionLithium 4,5-dicyano-2-trifluoromethylimidazole sits in a category of high-value electrolyte ingredients used in battery cells that require tight performance tolerances. According to IndexBox, the market’s growth outlook is tied to adoption of advanced electrolyte systems, where formulators are looking for compounds that support stable operation under demanding conditions.

In practical terms, the appeal of such materials lies in their ability to help batteries perform more reliably across charge-discharge cycles. As battery manufacturers aim to extend product life and improve safety margins, even relatively small-volume additives can become strategically important. That makes the segment attractive not only to chemical producers but also to battery developers seeking differentiated performance.

Advanced batteries are reshaping the chemicals mix The report points to a broader change in the battery industry: the chemistry inside cells is becoming more sophisticated, and suppliers of speciality inputs are being pulled into that transition. Traditional commodity chemicals are no longer enough for many next-generation applications. Instead, manufacturers are increasingly selecting materials that can support faster charging, better durability and more stable operation over time.

This creates an opening for suppliers of niche compounds such as lithium 4,5-dicyano-2-trifluoromethylimidazole. The market’s trajectory will likely depend on how quickly battery producers scale advanced formulations and how successfully additive makers can maintain the purity levels and production consistency required by the sector. In a market shaped by quality thresholds, supply reliability can matter as much as raw demand.

What could shape the forecast to 2035 While the report does not frame the segment as a mass-market chemical, it indicates that growth will be linked to the gradual expansion of advanced battery manufacturing. That means the strongest demand could come from applications where performance matters more than cost alone, including premium electric vehicles, grid storage and other high-specification energy systems. Another factor is the continuing push for battery innovation. As research teams work on improving energy density and reducing degradation, electrolyte additives are likely to remain part of the discussion around cell design. For suppliers, that could translate into a market that is smaller than mainstream battery materials but more resilient than many commodity niches because of its technical barriers and performance-led demand.

Implications for chemical suppliers For speciality chemical companies, the opportunity lies in positioning early for a segment that sits at the intersection of battery innovation and materials engineering. Products used in electrolyte formulations often face stringent qualification processes, which can create stickier customer relationships once a compound is approved. That dynamic can favour producers with deep process control and the ability to meet exacting specifications. At the same time, the market is likely to remain sensitive to shifts in battery chemistry. If alternative additive systems gain traction, or if cell architectures change materially, demand patterns could move quickly. Suppliers therefore need to track not just current battery production volumes but also the direction of future chemistries, especially those linked to safety and performance improvements.

A niche market with strategic importance IndexBox’s outlook suggests that lithium 4,5-dicyano-2-trifluoromethylimidazole will remain a specialised but increasingly relevant material in the battery value chain through 2035. The compound may not be widely known outside the industry, yet its role reflects a larger truth about the energy transition: progress in batteries often depends on a long tail of high-performance chemicals that never make headlines but are essential to the final product. As electrification deepens and battery expectations rise, the market for such additives is likely to benefit from the same forces reshaping the broader energy storage ecosystem. For chemical makers, that could mean a long but selective growth path, built on technical credibility rather than volume alone.

text:
By Joey Harris | Indianapolis Business Journal

A new report out of Indiana’s Office of Energy Development says projects that boost power generation in the state need to be built quicker.

Indiana’s Strategic Energy Growth Task Force wrapped up deliberations about the report and its 10 recommendations in July and the document was posted on the Office of Energy Development’s website earlier this month. The task force was founded by an executive order from Gov. Mike Braun.

Recommendations include making the state a hub for energy-hungry industries willing to pay for new infrastructure, bringing communities on board with energy projects early and changing certain regulatory processes to let some projects move ahead quicker.

Some of the recommendations could become legislation that the administration pushes and others include potential actions for state agencies, said Secretary of Energy and Natural Resources Suzanne Jaworowski. Other action items include directions that the administration would like to see industry take on its own, she said.

“Sometimes it’s just casting a vision and doing education and outreach of where we want to go and we see the private sector come in and deploy those solutions,” she said.

Almost all of the recommendations are aimed at speed.

“Frankly for industry right now, it’s speed to electrons, it used to be a company would look for a place to find a site to locate whatever it is they were doing, right now, people are looking for where can I get electricity?” Jaworowski said.

The task force was comprised primarily of Braun’s administration or regulatory appointees but also included representatives from various parts of the energy industry and large industrial power users.

Almost every member of the task force voted in favor of the recommendations, except two — representatives of the Mid-continent Independent System Operator, the group that manages the power grid for most of the Midwest, and the Indiana Energy Association, which represents utilities in the state.

MISO told IBJ that it abstained because it remains agnostic to state policy.

The abstention of the Indiana Energy Association could be more notable.

At the time of the vote, Indiana Energy Association President Danielle McGrath said that the group did not oppose the report but expressed concerns about some potential regulatory changes discussed in it.

Indiana utilities have been outspoken in favor of maintaining the state’s vertically integrated regulatory compact, in which the companies have a monopoly over what projects serve customers in their territories. The report, however, said the state’s existing structure can slow down investment from major industry.

In a statement to IBJ McGrath said the group supports many of the recommendations.

“We believe Indiana’s current regulatory structure has enabled us to successfully meet the needs of both existing customers and the growing demands of large-load economic development,” she said.

Jaworowski said, “nobody wants to deregulate the state for electricity.” But she said the Braun administration sees an increased role for non-utility energy producers — frequently referred to as independent power producers — to bring more power on the grid quicker to meet demands while shielding customers from financial risks.

She said that the administration does not want to create competition for the utilities, but she said there is more room for collaboration on top of what already exists.

“We’re seeing independent power producers building natural gas plants and then Indiana Michigan Power Co. has already purchased one,” she said. “It’s more about how do we make that independent power producer’s opportunity to work with a utility, to quickly build what we need to build here, but keep the utilities involved in that process. Eventually [the] utility can have a power purchase agreement, they can maybe purchase the asset, but we get that energy generation deployed quickly.”

Other pathways the reported cited for bringing more energy to the grid include having counties establish specific zones for energy development, providing extra payments to counties from wind and solar projects if they have renewable-friendly zoning, publicly financing energy projects and boosting efforts to expand the deployment of grid-balancing battery storage systems.

The report also envisions ways for the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to move more quickly. That could include certain changes to the way critical infrastructure projects and rate cases move through the process.

Jaworowski pointed to a recent Indiana Michigan Power request to reduce rates as an example.

“Even in a case where they’re saying, ‘we want to lower our rates,’ the case takes nine months,” she said.

Jaworowski said the end goal is creating an environment in which high-demand customers like data centers can easily come to Indiana while paying all of their costs, which she said is happening despite no state law mandating it.

One law does offer an expedited pathway for data center service agreements if a utility proves that 80% of the costs will be borne by the data center developer.

“I don’t see the need right now to put that into policy,” Jaworowski said, adding, “having a large-load user — even if that large-load user isn’t paying for new generation, they’re just paying the cost of the energy they’re using — that lowers the cost for everybody around.”

Critic responds

That’s a claim disputed by Ben Inskeep, program director for the consumer and environmental group Citizens Action Coalition.

“Our problem is we have too much load growth, too fast right now. It’s completely out of control, and it’s completely infeasible that we can meet it,” he said. “Even if we eliminated every regulation in the book, just based on the timelines of these projects and the fact that there are backlogs to get labor, to get equipment. … Supply can’t respond to demand.”

Inskeep was also critical of many of the report’s recommendations and argued they were unclear or didn’t mesh with the body of the challenges that the report laid out. He pointed to a recommendation to allow quicker regulatory reviews for certain “critical infrastructure” projects.

“What actually needs an accelerated timeline? We have hyper-accelerated timelines in Indiana where things can be built very quickly without regulatory review,” he said. “I’m just completely flummoxed what this is getting at and the purpose of this. … They’re using these very nebulous and vague terms to propose some sort of legislation with an unknown endpoint.”

Some suggestions, such as payments to communities with zoning rules favorable to renewable energy could be helpful, he said, though the specific recommendation from the report may be insufficient to bring more renewable energy to the grid. Public financing of energy projects could also be a useful avenue to improve affordability, Inskeep said.

Still, the push to move fast to incentivize the buildout of data centers would have negative consequences if seen through, he argued.

He was also critical about the lack of inclusion of environmental groups on the task force.

“Not really any critical perspectives or alternative perspectives it seems like,” Inskeep said.

Synopsis

US President Donald Trump is campaigning in Michigan, which is crucial for the upcoming midterm elections. Former President Barack Obama previously rallied for Democrats, emphasizing the importance of this Senate race. The competition is between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator if elected. Rogers has made claims about El-Sayed's connections to terrorist groups, which El-Sayed denies.

Detroit: US President Donald Trump will rally Republicans in eastern Michigan on Sunday, a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's midterm elections.

Michigan has one of the nation's most competitive US Senate contests, an open-seat race between former Republican Representative Mike Rogers and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that will help decide control of the chamber.

Also Read: US Midterm Elections 2026: Where could Indian-American voters make a difference?

Despite repeatedly attacking El-Sayed from the Oval Office and at rallies across the country, the Republican president had not yet campaigned in Michigan this year.

If he wins, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint El-Sayed as a Muslim extremist and repeatedly mocked his middle name, Mohamed, a common Muslim name.

Live Events

El-Sayed has dismissed the accusation and, in a recent advertisement, defended his religion, saying, "Faith is a thing there's just too little of in Washington."

Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

"If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers said at a debate last week.

El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the group and says it is "shameful" for Rogers to question his allegiance to the United States.

At Saturday's rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks on El-Sayed as an attempt by opponents to make him look "less patriotic and less American than they are."

The former president compared it to his experience as the target of false claims that he was born in Kenya.

"We have seen this movie before," Obama said. "I starred in it ... This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul."

Trump's rally in Port Huron, part of an area of Michigan that he won in the 2024 presidential election with more than 66% of the vote, will also highlight the US-Canada tariff standoff.

The trade fight has affected the Detroit-based US auto industry, prompting Rogers to distance himself from the president's policy.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US Senate and US House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

Key Points

Interested in Aclara Resources Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

Aclara Resources is pursuing an integrated rare-earth supply chain spanning ionic-clay deposits in Chile and Brazil, a planned separation facility in Louisiana, and a metals-and-alloys operation focused on heavy rare earths such as dysprosium, terbium and yttrium.

The company targets mine production at Penco in late 2028 and Carina in mid-2029, with Louisiana separation expected to begin in late 2028 and metals production in early 2029, subject to financing and execution.

The integrated plan is estimated to require about $1.7 billion in construction capital. Aclara is seeking customer offtake agreements and potential U.S. government-backed financing, including an Export-Import Bank letter of interest for up to $750 million.

Aclara Resources (TSE:ARA) outlined plans to build an integrated rare-earth supply chain spanning two ionic-clay deposits in South America, a separation facility in Louisiana and a metals-and-alloys operation, with management emphasizing its focus on heavy rare earth elements including dysprosium, terbium and yttrium.

At the company's investor day in New York, Chief Executive Officer Ramón Barúa said Aclara's strategy is centered on producing materials that are scarce outside China and are needed for permanent magnets, power-generation equipment, aerospace applications and other technologies. He said the company intends to become a long-term supplier rather than develop assets for sale.

→ Lam Research's Earnings Beat Wasn't the Real Story—Its 2027 Outlook Was

Barúa said Aclara has invested more than $300 million over roughly eight years to advance its assets and technology. The company's principal mining projects are the Penco deposit in Chile and the Carina deposit in Brazil, both ionic-clay deposits that management said contain relatively high concentrations of heavy rare earths.

Project timelines and processing plans

Chief Operating Officer Hugh Broadhurst said the company's mines are designed to produce a high-purity mixed rare-earth carbonate product known as SPREC. The material would be shipped to a planned 82-acre site in Port of Vinton, Louisiana, where Aclara intends to separate it into individual rare-earth oxides and subsequently produce metals and alloys.

→ Tesla's Flying-Car Hype Hits an Earnings Reality Check

Aclara said it has completed basic engineering and obtained a key air permit for the Louisiana site. The company is targeting the start of separation operations in late 2028 and metals production in early 2029, subject to financing and project execution.

Penco: Aclara recently released an updated preliminary economic assessment for the Chile project, which is expected to have a 17-year mine life. The company has received an environmental license and expects to complete a feasibility study in the first quarter. It is targeting mine production in late 2028.

Carina: The Brazilian project is expected to have an 18-year mine life, according to management. Aclara completed a feasibility study in April and is pursuing environmental licenses. Management said it expects first production in mid-2029.

Louisiana: The planned downstream operation, called Project Dynamo, would use solvent extraction and mixer-settler equipment to produce oxides including neodymium-praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium.

Broadhurst said the company selected conventional solvent extraction because it is commercially proven, though applying it to heavy rare earths remains complex. Aclara is operating a pilot-scale separation circuit at Virginia Tech's Corporate Research Center and said it has produced market-grade neodymium-praseodymium oxide. The company expects samples of dysprosium and terbium at target specification in the fourth quarter.

→ Is Texas Instruments Setting Up for Its Next Big Breakout?

The company also said it has operated a metallization demonstration plant at CAP's Huachipato site in Chile. Broadhurst said the facility has produced about 500 kilograms of neodymium-praseodymium metal and reached a targeted production capacity of 175 kilograms per day.

Funding, offtake and economics

Chief Financial Officer Francois Motte said Aclara estimates the integrated supply chain would require approximately $1.7 billion of construction capital. The Carina project represents the largest component, with estimated investment of $780 million, while the expanded Louisiana separation facility is estimated at $494 million.

The company said the U.S. Export-Import Bank has issued a non-binding letter of interest for up to $750 million in potential debt financing for the Louisiana industrial facilities. The U.S. International Development Finance Corp. has invested $5 million in Carina and holds an option to provide additional financing, according to management.

Aclara has also signed three non-binding memorandums of understanding with end customers, Motte said, and is pursuing additional agreements. Management said future offtake contracts would likely include minimum-price floors during the initial project payback period, while potentially retaining exposure to higher market prices after capital costs are repaid.

Motte said the company's integrated model implies approximately $3 billion in value and cited unlevered project internal rates of return of roughly 26% to 27%. He said that, once financing is incorporated, leveraged returns could rise to 40% to 45%, though these outcomes depend on commodity prices, financing and project execution.

Technology and ESG focus

Aclara said its circular mineral harvesting process uses dilute ammonium sulfate, a common fertilizer, to release rare earths from near-surface clays. Management said the process avoids blasting, crushing and milling, recycles 99% of its main reagent and recycles 97% of water used in the plant. The company also said the process does not require a conventional tailings dam.

Head of Technology and AI Projects Mauricio Carrasco said Aclara is working with Argonne National Laboratory to develop digital-twin models of its separation process. The models are intended to help optimize operating conditions and shorten plant ramp-up periods. The company is also using satellite imagery and artificial intelligence through a Stanford University Mineral-X collaboration to identify prospective exploration areas.

Executive Vice President José Augusto Palma said Aclara is pursuing environmental and social standards aligned with International Finance Corp. requirements and the Equator Principles. In Brazil, he said the company is working toward a preliminary license for Carina and expects a decision by the end of the first quarter, followed by further installation approvals before construction.

Aclara Resources Inc (TSX: ARA), a Toronto Stock Exchange listed company, is focused on building a vertically integrated supply chain for rare earths alloys used in permanent magnets. This strategy is supported by Aclara's development of rare earth mineral resources hosted in ionic clay deposits, which contain high concentrations of the scarce heavy rare earths, providing the Company with a long-term, reliable source of these critical materials. The Company's rare earth mineral resource development projects include the Carina Project in the State of Goiás, Brazil as its flagship project and the Penco Module in the Biobío Region of Chile.

text:
Programme aims to ease energy costs, increase private investment and expand support for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises and job creation

The Board of Directors of the African Development Bank Group (AfDB) has approved a US$503.75 million (6.62 billion Botswana pula) loan to enable Botswana to cushion the impact of the global energy shock and support structural reforms for private sector-led economic growth and job creation, particularly for women and youth. One of the Bank’s largest operations in the country, the financing is designed to deliver tangible benefits to households.

Through the Economic Competitiveness and Transformation Support Program (ECTSP), the loan will fund fiscal and private sector reforms, aiming to lift non-mining tax value to 11.8 per cent of GDP for 2027/28, raise private investment to 30 per cent by 2028, and expand support for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) and job creation.

Precision work in Botswana on a wire harness, a component exported to South Africa’s automotive assembly plants

The approval supports the government’s ongoing efforts to mitigate the impact of the Middle East conflict on the cost of living across Botswana. A prolonged downturn in the natural diamond market—which accounts for about 30 per cent of GDP and nearly 80 per cent of exports—contributed to economic contractions of 2.8 per cent in 2024 and 0.7 per cent in 2025. The Middle East crisis has increased the energy bill and contributed to economic contraction.

“Botswana has clearly defined its priorities in National Development Plan 12 and Botswana’s Transformation Programme. Our role is to help finance the adjustment, while protecting those least able to bear its costs,” said Moono Mupotola, the AfDB’s Deputy Director General for Southern Africa and Country Manager.

In August 2025, payment arrears to suppliers of medicines and medical equipment contributed to a public health emergency. Unemployment stands at 21 per cent overall and 28.9 per cent among young people, 37 per cent of whom are not in education, employment or training.

“These are time-bound, measurable reforms, each supported by technical assistance to ensure delivery. Adoption alone is not our goal; implementation is,” said Abdoulaye Coulibaly, the AfDB’s Director for Governance and Economic Reforms.

What the operation will change and who will benefit

The programme supports a directive the President of Botswana issued on 6 April 2026, suspending fuel, road, and security-of-supply levies for six months. This measure limits the increase for motorists to about P0.58 per litre and is expected to reduce inflation by 1.6 percentage points, easing pressure on transport fares and household food costs nationwide.

In parallel, supplementary monthly payments are being provided for three months to old-age pensioners, disability grant recipients, destitute cash beneficiaries, and home-based care patients. The support will reach an estimated 279,000 older and other vulnerable people, including households least able to absorb a sudden rise in prices.

Over the medium term, the reforms aim to expand access to energy, assets, and economic opportunities. A fully costed National Electrification Action Plan will advance implementation of Mission 300’s National Energy Compact for Botswana, which seeks to lift household electricity access from 79.5 per cent in 2025/26 to universal access by 2030. Connecting more homes requires additional power supply. The country will therefore hold at least one competitive renewable energy auction, inviting private developers to build new solar and wind capacity.

Separately, expanding the Francistown fuel depot from 38 million to 98 million litres will strengthen the security of fuel supply.

Land administration reform is expected to give 4,300 more families secure titles within a year, raising the national total from 19,682 to about 24,000 and allowing land to be used as collateral. The programme targets 3,292 active MSMEs and 3,935 direct jobs by 2027/28, with women-owned firms accounting for 93 per cent of supported enterprises and the youth share of jobs created rising from 15 to 20 per cent.

Full implementation of e-procurement is expected to cut procurement costs by 5 to 15 per cent, freeing resources for frontline services. Together, these measures contribute to broader efforts to unlock the Botswana Economic Transformation Programme’s pipeline of 186 projects valued at Botswana pula 514 billion, with a long-term goal of creating 512,000 jobs by 2036.

The operation is the first phase of a two-year programmatic series for 2026/27 and 2027/28. Co-financed by the OPEC Fund with US$170 million, it builds on earlier Bank support to Botswana in 2025, under which VAT collections rose by 15.5 per cent to 14.397 billion pula, and the country’s business regulatory environment score reached 4.8 out of 6, above the 4.7 target.
